<meta>This is the title page for the 1605 printed edition of Rabanus Maurus’s "De laudibus sanctae crucis" (In Praise of the Holy Cross). The work was originally composed in the 9th century and is famous for its "carmina figurata" (patterned poems) where text and image intertwine.</meta>

# MAGNENTIUS RABANUS
# MAURUS
## **A WORK ON THE PRAISES**
# **OF THE HOLY CROSS,**
## MARVELLOUS IN ITS LEARNING,
->in both verse and prose.<- <note>This refers to the "prosimetric" style, where the author provides a poem in a grid and then a prose explanation of its complex symbolism.</note>

# **NOTABLE FOR THE ANTIQUITY**
## OF THE AUTHOR [WHO LIVED NEARLY
->eight hundred years ago, first as Abbot of Fulda, and later<-
->as Archbishop of Mainz] as well as for the novelty of its writing style.<-

# **IN WHICH, THROUGH TWENTY-EIGHT FIGURES OR IMAGES,**
->*many mysteries of the Christian faith and many mystical numbers are subtly and*<-
->*ingeniously explained: of the Angels, of the virtues, of the 7 gifts of the Holy Spirit,*<-
->*of the 8 beatitudes, of the 4 Elements, of the 4 seasons of the year, of the 4 Evangelists*<-
->*and the Lamb, of the months, of the winds, of the 5 Books of Moses, of the name of*<-
->*Adam, of the Alleluia and the Amen, and the power and dignity of other things*<-
->***ARRANGED INTO THE FORM OF A CROSS.***<-
## SUBTLY AND INGENIOUSLY EXPLAINED.

<meta>This page continues from the title page of Rabanus Maurus’s "In Praise of the Holy Cross." It features a prefatory letter by the influential German humanist Jacob Wimpfeling, who was instrumental in the 1501 printing of this medieval manuscript.</meta>

JOHN <note>This "IOANNIS" likely refers to the signature mark or the printer Johann Pforzheim's workshop, used for organizing the printed sheets.</note>

# JACOB WIMPFELING
## OF SÉLESTAT TO ALL
### lovers of good literature.

->Heartiest Greetings.<- <note>original: "S. P." for *Salutem Plurimam*</note>

Rabanus the German <note>Rabanus Maurus (c. 780–856 AD), the author of the work.</note> composed a marvelous and most artistic work in praise of the Holy Cross, woven together in a most painstaking poem. Within it, he demonstrates how many mysteries of the Christian faith—many mystical numbers, the Angels, the virtues, the gifts of the Spirit, the beatitudes, the Elements, the seasons, the regions of the world, the months, the winds, the books of Moses, the name of Adam, and the power and dignity of other noble things—can be harmonized and adapted to the Holy Cross. He weaves verse into verse so that the figures themselves contain their own small verses, through which diverse images are represented. Yet, the legitimate order of the main poem is never broken or interrupted in its flow or meaning. Thus, the letters themselves usually fit into a double order <note>This refers to the "grid" style of the poems, where letters form words both horizontally as part of a poem and within a shape (the figure) to form a second set of words.</note>. After each poem, a prose discourse follows, which clearly explains the wonderful depth of the verses. O, what a distinguished work, worthy of all veneration, by which Germany (which gave birth to such a man) is deservedly rendered illustrious and glorious! 

Therefore, I beseech you, honest reader—whoever you are who is truly Christian—make this special book your own. Do so that you may see its novelty, praise the author’s genius, wonder at his excellent talent, and be kindled to a love of the Cross and the Crucified. Begin to be devoted to Him who suffered for you, and delight yourself in this sweet tree on which the salvation of the world hung—in which is all our hope, our refuge, and our medicine. Through it we are saved and set free; by it, you shall undoubtedly obtain the immortal fruit of your soul from the gift of God. Farewell, dearest reader in Christ. From the hermitage of Saint William, in the suburbs of Strasbourg <note>original: *Argentinensi*</note>, on the ninth of August <note>original: *quinto idus sextilis*</note>, in the year of our salvation 1501.

<meta>This page continues from the prefatory matter of the 1501 edition of "In Praise of the Holy Cross." While the previous page featured a prose address by Jacob Wimpfeling, this page presents a laudatory poem by the famous humanist Johannes Reuchlin, addressed to the printer Thomas Anshelm.</meta>

# JOHANNES REUCHLIN
## OF PFORZHEIM, DOCTOR OF LAWS,
->To Thomas Anshelm the Printer, in praise of<-
->Rabanus’s work on the Holy Cross.<-
->PRAISE. <note>original Greek: ΕΠΑΙΝΟΣ (Epainos)</note><-

I consider both you, O Thomas, and Pforzheim to be blessed,
Because through your efforts the work of Rabanus on the Cross shines forth.
The seeds of writing, once scattered throughout the world, now return—
An art which our ancestors hid away for those yet to come.
Let the mind that knows not how to look on shameful things draw closer:
Here, a more beautiful heaven lies hidden within a beautiful sky.
It is not the "cross" <note>The poet uses "crux" (cross) metaphorically to refer to the constellations or the mythical bindings of these figures.</note> of Andromeda, daughter of Cepheus, nor the "cross" of Ganymede
Or of Verres, that will be presented for your viewing in this book.
But rather the one to which the Creator of both men and gods was fixed—
He who is pure and innocent, atoning for our crimes.
This Cross of Rabanus shines more brightly than the one seen by Constantine,
That vision once painted in the sky with signs made of stars. <note>Refers to the vision of the Roman Emperor Constantine the Great, who reportedly saw a cross in the sky with the words "In this sign, you shall conquer."</note>
The bronze figure of the serpent, fixed to a pole, was able to heal; <note>A reference to the biblical "Brazen Serpent" (Numbers 21:9), a traditional Christian symbol foreshadowing the crucifixion.</note>
With our Cross, you shall be even more safe.
The spotted arrangement of letters scatters beautiful strokes
In various parts, so that their order marks out the shape of a cross.
In this, Rabanus easily defeated Apelles of Cos; <note>Apelles of Cos was the most famous painter of ancient Greece. Reuchlin is arguing that Rabanus's visual poetry is superior to classical painting.</note>
Compared to him, Parrhasius and Zeuxis <note>Two other legendary Greek painters known for their realism and skill.</note> will be as nothing to you.
Whether you read the book, you will see everything is most masterfully crafted; <note>original: Polydædala, a Latinization of a Greek term meaning "cunningly wrought" or "multifaceted," invoking the skill of the mythical inventor Daedalus.</note>
Or if you prefer to listen, a harmony sings out.
Therefore, let both of you—printer and city—grow into high titles
By this single, most splendid book of Rabanus.
Thomas Anshelm, you who print these pages with such skill;
And you likewise, Pforzheim, the fountain and origin of my own life.
O City, honor of craftsmen and maker of intellects,
O Glory, live on as the second parent of Rabanus’s work!

<summary>This page features a celebratory Latin poem by the humanist scholar Johannes Reuchlin, praising the printer Thomas Anshelm for publishing Rabanus Maurus's medieval masterpiece. Reuchlin compares the visual and spiritual beauty of the work to classical painting and biblical miracles, celebrating Pforzheim's role in the rebirth of learning.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Reuchlin, Thomas Anshelm, Rabanus Maurus, Pforzheim, typography, printing history, visual poetry, carmina figurata, Humanism, Holy Cross</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory matter of the 1501 edition of "In Praise of the Holy Cross." It follows a poem by Johannes Reuchlin. Here, Sebastian Brant—the famed author of "The Ship of Fools"—offers his own poetic commendation of Rabanus Maurus’s work to Nicolaus Keinbös, a priest and member of the Knights Hospitaller.</meta>

# TO A MAN OF GREAT GENIUS
# AND A MOST DILIGENT INVESTIGATOR
## of good things, Brother Nicolaus Keinbös: of the Order of Saint John
## of Jerusalem, parish priest of Durlach: an introduction <note>original Greek: σύστασις (systasis)</note>, or
## commendation by Sebastian Brant for the marvelous work on the praises of the Cross by Rabanus
## Maurus, Abbot of Fulda.

Nicolaus, because you recently sent me the sacred work of Rabanus
->Regarding the Cross, and regarding the beauty of the Cross,<-
I could not help but marvel at the daring of the work in many ways,
->Or judge it worthy of immeasurable praise.<-
And it was fitting: for what servant of Christ or of the Cross
->Would not himself also strive for the praises of the Cross?<-
But who will think themselves able to say things worthy
->In song for the marvelous and life-giving Cross?<-
Sense, tongue, and the power of genius fail in all
->Who attempt to sing of the Cross with a mortal mouth.<-
Yet that Rabanus, a learned father and the finest author,
->Dared the same, under various poetic auspices,<-
And he completed the mystery, the praises, and the glory of the Cross,
->And taught that the Cross is present in all things.<-
He traced the Cross from the heavens above, and from the first parent:
->Through all creatures and the very elements.<-
O, how great a labor did that divine father undertake?
->What an immense burden did he take up for the love of the Cross?<-
Watchful, he spent sleepless nights (without a doubt)
->So that he might continue the praises of the Cross.<-
Because of this, I am all the more indignant: I also curse
->The men of this time; I marvel at and grieve for these fickle people;<-
Not only those who are senseless, and flowing with sloth,
->Who do not worthily sweat or keep watch for the Cross:<-
But those who even violate, desecrate, and now defile it,
->Who despise, dread, and tear the Cross apart.<-
Moreover, they trample the venerable sign with their feet:
->And shamefully slaughter those marked with the Cross. <note>Brant likely refers to the contemporary conflicts between Christian Europe and the Ottoman Empire, as well as internal neglect of devotion.</note><-
Their own punishment awaits them at last; meanwhile, it delights us
->To join in singing the praises of the Cross with Rabanus.<-
And let us return, hold, and give thanks to the Lord:
->Who frees and blesses us by His own Cross.<-
A worthy merit from the heavens and from pious Christians
->Will follow you too, dear father Nicolaus,<-
Who wear a garment marked with the Cross: <note>As a member of the Order of Saint John (the Knights Hospitaller), Keinbös wore the distinctive habit featuring a white cross.</note> hence the arms of the Cross
->You love, you observe, and you strive to amplify.<-
You also provide the means by which this work might one day come
->Into the light: and receive life under your guidance.<-

<summary>A commendatory poem by Sebastian Brant addressed to Nicolaus Keinbös, praising the 9th-century work of Rabanus Maurus and lamenting contemporary neglect or desecration of the Cross.</summary>
<keywords>Sebastian Brant, Nicolaus Keinbös, Rabanus Maurus, Knights Hospitaller, Order of St. John, Durlach, Holy Cross, humanism, religious devotion</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory sequence of the 1501 Pforzheim edition of Rabanus Maurus’s "In Praise of the Holy Cross." It concludes the poem by Sebastian Brant addressed to the priest Nicolaus Keinbös and includes further commendatory verses by Jodocus Gallus and Theodoricus Gresemundus. The focus transitions from the content of the work to the skill of the printer, Thomas Anshelm (Thomas de Baden), and the enduring nature of the poetry.</meta>

Rightly, therefore, are you called Keinbôs <note>A wordplay on the German "Kein Böse," meaning "No Evil."</note>: because you live free from every crime, and depraved things do not please you. Whence you also seek the praises of the Cross and its trophy, and you instruct your natural genius in the good arts. Therefore, farewell; let the shadow of the Cross defend us, and let it receive and protect its servants with its wings. And may this Cross, which is to be venerated with perpetual beauty, also protect us forever; Amen.

# A FOUR-LINE POEM <note>original: Tetraftichon</note> BY JODOCUS
### Gallus to the Christians.

> Learn from those in the depths whom the sacred Cross alone redeemed,
> *With what piety it is worthy to embrace the Cross.*
> *Since nowhere else is such affection, labor, genius, and the power*
> *Of memory to be found: as they are so well scattered throughout this book.*

---

# BY THE SAME TO THE FAITHFUL,
### industrious, and diligent printer of Pforzheim, <note>original: Phorcensem</note>
### Thomas de Baden: <note>Referring to Thomas Anshelm, the printer, who was from Baden-Baden.</note>

> Continue as you have begun, learned master of printing <note>original: Chalcographe, literally "copper-writer" or engraver</note>;
> *To print marvelous marks with marvelous bronze.*
> You have a lively mind: a ready art, a sure practice at a moment's notice;
> And a fertile genius, and a learned hand.
> Hence, the figures of Rabanus which you have just produced with art,
> No one else in our world will fashion any equal to them.
> Therefore, go on: let the file <note>A common metaphor for the "polishing" or refining of a work.</note> (as you have begun) be applied to the art
> Which you alone almost possess; you alone shall bear the rewards.

---

# IN PRAISE OF THE POEMS
### of Rabanus, by Theodoricus Gresemundus,
### Doctor of Laws.

> Rabanus with his pen, Apelles <note>The most famous painter of ancient Greece, used here as the standard of artistic perfection.</note> with his tablets, indulged themselves;
> *Whatever either one painted with his hand seemed to breathe.*
> Devouring time has scraped away whatever ancient tablets the latter [Apelles] had;
> *The work of the former [Rabanus] shall live for all eternity.*
> You, the painted images, owe your life to the songs:
> *Even if the drawn line should perish, the songs do not.*

<summary>This page concludes Sebastian Brant's introductory poem and features commendations for the printer Thomas Anshelm, celebrating the technical achievement of printing Rabanus Maurus's complex "picture-poems." It emphasizes that while physical art may decay, the spiritual and intellectual power of the poetry is eternal.</summary>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory commendations for the 1501 edition of "In Praise of the Holy Cross." Following the previous page’s poem by the humanist Johannes Reuchlin, this page features a dedication by Sebastian Brant—author of the famous "Ship of Fools"—to Nicolaus Keinbös, who helped bring this complex work to the press.</meta>

# TO A MAN OF GREAT INTELLECT
# AND A MOST DILIGENT SEEKER
->of good things, Brother Nicolaus Keinbös: of the Order of Saint John<-
->of Jerusalem, parish priest of Durlach: a recommendation <note>original Greek: σύστασις (systasis)</note> or<-
->commendation by Sebastian Brant regarding the wonderful work of Rabanus<-
->Maurus, Abbot of Fulda, *On the Praises of the Cross* .<-

Because you recently sent me, Nicolaus, that sacred work
  Of Rabanus concerning the Cross and its beauty,
I could not help but marvel at the daring of the feat in many ways,
  Or deem it worthy of anything less than immoderate praise.
And it was fitting: for what minister of Christ or of the Cross
  Would not himself also strive to sing the praises of the Cross?
But yet, who will think himself able to speak worthy things
  In a poem about the wonderful and soul-saving Cross?
Sense, tongue, and the power of intellect fail in all men
  Who attempt to sing of the Cross with a mortal mouth.
Yet that Rabanus, a learned father and excellent author,
  Dared this very thing, under the various guidance of his song;
He completed his study of the mystery, the praises, and the beauty of the Cross,
  And taught that the Cross is present in all things.
He traced it from the heavens above, and from our first father <note>Refers to Adam; medieval tradition held that the wood of the Cross came from a seed or branch of the Tree of Knowledge.</note>:
  Tracing the Cross through all creatures and the elements.
Oh, how great a labor did that divine father undertake?
  How great an immense burden did he take up for the love of the Cross?
Ever-watchful, he spent sleepless nights (without a doubt)
  So that he might continue the praises of the Cross.
For this reason I am the more indignant: I even curse the men
  Of this current age; I marvel at and grieve for the frivolous;
Not only the senseless ones who, overflowing with sloth,
  Do not worthily toil or keep watch for the Cross:
But they even violate, desecrate, and now defile,
  Despise, shudder at, and tear the Cross apart;
Moreover, they trample the venerable sign with their feet:
  And they shamefully slaughter those marked by the Cross <note>Likely a reference to the ongoing conflicts with the Ottoman Empire, where Christians—the "cross-marked"—were killed.</note>.
Their own punishment awaits them at last; meanwhile, it delights us
  To sing the praises of the Cross together with Rabanus.
And let us return, hold, and give thanks to the Lord,
  Who frees and blesses us by His own Cross.
A well-deserved merit from the heavens and from pious Christians
  Will follow you too, dear father Nicolaus,
Who wear the garment marked with the Cross <note>As a member of the Order of St. John (Knights Hospitaller), Keinbös wore a habit featuring a distinctive white cross.</note>: for this reason
  You love, observe, and strive to amplify the weapons of the Cross.
You also provide the means <note>Brant is thanking Keinbös for providing the financial or material support needed to print this expensive, typographically difficult book.</note> by which this work might one day come forth
  Into the light: and take up its life under your guidance.

<summary>Sebastian Brant dedicates a poem to Nicolaus Keinbös, a priest of the Order of Saint John, thanking him for his role in publishing Rabanus Maurus's work and contrasting Rabanus's devotion with the perceived impiety of the early 16th century.</summary>
<keywords>Sebastian Brant, Nicolaus Keinbös, Rabanus Maurus, Order of Saint John, Knights Hospitaller, Durlach, printing patronage, devotion, Holy Cross</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the introductory poem by Sebastian Brant to Nicolaus Keinbös and includes further commendatory verses by humanists Jodocus Gallus and Dietrich Gresemund. It specifically praises the technical achievement of the printer, Thomas Anshelm (referred to here as Thomas de Baden), for successfully reproducing Rabanus Maurus’s complex grid-poems.</meta>

You are rightly, therefore, called "Keinbös" <note>A wordplay on the German name "Keinbös," meaning "No-evil."</note>: because you live free
    From every crime, nor do wicked things please you.
Thus you also seek the praises and the trophy of the Cross,
    And you train your intellect in the good arts.
Therefore, farewell; let the shadow of the Cross defend us, and let it 
    Receive and protect its servants with its wings:
And may this Cross, which is to be worshipped for its eternal beauty,
    Also protect us forever; Amen.

# A TETRASTICH TO THE CHRISTIANS BY JODOCUS
->Gallus.<-

Learn, you whom the holy Cross alone redeemed from the depths,
    *With what piety it is worthy to embrace the Cross.*
*Since nowhere else are affection, labor, genius, and the power*
    *Of memory so well distributed as in this book.*

# BY THE SAME AUTHOR TO THE FAITHFUL,
->industrious, and diligent printer of Pforzheim,<-
->Thomas of Baden:<- <note>Thomas Anshelm of Baden (c. 1470–1522), a prominent printer who moved his press to Pforzheim. He was celebrated for his technical ability to print the complex "carmina figurata" (grid poems) found in this volume.</note>

Continue as you have begun, O learned master printer <note>original: *chalcographe* (copper-engraver/writer in bronze). In this era, the term referred to the skill of working with metal type and engraving.</note>;
    To print wonderful marks with wonderful bronze.
You have a lively mind: a ready art, a sure practice 
    Refined by time, a fertile wit, and a learned hand.
Hence, no one else in our world will fashion figures equal 
    To these of Rabanus which you have now produced with your art.
Therefore, come: let the file <note>A metaphor for the "final polish" or correction of a literary or artistic work.</note> (just as you have begun) be applied to the art 
    Which you almost alone possess: you shall bear the rewards alone.

# IN PRAISE OF THE POEMS
->of Rabanus, by Dietrich Gresemund,<-
->Doctor of Laws.<-

Rabanus devoted himself to the pen, as Apelles <note>The most famous painter of ancient Greece, often used as a shorthand for artistic perfection.</note> did to his tablets;
    *Whatever each one painted with his hand seemed to breathe.*
*Devouring time has scraped away those ancient tablets of the latter:*
    *But the work of the former shall live for eternal time.*
*You owe the life of the painted image to the poems:*
    *Though the line may perish, the poems do not perish.*

<meta>This page continues the introductory commendatory verses for Rabanus Maurus's work "On the Praises of the Holy Cross." The previous page ended mid-sentence in a poem by Jodocus Gallus praising the printer Thomas Anshelm; this page begins with a final short poem by Gallus followed by two poems by the Heidelberg humanist Joannes Gallinarius (Johann Henlin, d. 1506).</meta>

# ANOTHER POEM BY THE SAME AUTHOR
## to the same subject.

Behold the verses of Rabanus, shaped with wonderful craftsmanship, if you are someone of a joyful spirit.
However you read them, meaning arises along with the song:
For every single letter serves in many ways. <note>This refers to the "carmina figurata" (shaped poems) where letters form part of both a horizontal verse and a visual grid image.</note>
And what is more marvelous is that each image dwells within its own rhythmic counts: for the poet, these were no labor at all.
For although these poems are composed by a law that is far from easy,
Yet they all flow with an easy grace.

---

# AN ELEGIAC POEM BY JOANNES
## GALLINARIUS of Heidelberg to the lovers of Christ,
## that they may read Rabanus on the praise of the Holy Cross.

*IF anyone desires to run through the song of praise <note>original: pæana</note> for the Cross of Christ,*
*Let him direct his step here with a swift pace.*
*Rabanus, the greatest glory of the German people,*
*Composed <note>original: lusit (literally "played"), a common term for poetic composition</note> this noble work with a marvelous song.*
*The German land has produced nothing like it, nor the Italian earth,*
*And neither has Spain <note>original: Tartessus</note>, nor the Rhone, nor the Saône <note>original: Arar</note>.*
*He does not make a noise here about the flames of Helen [of Troy], nor the wound*
*Of unhappy Elissa <note>Dido, the tragic queen of Carthage</note>, nor the beds of the descendants of Tantalus:*
*He does not sound the boiling battles of untamable Mars,*
*Nor does he try poems made in Eastern rhythms:*
*But he sang of the sacred marks of the triumphant Christ—*
*The weapons with which He conquered the Stygian leader <note>The ruler of the underworld; Satan</note>,*
*At which the ghosts of the depths of Erebus, the shadows of the wicked,*
*The Tartarean Pluto, and Persephone tremble.*

---

# TO THE MUSES, THAT THEY MAY
## adorn and surround Rabanus with a crown made from all types of spices,
## an Elegiac poem by Joannes Gallinarius of
## Heidelberg.

Bind the temples of the poet Rabanus with the virgin laurel,
O Muses of Castalia <note>original: Castalides, the Muses associated with the sacred spring on Mount Parnassus</note>, and with the hair of Pallas Athena.
Let green ivy not be lacking, nor the myrtle woods;
Let lilies and purple roses come together.
Cinnamon, wild thyme, boxwood, narcissus, spice-plant,
Incense, violets, nard, balsam, myrrh, and thyme,

<meta>This page continues the introductory commendatory poems for Rabanus Maurus's "On the Praises of the Holy Cross." The previous page concluded mid-poem with Joannes Gallinarius calling upon the Muses and various lands to witness Rabanus's achievement. This page completes his poem and includes contributions by Georgius Symlerus.</meta>

Come here, Terebinth trees, Walnut trees, and sea-roses;
Come here, Cyparissus, along with the forest-god Silvanus. <note>In mythology, Cyparissus was a youth turned into a cypress tree, a symbol of mourning or devotion.</note>
Bind together whatever is produced in the gardens of Panchaia, <note>Panchaia was a mythical island in the Indian Ocean famous for its incense and perfumes.</note>
Whatever the Cilicians possess, or the Idalian grove. <note>Idalium, on Cyprus, was a grove sacred to the goddess Venus.</note>
Whatever the dark Indian seeks in the Red Sea <note>original: Erythræa</note> seaweed,
Whatever the Pactolus or the Tagus rivers themselves carry. <note>The Pactolus and Tagus were rivers famous in antiquity for having gold in their sands.</note>
Let Mount Tmolus also bring hither its saffron scents:
And let the honey-bearing mouths of Hyblaean bees bring their honeycombs.
Let the Hyperborean Griffins and the beasts of the Caucasus
Bring crystals from the icy peak of Mount Taurus.
Let the snowy swans from the shore bring amber <note>original: electra</note>,
The tears of the river Eridanus and of the sisters of Phaethon. <note>In myth, the sisters of Phaethon wept amber when he fell from the sun-chariot into the Eridanus (the river Po).</note>
You too, Hamadryads and Napaeae, sisters of the plain,
Pluck every kind of fragrant grass,
Bind precious gems with interwoven flowers,
And you, Muses of Pieria, circle the brow of Rabanus.

## A SIX-LINE STANZABY THE SAME AUTHOR.

*With a Daedalian talent, Rabanus drew the threads,*
*And the fibers to be guided in a labyrinthine way.* <note>The term "Daedalian" refers to Daedalus, the mythical inventor of the labyrinth; it here praises the complex "grid" structure of the poems.</note>
*Though you may be a Theseus relying on the power of Ariadne,*
*A Daedalus in your genius, or Virgil <note>original: Maro</note> himself in your verses:*
*Yet by no art are you able to equal this poet,*
*Therefore the glory shall be greater for so great a seer.*

# IN PRAISE OF THE POEM

->by the industrious and quite remarkable Georgius Symlerus of<-
->Wimpfen, regarding the creator.<-

HOW great are the names of Rabanus in the land of Mainz? <note>original: Moguntinæ</note>
Names that shall now possess perpetual trust,
Where the horn-bearing <note>original: Corniger; rivers were traditionally personified as gods with horns.</note> Rhine glides with gold-bearing waves,
And the Belgian cuts the shallows on the German shore.
This leader is our honor (though antiquity might imagine greater things),
A glowing glory for the Germans and the nobility,
He has shown by proof what our land and what the Italian earth
Can do, while he summons his unusual lyre. <note>original: chelyn (from the Greek for tortoise-shell lyre)</note>
Now let the golden rocks of the Tarpeian Thunderer <note>Jupiter's temple on the Capitoline Hill in Rome.</note> fall silent,
And the machine called the lighthouse <note>original: phari</note> of Ptolemy:
Henceforth let the inextricable maze of Crete be silent,
Which they say the hands of Daedalus were able to build.

## ANOTHER POEM BY THE SAME AUTHOR
->on the same subject.<-

Behold the verses of Rabanus, polished <note>original: "tornatos," literally "turned on a lathe," implying the mechanical precision of his grid-based poetry.</note> with wondrous skill, if you are someone of a happy disposition.
However you may read them, a meaning arises with the song:
For every letter serves in many ways. <note>This refers to Rabanus's "carmina figurata," where letters form both horizontal verses and vertical or diagonal shapes/images.</note>
And what is more marvelous: an image dwells within its own meters;
these were no labor at all for the poet.
For although these poems consist of a difficult law <note>The "law" refers to the strict constraints of fitting poetry into a mathematical grid.</note>,
yet they all flow with an easy grace.

# AN ELEGIAC POEM BY JOANNES
->GALLINARIUS of Heidelberg to the lovers of Christ,<-
->that they may read Rabanus on the praise of the Holy Cross.<-

*If anyone desires to run through the songs of praise for the Cross of Christ,*
*Let him direct his step here with a swift pace.*
*Rabanus, the greatest glory of the German people,*
*Composed this noble work with miraculous song.*
*The German land has brought forth none like him, nor the Italian land,*
*Nor Tartessus, nor the Rhone, nor the Saône.* <note>Tartessus was an ancient region in southern Spain; the Rhone and Saône are major rivers in Gaul (modern France).</note>
*He does not make a noise here of the flames of Helen, nor the wound*
*Of the unhappy Elissa, or the marriage beds of the house of Tantalus:* <note>Elissa is another name for Dido, the Queen of Carthage; the house of Tantalus refers to the tragic myths of the Pelopids.</note>
*He does not sound the burning battles of untamed Mars,*
*Nor does he approve of poems made in the worldly manner;*
*But he sang of the sacred wounds of the triumphant Christ,*
*The weapons with which He Himself conquered the leader of the Styx,* <note>The "leader of the Styx" refers to Satan or Pluto, the ruler of the underworld.</note>
*At which the springs of the underworld, the spirits of the dead, and the wicked shadows tremble,*
*As do Tartarean Pluto and Persephone.*

Come here, you Terebinth trees, and Walnuts, and Sea-roses; come here, Cyparissus, along with Silvanus <note>Silvanus was the Roman god of the woods; Cyparissus was a youth in mythology who transformed into a cypress tree.</note>.

### A SIX-LINE STANZABY THE SAME AUTHOR.

With Daedalian <note>Referring to Daedalus, the mythical inventor and builder of the Labyrinth; this praises the intricate, "labyrinthine" structure of Rabanus's grid-poems.</note> talent, Rabanus drew out his threads, and the strings must be guided in a labyrinthine manner.
Though you be a Theseus relying on the power of Ariadne, or a Daedalus in ingenuity, or even Virgil <note>original: "Maro," the family name of the poet Virgil.</note> himself in verse:
Yet by no art can you equal this poet; therefore, the glory for so great a bard shall be all the greater.

# FOR THE PRAISE OF THE POEM
## by the industrious and most unusual Georgius Symlerus of Wimpfen,
## regarding the creator.

How great is the name of Rabanus in the land of Mainz? <note>original: "Moguntinae terrae," referring to the Archbishopric of Mainz where Rabanus served.</note>
A name that shall henceforth possess eternal trust,
Where the horned Rhine <note>The river god Rhine was often depicted with horns to symbolize its power and its multiple branching mouths.</note> glides with gold-bearing waves, and the Belgian cuts through the shallows on the German shore:
This leader is our honor (though antiquity may invent greater things), a shining glory for the Germans and their nobles.

Here let wonders be joined for you in a resounding theater: and the ancient, celebrated fame of the baths.

### A FOUR-LINE STANZA BY THE SAME AUTHOR.

This primary praise is owed to our poet, 
Because he revealed a useful work to the followers of Christ: 
And he painted the signs of the Cross, to be venerated by all, 
In rosy blood: and the warfare of the most high God.

### Vincent in the *Mirror of History*, Book 25, Chapter 28. <note>Vincent of Beauvais (c. 1184–1264) was a Dominican friar who wrote the *Speculum Maius*, the most famous encyclopedia of the Middle Ages.</note>

Rabanus the Sophist <note>In this medieval context, "Sophist" is a title of respect for a master of rhetoric and learning.</note>, and second to none of the poets of his time, became the Abbot of Fulda. He discussed many things from the Holy Scriptures; he also composed a book about the praise of the Holy Cross, distinguished by a variety of figures, in a difficult and wondrous poem, and he sent it to be offered to Pope Sergius.

### Antoninus in his *Chronicles*, Part Two, Title 14, Chapter 5, Paragraph 1. <note>Saint Antoninus of Florence (1389–1459) was an Archbishop and influential chronicler.</note>

He alludes to and supports these same things in almost the same words that Vincent used.

### Odilo, Abbot of Cluny, in a sermon on the praise of the Holy Cross, says the following: <note>Odilo (c. 962–1049) was the influential fifth Abbot of Cluny.</note>

Rabanus, abundantly learned in secular science, Catholic in faith, and fully instructed in spiritual knowledge, wove such a work concerning the praise of the Holy Cross, and perfected it in the weaving, that nothing more precious to look upon, more lovely to read, sweeter to remember, or more laborious to write can be found.

### *Martin of Opava in his Chronicles, under Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne.*

At that time flourished the monk Rabanus, Abbot of Fulda, a great poet and most distinguished in the science of Theology.

---

### *Platina in his life of Gregory IV.* <note>Bartolomeo Platina was a 15th-century historian of the papacy.</note>

There are those who write that, at the request of Louis <note>Louis the Pious</note>, Gregory established the celebration of All Saints on the first day of November. They also note that this matter was greatly praised in both verse and prose by the monk Rabanus, a distinguished theologian; for as a man of learning, he was remarkably skilled in both styles of speaking for that era. The same Rabanus wrote commentaries on the Book of Chronicles <note>original: "Paralipomenon," the Greek-derived name for the Books of Chronicles</note> and the Book of Maccabees. He also delivered quite elegant sermons to the people, but the one he gave during the celebration of All Saints is most highly praised.

---

### *Werner Rolevinck, a Carthusian of Cologne, in the "Fasciculus Temporum" under Louis I.* <note>The "Fasciculus Temporum" (The Little Bundle of Times) was a popular 15th-century world chronicle.</note>

Rabanus, poet and monk, and later Abbot of Fulda. Afterward, as the Archbishop of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinus"</note>, he flourished as a great Teacher <note>original: "Doctor"</note> and wrote many works.

---

### *Giacomo Filippo Foresti of Bergamo in his "Supplement of the Chronicles."*

Rabanus, monk and Archbishop of Mainz, was a most famous theologian and a notable poet, excelling greatly in both prose and verse.

---

### *Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, in "On Ecclesiastical Writers."* <note>Trithemius was a famous 15th-century polymath and bibliographer.</note>

Rabanus the German <note>original: "Theutonicus"</note>, from the city of Fulda in Buchonia: a man most erudite in the divine scriptures and nobly learned in secular letters. He was a philosopher, rhetorician, astronomer, and a most subtle poet, such that Italy never produced his like, nor did Germany bear his equal. He wrote many volumes in both verse and prose, especially regarding the Holy Scriptures on almost both Testaments, and "In Praise of the Holy Cross" <note>original: "de laude sanctae Crucis"</note>, which begins with the words, "Lord, King of Kings" <note>original: "Rex regum Dominus"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the introductory poetic sequence of Hrabanus Maurus's "De laudibus sanctae crucis" (Praise of the Holy Cross). # THE INTERCESSION OF ALBINUS
<note>Albinus is the Latin name for Alcuin of York (c. 735–804), the preeminent scholar of the Carolingian Renaissance and mentor to Hrabanus Maurus.</note>
->on behalf of Maurus.<-
<note>Maurus is the nickname Alcuin gave to his favorite pupil, Hrabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), after St. Maurus, the disciple of St. Benedict.</note>

Holy prelate of God, living through the ages by your merits,
    Receive with a pious spirit the cause we bring before you.
Indeed, when I was the guardian and humble minister
    Of this Church, reading the sacred teachings,
I taught this boy the speech of the divine word
    Through the precepts of ethics and the study of wisdom.
He is a Frank by birth, and an inhabitant of the forest
    Of Buchonia <note>The "Beech Forest," the region surrounding the Abbey of Fulda in Germany.</note>, sent here to learn the words of God:
For his own Abbot, the ruler of the flock at Fulda,
    Directed him here to your house, O Father,
So that as a student he might study the art of poetic meter with me,
    And joyfully prepare himself in the Holy Scriptures according to the rites.
But when he had completed thirty years <note>original: "sex lustra." A lustrum is a five-year period; Hrabanus was around 30 when he finished this work.</note>, attempting now to write,
    He produced this book by his art for the praise of Christ:
In which he has set down symbolic numbers and figurative shapes <note>A reference to the "carmina figurata" (grid poems) that follow, where letters form shapes and hidden meanings through numerology.</note>
    In the proper way, so that he might reveal the nourishing gifts of God.
[He writes of] what honor the Passion of Christ confers upon the world,
    And how He conquered the ancient serpent <note>original: "chelydrum," a Greek-derived word for a serpent or water-snake, representing the Devil.</note>;
Things which the holy Prophets sang would come to pass,
    And which the books of the Law rightly provided in their writing.
And because he remembers that he was nurtured in the illustrious house
    Of this very place, he brings these gifts to you.
Though these gifts may be unworthy and poor, yet as a
    Gentle patron, I pray you receive them piously,
And return this pledge to the One enthroned on high, who provided it,
    Urgently seeking pardon for the craftsman.
He has done as much as he could—though it is not as much as he,
    The debtor, ought to have given in order to return thanks to God:
O holy one, pour out abundant prayers to the powerful Lord
    For the crime of this miserable man, and thus help your servant,
Who confesses that he himself has done many shameful things,
    Such as a playful age <note>A reference to the common errors or "follies" of youth.</note> is accustomed to commit.
But a firm hope remains, and the great goodness of the Thunderer <note>original: "tonantis." A classical poetic title for God, borrowing the epithet of Jupiter.</note>
    That the almighty Physician will save him:
He who released the world's debts with His own blood,
    And washed away many crimes in the sacred fountain.
Only do you, by your sacred prayers and merits,
    Commend him to Christ, and thus he shall be blessed;
May he complete this present life, and be preserved in safety
    For his future homeland; O holy one, protect your own.

<summary>A commendatory poem written by Alcuin of York introducing his student Hrabanus Maurus and presenting Hrabanus’s complex poetic work on the Holy Cross to a saintly patron.</summary>

<meta>The signature Bb indicates this page belongs to the preliminary matter of Hrabanus Maurus’s "In Praise of the Holy Cross" (De laudibus sanctae crucis), a famous 9th-century work of figure poems. The author is addressing Pope Gregory IV.</meta>

# COMMENDATION OF THE POPE.

Prince of the Apostolic See <note>original: "Sedis Apostolicę princeps". The Apostolic See refers to the Episcopal jurisdiction of the Pope in Rome.</note>, golden light of Rome,
Both the glory and teacher of the people, and their nourishing love.
You are the head of the church, the first patriarch throughout the world,
Renowned for your merits, and powerful in your piety.
Salt of the earth, light of the world, and the illustrious city of Christ,
Offering the path of perpetual light to the people.
Your tongue has the power to open and close heaven,
An ethereal key-bearer <note>A reference to the "Keys of Heaven" granted to St. Peter, whose successor the Pope is.</note> stationed upon the earth.
You stand as the restorer of the homeland, its hope, ruler, and honor.
A sweet love to all, worthy of the love of God.
The times of this life are now full of dangers:
Wars stir the nations, and the enemy rages everywhere,
Wherefore there is great need for your strong protection:
May it succor the wretched, whom the enemy hates.
Rescue the flock committed to you, O Shepherd, from the enemy,
With your holy warnings and your sacred prayers.
So that your praise may remain, and your reward, and your glory forever,
Holding blessed realms with Christ in the heavens,
Joined for eternity to the apostolic prince Peter,
Whose place <note>original: "vicem". The Pope is the "Vicar of Peter" or "Vicar of Christ."</note> you yourself hold on earth.

->*He offers a gift to the Pontiff.*<-

O Prelate beloved by God, I pray to you, Pope Gregory,
That you might count me, a wretch, among your own sheep.
May you be a true protector of your servant, and restore him
To the eternal Lord through your prayers—
He who offers his whole self, and provides these small gifts,
Commending both himself and his belongings to you at once.
Through you, may this nourishing praise of the Cross now stand more acceptable,
These gifts sent to the apostolic prince Peter:
Which were composed to the praise of Christ in an earlier time,
When it pleased me to play with versifying song.
I believe indeed that through you I can obtain
The life which I cannot reach through my own merits.
May the eternal God, the most gentle author of the world,
Protect and rule you for a long length of time,
That you may be well, flourish in health, and seize prosperity:
Here, and in the eternal realms above, may you reach your goal.
May He who does not sleep keep you vigilant forever:
And restore the merit of your name.
So that as a cautious pastor you may watch, may you be "Gregory" <note>The name Gregory comes from the Greek "gregorein," meaning "to be watchful" or "vigilant." Hrabanus is making a pun on the Pope's name here.</note>
Holy one, to your sheep: blessed Pope, farewell.

<summary>This page contains a formal poetic dedication by Hrabanus Maurus to Pope Gregory IV, praising the papacy's role as the successor of St. Peter and presenting the book "In Praise of the Holy Cross" as a spiritual offering.</summary>

<meta>Following the dedication to Pope Gregory IV, this page marks the formal presentation of the work to the Carolingian Emperor Louis the Pious (reigned 814–840 AD). This is one of the most famous "picture poems" in the manuscript, where the text and the image of the Emperor are inextricably linked.</meta>

# THE DEDICATION TO THE EMPEROR LOUIS

->**A POEM IN THE FORM OF AN IMAGE**<-

King of kings, Lord, governing the world by your authority,
Who, reigning by eternal right, hold the immortal scepter of empire,
When you released the many sins of our forefathers upon the cross,
Where you had placed the reins of justice.
Therefore, you wish for all your servants to hope for a blessed life
Above the stars; from this, O Christ, you quickly gave the right to life.
And now there is a gift, but it is of God and of your Father.
Now all the ages were long ago amazed by your name;
Behold, turn that which the friendly nature of the High Christ-worshipper <note>The "High Christ-worshipper" refers to the Emperor himself as a devout leader.</note>
Carries, to be performed in a well-worn way.
Through this law, Hrabanus <note>The author, Hrabanus Maurus, inserts his own name here into the grid.</note> desired to take up the law,
And as is fitting, the <term>Augustus</term> <note>A title for the Roman/Carolingian Emperor, implying majesty and semi-divine status.</note> honors the whole world by his nod.
For this profit comes forth from such a great and steering pole,
That the world may be made so that it prays with the mouth of Caesar for a helmet.
Dedicated to the pure <term>Augustus</term>, [I offer] from here a nourishing and beautiful crown.
For the divine virtue appears as the foremost right hand with skillful art,
And the lineage persuades us; we all ask for a triple triumph,
Now a nourishing and just one, so that justice may reign everywhere.
May this [justice] be clothed in flint and bound by a friendly circle,
While the breastplate <note>The Emperor is depicted wearing a <term>lorica</term> (breastplate), symbolizing both physical and spiritual protection.</note> asserts itself thus prepared for what is pleasing.
Let us pray that Christ piously always protects him as a friend,
So that no one may press him down with a javelin, but he rises up.
Either by divine law or in that sin, the enemy desires dire things,
But the Defender of the art shows him to be firm and lovable.
Justice adorns him, and the woolly [cloak] holds the draft of the head.
May there be an omen, and may the whole empire remain safe in the world by this act.
Behold, the entire Greek realm rules, and they bestow gifts through the common good,
And the Persian gives likewise, and his offspring seeks the revived things.
The nation and the joyful people piously grant a successor to the lineage.
May the Muse live, and may God remain; He knows how to protect and love you.
While he gives hope everywhere by holding the scepter received from God,
Until he drives away the matter from the era with a draft from [divine] art.
I seek that the laws will hold you, and that weapons may not be absent,
And to settle quiet things, to solidify the earth against insolence.
How solid he remains! He has acted as a servant to the <term>Augustus</term>.
The transformer of the world declares the bright tributes of Christ,
Giving by the right of worship while he prepares mindful trophies.
Whithersoever this name goes, may it be everywhere a prayer from the mouth.
Surely the heart thunders and urges that the divine be properly loved;
Let there be trembling, and let the good things of the divine gift be loved.
From there, he benefits the world, moist and serene, even in unlawful things;
Thus he casts them away, and follows the harbor given by the cross.
For this is given to you, always chaste and pious;
O Caesar, you see now a generous thing, so that you may terrify the enemy camps,
Giving hope and fleeing the hostile fears of your enemy.
You are more pious, and this nation asks for a very pleasing sound.
May the spirit come to us at the command of the parent;
For I wrote some time ago a little book in praise of Christ,
In verse and prose, which I now, O Emperor,
Offer to you, Holy One, gladly; the image of him stands before it,
Standing armed with faith, it shows the victor everywhere.

<note>The figure of Emperor Louis the Pious drawn over the letters acts as a secondary poem. The letters touched by his halo, body, and staff form the phrase: **"TU HLRUDUVICUM CRISTE CORONA"** (You, O Christ, crown Louis).</note>

***

The text intertwines the Emperor's worldly military defense with his spiritual role as a protector of the Church.</summary>

--- Page 23 ---
<meta>This page continues the sophisticated "picture poem" (carmen figuratum) dedicated to Emperor Louis the Pious. In the original manuscript, the letters of this poem are arranged in a grid, and certain letters are highlighted to form the physical image of the Emperor dressed as a Roman soldier, holding a cross. This text provides the theological and political justification for his rule, weaving together the authority of Christ and the authority of the Carolingian throne.</meta>

# ON THE IMAGE OF THE EMPEROR <note>Original: De Imagine Cæsaris</note>

King of kings, Lord governing the world with your power,
You who hold the immortal scepter of empire, reigning by eternal right:
When you loosened the many sins of our ancestors upon the Cross,
And when you had set the reins of justice;
Therefore, O Jesus Christ, you have quickly granted all your servants
To hope for a blessed life from this place, far above the stars.
This gift now belongs to Christ the God, and to your Father.
Now all the ages are rightfully amazed at your name,
Behold, that which is carried upon the head of the great worshipper of Christ <note>The "worshipper of Christ" refers to the Emperor himself, depicted in the poem's shape.</note>
Marks what must be done under his leadership;
And through a just throne, it is right for one who wishes to uphold the law
To do so; may the <term>Augustus</term> <note>A title for the Emperor signifying majesty and sacred authority.</note> cultivate the whole world by his nod.
For this benefit comes forth from such a great and turning pole,
That the world may know to pray for a helmet by the counsel of Caesar;
From here, he offers a nourishing crown of praise purely to the Augustus.
For divine virtue prepares the right hand with the best art,
And may your offering, O Jesus, grant a triumph; we all ask
Now for a nourishing one for the just man, so that justice may reign everywhere.
May he be clothed in flint and bound by a friendly circle,
While the breastplate <note>In the visual poem, the text forming the Emperor’s torso describes his spiritual "armor."</note> brings a pleasing protection thus prepared.
Let us always hope for a friend whom Christ piously
Protects in reality, whom no spear-thrower can strike; but let the thief
Or the enemy perish in that dire crime of audacity.
The defender of art shows that the firm law must be loved,
Adorned with beauty, he holds the draught of Caesar’s authority,
And may every omen be favorable, and the empire remain safe in the world.
Behold, the kingdoms of the Greeks give gifts through every age,
And the Persian gives as well, and so his side encompasses his offspring.
The nation and the people, a joyful progeny, piously grant a song;
It helps the one producing the Muse to remain; he knows how to love the shield
And hope, while the exile holds the scepters, as long as he gives the matter of faith 
Everywhere with a draught, until he drives away the ages from his art.
Those weapons which beautifully uphold the laws shall not be an elder of wickedness,
And he who settles the arrogance of the earth must be strengthened;
As long as he is firm, the Augustus remains and protects the sheepfold.
The world transforms when it prepares the bright tributes of Christ,
While, mindful of the right of worship, it equally grants the trophies it prepares,
Which carry this name everywhere; indeed, it thunders
From the mouth of the devoted, and urges the heart to be loved for a long time.
Let there be a trembling, for there is a good fame by divine gift;
From there, the world profits, the overflowing sea and the illicit things;
Thus he reaches the harbor, gives himself to the Cross, and follows Jesus.
For this has been given to you, O always chaste and pious
Caesar, in a grand vision; but you terrify the camps of the enemy,
And a deep fear puts the enemy's hopes to flight.

Having established the visual metaphor of the Emperor as a soldier of Christ, the text now transitions into a formal "Declaration" or "Exposition" (Declaratio), which serves as a prose commentary explaining the spiritual and political significance of the Emperor’s role as the defender of the faith and the rightful heir to the Roman and Frankish legacy.</meta>

# ON THE IMAGE OF THE EMPEROR <note>original: "De Imagine Cæsaris"</note>

This people, so devoted and grateful, asks your mind—so inclined toward mercy—to hear us at the commands of the Father. For I have recently composed a little book in praise of Christ, in both verse and prose, which I now, O <term>Commander</term> <note>original: "Induperator," an archaic Latin form of "Imperator," used here to evoke ancient Roman dignity</note>, offer to you, holy and willing. His image stands before this work, shown armed with faith, appearing as a victor everywhere.

->DECLARATION<-

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'O' featuring floral or scrollwork design, marking the beginning of the primary text block.</image-desc>

O Christ our Savior, King of kings and Lord of lords, who governs the world by Your own power, and reigning by eternal right, holds the incorruptible scepter over all things: You erased the many sins of our ancestors upon the Cross when You established the reins of justice for the human race, and granted Your faithful the ability to hope for a blessed life in heaven and to obtain it swiftly. Therefore, it is by the gift of Your most generous self and of Your most powerful Father that Your ineffable name—once terrible to all ages—is now worn upon the brow of this most pious prince with honest devotion, a name celebrated and venerated by all.

From this, it is also shown that by his authority and protection, the <term>Augustan Empire</term> <note>original: "Augustum imperium"; referring to the Roman imperial title "Augustus" adopted by the Carolingian rulers</note> is firmly held. Through just judgment, power is taken away from every greedy person and every enemy of the Christian religion, so that the whole world may be ruled by the nod of a religious prince. Indeed, the most ample distribution of his gifts proclaims this everywhere, stirring the peoples of many lands to the praise of the venerable Emperor, so that by common counsel they may all alike seek his protection.

This is what we, Your servants, O gentle Savior Christ, ask as suppliants: that through the banner of the holy Cross, Your most sacred virtue may imbue his right hand with divine skill and grant the triumph of justice everywhere. This Cross also clothes him in a breastplate of faith harder than <term>adamant</term> <note>A legendary stone of indestructible hardness, often identified with the diamond; here symbolizing unbreakable spiritual resolve</note>, which provides both the most fitting ornament and the strongest fortification.

Wherefore it is necessary that we, together with all the Christian people, desire the grace of his friendship. The Lord Christ so protects and guards him that no one plotting against him can harm him in any way, nor stain his most just fame with any crime. Instead, the almighty Defender and Helper of his good zeal and good will sets before us a model of constancy and true innocence to be imitated. It is God’s will that the most noble Caesar may find success in every act, and that his Empire remain safe on both land and sea.

For the nations of the Greeks bring most precious gifts to him; likewise do the kingdoms of the Persians. Other nations also frequent his side to protect both him and his offspring. Most especially, the people of **Germany** and the people of the **Franks** (from whom his noble lineage drew its origin) sing his praises, wishing him life and continuous prosperity. Even the exile, whoever wandered from his own home in former times, now hopes for a swift return by loving the Emperor's triumphs. By holding the scepter, he spreads the word of faith everywhere, until he purges his people from the ancient habit of sin. With Christ’s help, he will firmly uphold the laws of the Catholic faith, so that he does not hurl the arrows of the Word in vain; rather, let them be weapons powerful to God for every good work, and, strengthened by the faith of Christ, let them tame the insolence of the flesh. O how solid in faith and stable in the Christian religion he remains, who diligently guards the sheep committed to him at every hour, and strenuously demands the performance of the Lord’s service and divine worship from all who obey him.

<header>->DECLARATION.<-</header>

...seeks, while it shows that the banner of the heavenly King is to be venerated by all, and directs its teachers everywhere to preach the Gospel of Christ: so that they may soften the hard-hearted with their words and, with the help of divine grace, lead them to perceive the sweet fragrance of virtues: so that they may despise the luxuries of the world and, placing their hope in Christ, long to share in His sufferings. Behold, O most merciful and most holy Emperor, I offer you this present gift, being subject to you with all devotion: you who stand terrible to your adversaries, pursuing the backs of your enemies, yet are gentle to the devoted, mercifully granting pardon to those who have turned to you. Every race, every nation seeks to do your will; and we, your wretched servants, desire to approach your mercy with humble service and long to comply with its wishes in all things. For the little book which I composed some time ago in praise of the Holy Cross, in both prose and verse, I now humbly offer to your Serenity, praying that you—who are fittingly adorned with the shield of faith, the breastplate of justice, and the helmet of salvation—might deign to fortify us who serve as soldiers for Christ under your protection, and lead us, with the Lord’s help, to the harbor of eternal salvation for the increase of your rewards.

Furthermore, the present image of the most serene Emperor Louis <note>original: "Hludouici"</note> contains fifteen verses written in <term>dactylic tetrameter</term> <note>a rhythmic poetic meter consisting of four "feet" or beats per line</note> in this manner: **"Jesus Christ, may Your sign upon his head grant a nourishing helmet to the August one. May Your excellence make his right hand invincible, and may Your power, O Jesus, grant him triumph. May justice clothe the just man, and may the breastplate always protect Your beloved friend, which no enemy may strike down with a spear. But let the whole Empire of Caesar remain firm in its actions through every age. And so may the joyful offspring of his lineage succeed him and remain holding the scepter, as long as the ages hold their own laws and the solid orb of the earth remains; while Christ's name is remembered everywhere, and he preaches the word of the Lord of his own accord."**

In the circle that surrounds his head <note>referring to the halo in the illustration</note>, these two verses in <term>Adonic meter</term> <note>a short, melodic verse form often used in choruses</note> are contained: **"May You, O Christ, crown Louis."**

The Cross, indeed, which his right hand carries, holds these verses in <term>Asclepiadean meter</term> <note>a classical Greek and Latin lyric meter</note>: **"In Your Cross, O Christ, is true victory and salvation; You rule all things rightly."**

The shield, truly, which his left hand holds, is written in <term>elegiac meter</term> <note>a poetic form often used for inscriptions or dedications</note> in this manner: **"For the shield of faith drives away wicked weapons. This part protects the famous trophies of the August one. A devoted heart, relying on a divine gift, always puts the enemy camps to flight, remaining unharmed."**

<meta>This page serves as the formal prologue to the work, following the specific dedication to Emperor Louis the Pious. Here, the author, Hrabanus Maurus, explains his theological motivations and the symbolic purpose of the book, transitioning from the political dedication to the spiritual heart of the project: the praise of the Holy Cross.</meta>

### HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE.

<margin>16. Because of the likeness</margin>Divine law exhorts us to offer gifts to the Lord, and it excludes no one, but rather seeks a voluntary offering from all. This is as the Lord commanded Moses, saying: "Speak to the children of Israel, that they may bring me first-fruits <note>original: "primiticias"; referring to the biblical tradition of offering the first part of a harvest to God</note>; from every man who offers it willingly, you shall receive them." In this, no room is given for excuse, since a ready will is sought and no necessity is imposed, but it is left to each person’s own judgment. Therefore, reading these things myself and devoting my mind to them, I offered these "first-fruits" produced in praise of the Holy Cross. This Cross is the column of the celestial building, in which the house of Christ is constructed. I offer this to that internal Judge <note>God</note> who beholds me, not with a proud intention, but with humble devotion, wishing to contribute whatever I can by His grace to His praise. He, judging not by the appearance but by the heart, does not weigh the quantity of the gift, but the depth of the devotion.

Indeed, I do not think I can add any glory to the Holy Cross, which clarifies all things by its own brightness; rather, I preach its brightness and eternal majesty with whatever praises I can to my fellow servants. I do this so that, by reading it often and looking upon it diligently, we may constantly meditate on our redemption within it and give thanks unceasingly to our Redeemer. For though He lacked nothing and possessed an eternal kingdom together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, He "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant" <note>A reference to the biblical book of Philippians 2:7</note>, becoming obedient to the Father even unto death—specifically, death on a Cross. Once also, the Just died for our sins, the Unjust, so that He might offer us to God and make us a kingdom and priests to God the Father.

Therefore, I ask that whoever looks upon the text of this work should not immediately cast it aside in scorn because of the lowliness of the artist <note>The author, Hrabanus Maurus, here adopts a traditional tone of humility</note>. Instead, if they are willing and able, let them read it. By looking with the eye of sound faith and judging through the authority of the Divine Scriptures, let them attribute whatever they find to be spoken rightly and according to the universal faith to Him from whom all good comes. If, however, they find anything stated less correctly or thoughtlessly, let them attribute it more to my lack of skill than to malice; for I always desire the righteousness of the universal faith as much as I can and learn it eagerly, striving to keep its laws as much as heavenly grace allows.

And so, to anyone whom I seem to have erred, I humbly suggest that they do not delay in making my error known to me—either by voice if I am present, or by writing if I am absent. But if, because of the distance of the lands or some other impossibility, they can do neither of these, or if it is established that I have departed from this present life, I pray that they would plead with the most merciful Judge for my guilt. May He, from whom nothing of human infirmity is hidden, dissolve the chains of my error and grant me pardon for my sins by the grace of His forgiveness. I hope to do the same as long as I live in this body—that is, to pour out prayers daily for my errors and those of others, so that the Pious One may, by His grace, both correct those who wander and grant indulgence to those who have erred.

For the rest, I advise the reader to maintain the order of this writing and not neglect to preserve the figures <note>term: "figuras"; refers to the "carmina figurata" or picture-poems where words are arranged to form images</note> made within it, lest the value of the work be lost and the utility of the reading be diminished. To make this easier, I have taken care to explain the logic of each figure in a prose style on the following page, subjoining its explanation together with the verses that are written within it. If it moves anyone to wonder why, since I decided to write verses of the same number for each page, I have interspersed certain marks or points among them, let them know that I have done this not so much by necessity as by choice, so that the sense and the speech in them might be clearer. I have not done this commonly or frequently, nor without authority...

<summary>Hrabanus Maurus introduces his work as a spiritual offering ("first-fruits") dedicated to the Holy Cross, emphasizing that the project is born of devotion rather than a desire for artistic glory. He provides instructions for readers to respect the complex visual and poetic structure of the book and asks for charitable correction of any errors.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical and spiritual introduction to the work. The text begins mid-sentence, concluding a thought on the "authority of the ancestors" before explaining the specific orthographic and poetic rules the author followed to create his complex grid poems. This provides essential context for why the letters are arranged in such a specific, mathematical way.</meta>

->### PROLOGUE.<-

...with the authority of our ancestors. For I do not recall having placed points <note>original: "punctos"; referring to punctuation marks or decorative dots used to separate words or sections in the grid</note> anywhere within these verses, except where the word *quae* was a pronoun, or *que* was a conjunction, or where *us* was the final syllable of a word. This is the same method that Porphyrius <note>Publius Optatianus Porphyrius (4th century AD), a poet famous for "carmina figurata" or pattern poems, which served as the model for this work</note> followed. It was according to his example that I learned how to space out the letters, and in some places, I used a small line <note>a macron or overline</note> above a preceding vowel to represent the letter *m*. I also employed *synaloepha* <term>synaloepha: the blending of two vowels into one syllable, common in classical poetry</term> in appropriate places within the writing, which Titus Lucretius <note>the Roman poet and philosopher, author of *On the Nature of Things*</note> is often found to have done. I also occasionally suppressed the letter *u* when placed between *q* and another vowel; similarly, it is established that *h* is not a true letter but merely a mark of breathing <note>original: "nota aspirationis"</note>.

If, however, a great deal of power is granted to all poets—who observe only the type of meter and the rules of poetic feet—to use *metaplasms* <term>metaplasms: the intentional alteration of a word's spelling or sound to fit a poetic meter</term>, figures, tropes, and all the other devices granted so abundantly to poets by the grammarians, then why should it not be granted to me? I have taken care to observe not only the correct types of meter and legitimate poetic feet, but also the sequence and number of letters, and the precise measurement of the visual figures.

Above all, I beseech everyone who reads this work: do not let the stings of envy provoke you against me. Do not strive to tear down my labor. While I have struggled to prepare this work for the praise of God, let no one seek to destroy it, for in doing so he harms himself more than he harms me. If he cannot bear to hear the glory of the Holy Cross through my humble efforts, he risks offending the Crucified King and may fail to attain the grace of redemption <note>original: "redemptionis"</note> which is found in the Cross.

<summary>Hrabanus Maurus explains the technical rules of his poetry, such as his use of punctuation and vowel elision, citing classical authorities like Porphyrius and Lucretius to justify his complex "word-grid" format. He concludes with a stern warning to critics, framing his work as a devotional act for the praise of God and the Holy Cross.</summary>

->### PREFACE.<-

<image-desc>A carmen quadratum (square poem) where the text is meticulously arranged in a perfect grid of 36 rows by 35 columns of letters, enclosed in a rectangular frame. Certain letters are rubricated (printed in red ink), forming a visual and symbolic structure within the block of text. **M**use, now daring through studies to speak of the divinity, **n**ow
Our [soul] desires equally in song and in discourse
Of the gifts of the highest Father, which He gave generously to the world,
And of the holy trophies of the King enthroned on high at once.
Which is the holy Cross, full of the power of the Crucified One,
A venerable lineage fit for all good destinies.
This, I, born of poor stock and lacking in wealth of speech,
**T**empted here, a servant, to provide a source, and from this I shall arise.
Nor do my deeds purify me, so that I should believe myself worthy
Of such a gift, nor that I am thus upright in mind.
But for me, God’s generous goodness is the greatest hope of my prayer,
It is the praise which, gladdening me, made me ready.
He did not despise the widow's meager mite, <note>original: "rara minuta"; referring to the biblical story of the widow's mite in Luke 21:1-4, where a small gift given in faith outweighs the large sums of the wealthy.</note>
But the all-holding Judge Himself accepted it with approval.
And He, ruling the world, who alone and as one creates
All lovely and good things, has blessed this work with the praise of love.
For indeed it is a commandment and by the Law required for everyone
That they should give fitting gifts to the honorable temples of God.
Some gave silver, **p**art gave bright gifts of gold,
Some bestowed gems, and some gave dyed fabrics.
Certain ones gave wood and oil and precious pigments,
And everywhere the great house shows many shining thing**s**.
Yet others had brought even the hair of goats,
Nor were they despised for bringing these gifts to God.
Therefore I ask, though you be rich in coin,
Do not wish to despise these humble things I bring.
Though one may bring immense treasures in great
Processions to fill the temples of God,
**H**ere I am not moved, nor **c**onfounded by an impious look,**u**
**S**o rejoicing, I **s**urvey his gifts increase for him.
**I** do not wish that he should have my gifts for himself,
**S**o rather let him make these gifts, of whatever sort, for God.
**E**xprobrated <term>exprobrated: rebuked or reproached</term> by God is he who despises the humble person,
**C**oncerning whose offspring this man is, and to whom every man belongs.
**E**n! <note>original: "En"; a Latin exclamation meaning "Behold!" or "Look!"</note> As much as I give, Jesus the Lover gives to me;
May all His deeds be holy here, and may He take everything tha**t**.

# ### First Figure. Concerning the image of Christ stretching out his arms in the manner of a Cross, and concerning his names pertaining to either his divine or human nature.

->**THE POEM WITHIN THE GRID**<-

<note>This page is a masterpiece of Carolingian "technopaegnia" (artistic wordplay). The main text is a grid of letters that can be read horizontally as a poem. However, certain letters are highlighted in red to form a picture of Christ. These highlighted letters form additional, hidden "interwoven verses" that describe the parts of the body they form (the halo, the hands, etc.).</note>

This offspring of the Lord and the Lord of lords is everywhere here.
With hands outstretched in the manner of one forming the Cross, behold, he is to be held.
He teaches that this one King justifies and cherishes the flock.
And thus in this manner they weary; Jesus Christ <note>original: "IHS XPS"; a common medieval abbreviation for the Greek "Iesous Christos."</note> sanctifies his members by this feast.
They rightly prove the people by law, and he responds as a parent.
For here the scripture of the Acts of the Apostles records the height of Jesus.
And I prove that the King of the Jews, by nodding, is the end of evils.
Who killed the King, he lives and remains powerfully.
He broke the weapons—alas!—completing the holy teachings by his struggle.
First he knows the evils, so that every man might flee from here.
<insert>Eternal</insert> Lord, the Author remains silent, the holy one is here in the world.
<insert>To be handed over</insert> All things befit the Highest, because we are redeemed by his blood.
<insert>The right hand</insert> snatched the prey; the holy one proves it from the deep.
<insert>On the Cross</insert> thus placed, God had given the crown from the heavenly citadel.
Here God is the Beginning, the Emmanuel, and the Origin of the end.
The Light and Image of the Father, the Splendor, Glory, and Christ.
Consubstantial <note>original: "homoousion"; a Greek term meaning "of the same substance," used to define Christ's equality with God the Father.</note> with the Father, the Word, Light from Light.
Equal to the Lord's hand, or the Power, Leader, and Prophet.
Whom we confess as the Only-begotten and truly the First-born.
The Nazarene, who is a stumbling block and a scandal to the wicked.
The Angel <note>original: "angelus"; here used in the ancient sense of "Messenger" or the "Angel of Great Counsel."</note> and the Stone, he climbs from here as the Door to the world.
Truth is clothed in a garment, which Christ teaches in his dogma.
He indicates and explains the law; this small garment also
signifies here what is covered in the rare letters.

<meta>This page continues the detailed theological explanation of the "First Figure" of Christ on the Cross. Following the poetic titles introduced on Leaf 11, the author now provides a prose commentary on the physical posture of the figure and a philological breakdown of Christ's various names in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin.</meta>

# EXPLANATION.

The Victim, since he is well-born from the Father without anything falling away;
Who felt losses and the wooden Cross, who is before all things,
Who was brought forth before all the starry stars and before the morning star <note>original: "luciferum"; here referring to the dawn star rather than the fallen angel.</note>.
He was born here from a Virgin mother, in a specific point in time,
And so that he might save man, he went here to the altar of the Cross,
He who is the eternal sower, Christ blessed forever.

---

Behold the Image of the Savior: by the position of his limbs, he consecrates for us the most healthful, sweetest, and most loving form of the Holy Cross. He does this so that we, believing in his name and obeying his commands, may have hope of eternal life through his passion. Whenever we look upon the Cross, let us remember him who suffered on it for us to snatch us from the power of darkness—swallowing up death so that we might be made heirs of eternal life. He has set out for heaven, with Angels and powers and virtues subject to him. Let us also reflect that we were not redeemed with corruptible silver or gold from the empty way of life inherited from our fathers, but by the precious blood of Christ, who is like a lamb without blemish and spotless. We are called to be holy and spotless in his sight in love, so that through these things we might become sharers of the divine nature, fleeing the corruption of worldly desire.

There are, in fact, names of our Redeemer contained in the verses on this very page—some derived from the substance of his divinity, others assumed from the arrangement of his taken-up humanity. These were chosen to show that the same mediator between God and men is both consubstantial <term>consubstantial: of the same essence or "stuff."</term> and coequal to the Father in his Godhead, and of the same nature and likeness as his mother in the humanity he assumed. This is because he perfectly took up our entire nature, yet remained without sin. The quality of these names can easily be understood through the reasoning woven below, determining whether they belong to his divine or his human nature.

For **Christ** <note>original: "Christus"</note> is named from the Greek word for "anointing" <note>original: "chrismate"</note>. In the Old Testament, priests and kings among the Jews were anointed with sacred oil; therefore, he is called "Christ" (the Anointed One) because he is both King and Priest. He was anointed not with physical oil, but with the "oil of gladness"—that is, the Holy Spirit—above all his companions. In Hebrew, **Christ** is called **Messiah**.

**Jesus** <note>original: "Hiesus"</note> is the Hebrew name which is **Soter** in Greek; in Latin, it is interpreted as **Salutory** or **Savior**, because he came bringing health and salvation to all nations.

**Emmanuel**, from Hebrew into Latin, means **God with us**; specifically, that God, born of a virgin, appeared to men in mortal flesh.

He is called **God** <note>original: "Deus"</note> because of his unified substance with the Father. He is called **Lord** <note>original: "Dominus"</note> because all of creation serves him. He is **God and Man** because he is both the Word and the Flesh.

He is called the **Only-begotten** <note>original: "Vnigenitus"</note> through the excellence of his divinity, because he is without brothers. Yet he is the **First-born** <note>original: "Primogenitus"</note> through his taking on of humanity, in which, through the adoption of grace, he deigned to have brothers for whom he would be the first-born.

He is called **Homousion** <note>original: "Homousion"; from the Greek "homoousios."</note> with the Father because of the unity of their substance; for substance or essence in Greek is called **Ousia** <note>original: "ysia"</note>. **Omoynum** <note>original: "Omoynum"; likely a medieval rendering of "homo-unon," signifying "same-one."</note> follows this, for the two joined together sound as "one substance."

He is the **Beginning** <note>original: "Principium"</note> because all things are from him and nothing exists before him. He is the **End** <note>original: "Finis"</note> because he deigned to be born humbly in the flesh and to die at the end of the ages; or because we refer everything we do back to him, and once we have reached him, we have nothing further to seek. He is the **Mouth of God** <note>original: "Os Dei"</note> because he is His Word.
