<meta>This page continues the catalog of Christ’s names and attributes begun on the previous leaf. It transitions from purely theological and substance-based names to metaphorical titles drawn from nature and physical objects, eventually leading into a technical description of how these words are physically arranged on the "First Figure" (the image of Christ on the Cross).</meta>

<page-num>LEAF III.</page-num>
<header># BOOK ONE.</header>

For just as we often say "this or that tongue" to refer to the words produced by the tongue, so the "mouth" is used to represent the Word of God, because it is the custom for words to be formed by the mouth. He is called the **Word**, however, because through him the Father created or commanded all things. **Truth**, because he does not deceive, but grants what he promises. **Life**, because he gives life to all. He is called the **Image** because of his equal likeness to the Father. **Figure**, because by taking on the form of a servant, through the likeness of his works and virtues, he designated within himself the image and immense greatness of the Father. He is the **Hand of God**, because all things were made through him. Hence also the **Right Hand**, because of the effect of the work of the entire creation which was formed through him. **Arm**, because all things are held together by him. **Power** <note>original: "Virtus"</note>, because he possesses all the Father's authority in himself and is capable of all things. **Wisdom**, because he reveals the mysteries of knowledge and the secrets of wisdom. **Splendor**, because he makes things manifest. **Brightness** <note>original: "Lumen"</note>, because he illuminates. **Light** <note>original: "Lux"</note>, because he directs the eyes of the heart toward contemplating virtue. **Sun**, because he is the enlightener. **The Rising** <note>original: "Oriens"; often translated as "Dayspring" or "East"</note>, because he is the source of light and because he makes us rise to eternal life. **Fountain**, because he is the origin of things, or because he satisfies the thirsty. He is also **Alpha and Omega**, because he is the beginning and the end. **Paraclete**, that is, the **Advocate**, because he intercedes for us with the Father and takes care to remove our faults. **Bridegroom**, because descending from heaven he joined himself to the Church, so that two might be in one flesh. He is called **Angel** <note>original: "Angelus", meaning "messenger"</note> because of the announcement of his Father's and his own will; thus he is read in the Prophet as the "Angel of Great Counsel," even while being the God and Lord of Angels. He is called **Sent**, because the Word was made flesh. He is called **Man**, because he was incarnated. **Mediator**, because he led us from death to life. **Prophet**, because he revealed the future. **Priest**, because he offered himself as a sacrifice for us. **Shepherd**, because he is the guardian. **Teacher**, because he is the one who shows the way. He is **Nazarene** from his place of origin. **Nazarean** from his merit, that is, "holy" or "clean," because he committed no sin.

Indeed, Christ even draws titles from other lower things to himself so that he may be more easily understood. He is called **Bread** because he is flesh. **Vine**, because we are redeemed by his blood. **Flower**, because he is the chosen one. **Way**, because through him we go to God. **Door**, because through him we enter into God's presence. **Mountain**, because he is strong. **Rock**, because he is the firmness of believers. **Cornerstone**, because he joins two walls from different directions—that is, from the circumcision and the uncircumcision <note>referring to the joining of Jewish and Gentile believers</note>—into one building of the Church; or because he makes peace between Angels and men. **Stone of offense**, because the unbelieving stumbled against him when he came in humility, and he became a **Rock of scandal**. He is called the **Foundation** because faith is founded on him, or because the catholic <note>universal</note> Church is built upon him. He is called **Lamb** for his innocence. **Sheep** for his gentleness. **Ram** for his leadership. **Kid** <note>original: "Haedus"; a young goat</note> for the likeness of sinful flesh. **Calf**, because he was sacrificed for us. **Lion** for his kingdom and strength. **Serpent** for death and wisdom. Also **Worm**, because he rose again <note>Medieval theologians often used the "worm" to symbolize the Resurrection or the Virgin Birth, as worms were thought to be born from the earth without seed</note>. **Eagle**, because after the resurrection he returned to the stars. Nor is it strange if he is represented by lowly symbols; for while he is the Son co-eternal with the Father before the ages, not scorning the lowliness of our nature, he was born in time as the Son of Man. For the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.

There are, therefore, five verses which are written surrounding the outward shape of the human body in a line. The first of these begins from the middle finger of the right hand, and so passes to the index finger, then raising itself to the thumb and ascending through the right arm, it ends at the crown of the head. It is as follows: **The right hand of the highest God, Jesus, created all things.** The second verse, descending from the head in a similar way, ends in the middle finger of the left hand: **Christ will loosen...**

<meta>This page provides a "Declaratio" (Explanation) of the image of Christ on the Cross, specifically interpreting the names and titles woven into the visual poem. It follows the list of attributes from the previous leaf, concluding the entry on the "Mouth of God" at the end of this section.</meta>

# EXPLANATION.

> ->The Victim, when spoken well of by the Father without failing:<-
> ->Who felt the wooden pains, who is before all things,<-
> ->Who was brought forth before all the starry heavens and the morning star.<-
> ->He was born here of a Virgin mother in a narrow point of time,<-
> ->And to save mankind, he went here to the altar of the Cross,<-
> ->Who is the eternal sower, Christ blessed forever.<-

Behold the Image of the Savior: by the position of his limbs, he consecrates for us the most healthful, sweet, and loving form of the holy Cross. This is so that we, believing in his name and obeying his commands, may have the hope of eternal life through his passion. Whenever we look upon the Cross, let us remember him who suffered upon it for us, to rescue us from the power of darkness—swallowing up death so that we might be made heirs of eternal life. He has gone into heaven with Angels, authorities, and powers made subject to him. Let us also reflect that we were redeemed from the empty way of life inherited from our fathers, not with corruptible silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot. Thus, we may be holy and immaculate in his sight in love, and through these things, we may become partakers of the divine nature, fleeing the corruption of desire that is in the world.

Indeed, on this very page, the names of our Redeemer are contained within the verses. Some of these names are drawn from the substance of his divinity, while others are taken from the administration <note>original: "dispensatione"</note> of his assumed humanity. This was done to show that the same mediator between God and men is both consubstantial and co-equal to the Father in his Godhead, and connatural and similar to his mother in his assumed humanity; for he perfectly took on our entire nature, yet without sin. The quality of these names can easily be understood through the reasoning woven below, whether they pertain to his divine or human nature.

For **Christ** <note>original: "Christus"</note> is named from the Greek word for "anointing" <note>original: "chrismate"</note>, which means "the Anointed One." In the Old Testament, priests and kings among the Jews were anointed with sacred oil. Therefore, he is called Christ because he is both King and Priest. He was not anointed with material oil, but with the "oil of gladness"—that is, the Holy Spirit—above all his companions.

In Hebrew, however, Christ is called **Messiah**. **Jesus** <note>original: "Hiesus"</note> is Hebrew, which in Greek is **Soter**; in Latin, it is interpreted as **Salutaris** or **Salvator** <note>meaning "the one who brings health or safety"</note>, because he came as the bringer of salvation to all nations. **Emmanuel**, from the Hebrew into Latin, means "God with us"—specifically because God, born of a virgin, appeared to men in mortal flesh.

He is called **God** <note>original: "Deus"</note> because of his shared substance with the Father. He is called **Lord** <note>original: "Dominus"</note> because creation serves him. He is **God and Man** because he is both the Word and the flesh. He is called the **Only-begotten** through the excellence of his divinity, for he is without brothers in that nature. He is called the **First-born** <note>original: "Primogenitus"</note> through his taking on of humanity, in which, through the adoption of grace, he deigned to have brothers to whom he would be the first-born.

He is called **Homousion** <note>original: "Homousion"; a technical term from the Council of Nicaea meaning "of the same substance"</note> with the Father because of the unity of their substance. For "substance" or "essence" is called **ousia** <note>original: "vsia"</note> in Greek. **Homousion** <note>original: "Omoysion"</note> when joined together sounds like "one substance." He is the **Beginning** <note>original: "Principium"</note> because all things are from him, and because nothing exists before him. He is the **End** <note>original: "Finis"</note> because he deigned to be born humbly in the flesh and to die at the end of the ages—or because whatever we do, we refer back to him, and once we have reached him, we have nothing further to seek. He is the **Mouth of God**, because he is God's Word.

<page-num>LEAF III.</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

For just as we often say "this or that tongue" to refer to the words spoken by the tongue, so the **Mouth** <note>original: "os"</note> is used to represent the Word of God, because it is the custom for words to be formed by the mouth. He is called the **Word**, however, because through him the Father created or commanded all things. He is **Truth**, because he does not deceive but grants what he promises. He is **Life**, because he gives life to all. He is called the **Image** <note>original: "Imago"</note> because of his equal likeness to the Father. He is the **Figure** <note>original: "Figura"</note> because, by taking on the form of a servant, he revealed the image and immense greatness of the Father within himself through the likeness of his works and virtues. He is the **Hand of God**, because all things were made through him. From this, he is also the **Right Hand**, due to the effect of the work of the entire creation which was formed by him. He is the **Arm**, because all things are held together by him. He is **Virtue** <note>or Power; original: "Virtus"</note>, because he holds all the Father's power within himself and can do all things. He is **Wisdom**, because he himself reveals the mysteries of knowledge and the secrets of wisdom. He is **Splendor**, because he makes things manifest. He is **Radiance**, because he illuminates. He is **Light**, because he directs the eyes of the heart toward contemplating virtue. He is the **Sun**, because he is the enlightener. He is the **Rising Sun** <note>original: "Oriens"</note>, because he is the source of light and because he makes us rise to eternal life. He is the **Fountain**, because he is the origin of things, or because he satisfies those who thirst. He is also the **A and Ω** <note>Alpha and Omega</note>, for he is the beginning and the end. He is the **Paraclete**—that is, the **Advocate**—because he intercedes for us with the Father and takes care to remove our faults. He is the **Bridegroom**, because descending from heaven he joined himself to the Church, so that two might be in one flesh. He is called **Angel** <note>or Messenger</note> because of the announcement of his Father's and his own will; hence, we read in the Prophet of the "Angel of Great Counsel," though he is the God and Lord of Angels. He is called **Sent**, because the Word was made flesh. He is called **Man**, because he was incarnated. He is the **Mediator**, because he led us from death to life. He is the **Prophet**, because he revealed future things. He is the **Priest**, because he offered himself as a victim for us. He is the **Shepherd**, because he is the guardian. He is the **Teacher**, because he is the one who shows the way. He is **Nazarene** from his location, but **Nazarean** <note>original: "Nazareus"</note> from his merit—that is, holy or clean—because he committed no sin.

Indeed, Christ also draws the names of other lower things to himself so that he may be more easily understood. He is called **Bread**, because he is flesh. He is the **Vine**, because we have been redeemed by his blood. He is the **Flower**, because he is the chosen one. He is the **Way**, because through him we go to God. He is the **Door**, because through him we enter to God. He is the **Mountain**, because he is strong. He is the **Rock**, because he is the firmness of those who believe. He is the **Cornerstone**, because he joins two walls from different directions—that is, from the circumcision and the uncircumcision <note>referring to Jews and Gentiles</note>—into the single structure of the Church; or because he makes peace between Angels and men. He is the **Stone of Stumbling**, because when he came in humility, the unbelieving stumbled against him, and he became a "rock of offense." He is called the **Foundation**, because faith is founded upon him, or because the Catholic Church is constructed upon him. He is called the **Lamb**, because of his innocence. He is the **Sheep**, because of his gentleness. He is the **Ram**, because of his leadership. He is the **Goat**, because of the likeness of his sinful flesh. He is the **Calf**, because he was sacrificed for us. He is the **Lion**, for his kingdom and strength. He is the **Serpent**, for death and wisdom. He is likewise the **Worm**, because he rose again. He is the **Eagle**, because after his resurrection he returned to the stars. It is no wonder if he is represented by humble symbols: for while he is the Son co-eternal with the Father before the ages, he did not despise the lowliness of our nature, but was born in time as the Son of Man. "For the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us."

There are, therefore, five verses which are written in a line surrounding the outer shape of the human body. The first of these begins at the middle finger of the right hand, and so passes to the index finger, then raising itself to the thumb and ascending through the right arm, it ends at the crown of the head. That verse is this: **"The Right Hand of the highest God, Jesus, created all things."** The second, descending from the head in a similar way, ends at the middle finger of the left hand; it is this: **"Christ will release..."**

<page-num>115</page-num>
<header>DECLARATION.</header>

...blood owed to the world. The third verse begins from the fourth finger of the right hand—which is called the **ring finger** <note>original: "medicus," the "medical finger," so called in antiquity because it was believed a vein ran from it directly to the heart</note>—and leading beneath the right arm through the **little finger** <note>original: "auricularem," the "ear-finger," used for scratching the ear</note>, it descends on the right side as far as the middle of the belly, and ends from the right knee at the base of the foot. Thus: *Placed thus on the Cross, loosening the bonds of the tyrant.* The fourth, beginning on the outer base of the right foot and ascending between the legs, reaches as far as the outer base of the left foot. Thus: *The eternal Lord led the blessed to the stars.* Likewise, the fifth, ascending from the outer base of the left foot to the knees, and from the middle of the belly through the side and left arm, reaches the ring finger. Thus: *And from his high citadel, God gave the crown of salvation.*

On the garment surrounding the thighs, there are these two **elegiac** <note>a classical poetic meter consisting of alternating lines of dactylic hexameter and pentameter</note> verses:
*He who contains the stars is covered here by a small garment, and he encloses the earth everywhere within his palm.*

Upon the hair of his head, it is written: *This is the King of Justice.* On the face and chin, the nipples and the navel, this is contained: *A just order for God.* On the crown surrounding the head: **King of kings and Lord of lords** <note>original: "Rex regum & Dominus dominorum"</note>. For on the cross which is placed next to his head, there are three letters—that is, **A, M, and Ω** <note>Alpha, Mu, and Omega</note>—which signifies the **beginning, the middle, and the end** <note>original: "initium & medium & finis"</note>, meaning that all things are encompassed by him.

## II. Figure. Concerning the figure of the Cross, which is written within a square, and shows that it encompasses all things.

<note>This page features a "pattern poem," a sophisticated form of medieval art where the text is arranged in a perfect grid. The letters highlighted in red (rubricated) in the original manuscript form the shape of a cross and a border. This visual "figure" contains its own hidden message, while the background text provides a longer hymn. Hrabanus Maurus designed these to show that the Cross is the underlying structure of the entire universe.</note>

## BOOK ONE

<note>This poem is an acrostic. If you read the first letter of every line downward, it spells out the Latin phrase: **O CRVC DVC MISERO LATO QVE REDEMPTIO MVNDO**, which translates to: "O Cross, lead the redemption for the wretched and the wide world." In the translation below, these starting letters are highlighted to preserve this hidden message.</note>

**O** Cross, who excels in all and rules in the highest heaven,
**C**elestial peoples and bright souls you receive there in the
**R**egions of the sky to be ruled; the nod and the fire of the Crucified One
**V**ery much gives you life everywhere, as you are reddened with the blood
**C**hrist shed, wherefore from the King you shall be called "Leader." <note>original: "dux"</note>
**D**evotedly seeking things human and divine through the touch
**V**ouchsafed by the One on the high throne; in the honor of praise
**C**hrist-worshippers you join together: and living with a sacred word,
**M**anifold praises you give forth from the summit of heaven.
**I**n the songs which the world offers on earth, and the exiled
**S**anctified world—the wind, the sea, and here the sun—
**E**xalts you, rejoicing with the mountains; the dry
**R**ural fields sing, and by your motion you grant songs to the stars.
**O**rient and Occident, the north wind, the south, and the breeze:
**L**et you hold the joy of the kingdom, that light may see light,
**A**nd open the heights of heaven, marking the divine power there,
**T**hrough the dispensing of God’s great gifts—He who made all things.
**O** Cross, who through Christ's flesh are blessed in triumph?
**Q**uite so many gifts the Creator of all gave to you out of love:
**V**erily, God Himself prepared for you by the gift of the Life-Giver,
**E**xtolling you well, so that the foul,
**R**ancid deceiver, the leader of the wicked, might not speak harshly—
**E**ven he who mocked the prey rescued from the light of the upper air,
**D**esiring to punish it by death, having been thrust down here for so long.
**E**nter, pious Cross of the Lord! What pious muse is able to
**M**agnify you so greatly, or to speak your praise:
**P**ure and beautiful you shine in worship, glory surrounds you.
**T**he dire yew tree flees, the reed and the pine
**I**ncline humble to your honor: and cedars, myrrh, and honey-scents
**O**ffer their fragrance—nard, myrrh, and cypress,
**M**astic, incense, stacte, amomum, balsam, and bdellium. <note>The poet lists these aromatic plants and resins to show that all of nature, even the most precious scents, bows in worship to the Cross.</note>
**V**anquished by your majesty, they bring their vows to you.
**N**oble though your name sounds harsh, you are greater in virtue; to the pious
**D**eliver this reward, when they go before the tribunal of Christ:
**O** Cross, who allowed the people to go free from broken Avernus. <note>original: "auerno" - A classical name for the entrance to the underworld, used by medieval writers to refer to Hell.</note>

<meta>This page provides the "Declaratio" (Declaration or Explanation) for the visual poem on the previous page. ### DECLARATION

But this figure proclaims that the Cross of Christ embraces all things in its four corners <note>original: "quatuor cornibus," literally "four horns," referring to the four points of the cross-shape</note>, whether they are in the heavens, on the earth, or under the earth—namely, all things visible and invisible, living and non-living. For the four corners of the Cross signify the four places in which rational creatures dwell: the celestial, the terrestrial, the infernal, and the supra-celestial. Regarding three of these, the Apostle Paul speaks when he says: *that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth.* We have Paul's testimony for these three; let us look for the fourth: *Praise the Lord, you heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord.* Thus, some things are called "celestial" and others "supra-celestial" <note>The author is arguing that the Cross reaches even higher than the stars, into the "waters above the heavens" mentioned in Genesis and the Psalms.</note>. 

Furthermore, there are four species of all creation in which every creature exists: <term>to be</term> <note>original: "esse," simple existence</note>, <term>to live</term> <note>original: "viuere," biological life</note>, <term>to feel</term> <note>original: "sentire," sensory perception</note>, and <term>to understand</term> <note>original: "intelligere," rational thought</note>. 
For some things merely "are," but they neither live, nor feel, nor discern—such as stones. Others "are" and "live," but they neither feel nor discern—such as shrubs and all the sprouts of the earth. Still others "are, live, and feel," but do not discern—such as the brute animals, which have the power of feeling but lack the underlying reason for understanding. Finally, there are those who "are, live, feel, and discern"—such as angels and humans, who subsist in their essence, live by their life, feel by their senses, and discern by their intellect.

There are also four affections of the soul itself, which living beings use for either good or evil. The ancients discovered these with great subtlety, and later generations accepted their findings as proven: namely, <term>to fear</term> and <term>to grieve</term>, <term>to desire</term> and <term>to rejoice</term>. If these are ordered and protected by the defense of the Holy Cross, they are proven to be life-giving in religious men, although the foolishness of certain "wise men" of this world <note>Likely a reference to Stoic philosophers, who argued that emotions were "diseases" of the soul to be eliminated.</note> considered them to be vices. If that were so, and if only sinners or the lost could possess them, they could not rightly be called "affections" (feelings), but rather "diseases." 

But since such movements of the soul are found in the holy Apostles and Prophets, who would be so foolish as to believe these affections are vices? Through them, those who resisted vices more than other men pleased God. Thus, the Apostle Paul speaks of fear: *I fear, however, that just as the serpent seduced Eve by his craftiness, so your senses might be corrupted from the charity that is in Christ.* He says of desire with confidence: *I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.* Regarding sadness—which others call grief—this same teacher of the Gentiles says: *For I have great sadness and continuous grief in my heart for my brothers, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh.* Writing to the Romans, he also says: *I rejoice in you, but I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil.* 

The Prophet David also says of fear: *The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever.* Likewise, he says: *Fear the Lord, all you His saints.* Regarding sadness, he says: *I was saddened in my exercise.* Of longing, he says: *My soul has longed to desire Your justifications at all times,* and *I have longed for Your salvation, O Lord.* Regarding joy, the same Psalmist, exhorting the saints of God, says: *Be glad in the Lord and exult, you righteous; rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord.* Therefore, anyone who wishes to rebuke this fear or grief, this desire or joy, rebukes the Apostle and the Prophet themselves. For through such affections, they not only pleased God, but they also exhorted others to do the same; and they blamed those who were devoid of these as being "without affection" among the criminal. Therefore, we do not sin by having these affections, but by using them poorly; for the proper nature of human affections [belongs] to man...

<meta>catchword: ...of man</meta>

# BOOK ONE. FOLIO VI.

of man indicates the creator: but quality signifies the good and evil will. Thus, the movements which are the emotions in all people become virtues in those who use them well, and in those who use them poorly, they become passions or disturbances, or as some prefer to call them, <term>infirmities</term> <note>original: "aegritudines," referring to spiritual or psychological sickness</note>. He uses these emotions well who seeks to do not his own will, but the will of God, so that he no longer lives for himself, but for Him who redeemed him through the shedding of His blood on the cross. Such a person can say with the Apostle: *For I through the law am dead to the law, that I might live unto God: I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ lives in me. And the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.* <note>Galatians 2:19-20</note> All these things, therefore, are fitting to the holy Cross, because in it Christ, the creator of all, has suffered. For the passion of Christ sustains heaven, governs the world, and pierces through the underworld. In it, the Angels are confirmed, the peoples are redeemed, the enemies are crushed, existing things are stabilized, living things are animated, sensing things are preserved, and thinking things are enlightened. 

From this, **fear**—drawn from the threat of punishment—sets the faithful free; **sorrow**, when it is healthy, cleanses the penitent from their sins; **desire** for the good germinates the fruits of the virtues; and **joy** gladdens those who trust in the hope of life. Indeed, the Author of all things foresaw this holy <term>machine</term> <note>original: "machinam," used here to mean a complex, divine structure or framework</note> for himself; He willed it to be constructed so that in it He might restore and unite all things through Jesus Christ our Lord. 

There are also two verses written upon the Cross itself, of which the first is: 
*O Cross, who are dedicated to the famous trophy of the Highest:* 
descending from the top to the bottom. 
The other is: 
*O Cross, who are the flesh of Christ blessed in triumph:* 
stretching from the right to the left of the cross. 

There are also four verses in the <term>quadrangle</term> <note>original: "tetragono," referring to the square border surrounding the cross</note> around the cross, of which the first, which is above the cross, is this: 
*O Cross, who excel above all and rule in heaven.* <note>original: "olympo," using the classical term Olympus to refer to the Christian heaven</note> 
The one below is this: 
*O Cross, who allowed the people to go out from broken hell.* <note>original: "auerno," using the classical term Avernus for the underworld</note> 
The one placed on the right, that is, in the <term>acrostic</term> <note>original: "anachrosticide," referring to the letters at the beginning of the lines</note>, is this: 
*O Cross, leader to the wretched and redemption to the wide world.* 
And the one on the left, that is, in the <term>telestic</term> <note>original: "telesticide," referring to the letters at the ends of the lines</note>, is this: 
*O Cross, banner for the holy and pious security for the age.* 

It should be noted that we have placed the letter **O**, which has the likeness of a circle, in the four corners of the quadrangle and in the four points of the cross, as well as in the center of the cross. This was done to show that the holy Cross binds all things together by its power, and joins those things which are above and those which are below in the veneration of Christ.

# DECLARATION.

But this figure proclaims that the Cross of Christ encompasses all things in its four **corners (horns)** <note>original: "quatuor cornibus," referring to the four points or extremities of the cross</note>, whether they are in the heavens, on the earth, or under the earth—all things, that is, visible and invisible, living and non-living. This is because the four corners of the Cross signify the four places where rational creatures dwell: the celestial, the terrestrial, the infernal, and the super-celestial <note>literally "above the heavens"</note>. Of these, the Apostle Paul also speaks:
> so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. <note>Philippians 2:10</note>

From Paul's testimony, we see three of these; let us look for the fourth.
> Praise the Lord, heaven of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord. <note>Psalm 148:4</note>

Again, some things are called celestial and others super-celestial. Alternatively, these signify the four categories of all creation—that is, **being**, **living**, **sensing**, and **understanding**—in which every creature exists. For some things only *exist*, but they do not live, nor feel, nor discern; such are stones. Others both *exist* and *live*, but they do not feel or discern; such are shrubs and all the sprouts of the earth. Still others *exist, live, and feel*, but they do not discern; such are the brute animals, which have the power of feeling, but lack the underlying reason for understanding. Finally, there are those that *exist, live, feel, and discern*, such as angels and humans, who exist in their essence, live their lives, feel through their senses, and discern through their intellect.

There are also four **affections** <note>emotions or states of being</note> of the soul itself, which living beings use for either good or evil. The ancients discovered these with great subtlety, and later generations, approving of their discoveries, adopted them: namely, **fear** and **sorrow**, **desire** and **joy**. If these are ordered and fortified by the protection of the holy Cross, they are proven to be life-giving in religious people, even though the folly of certain "wise men" of this world has considered them to be vices. If that were the case, and only sinners or the lost could possess them, they could not rightly be called "affections," but rather "diseases." But since such movements of the soul are found in the holy Apostles and Prophets, who would be so foolish as to believe these affections are vices? Through them, those who resisted vice more than other men pleased God. Thus, the Apostle Paul speaks of fear in this way:
> But I fear, lest as the serpent seduced Eve by his subtlety, so your minds should be corrupted from the charity that is in Christ. <note>2 Corinthians 11:3</note>

The same man says confidently of desire:
> I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. <note>Philippians 1:23</note>

And concerning sadness, which others call sorrow, the same teacher of the Gentiles says:
> For I have great sadness and continual sorrow in my heart, for my brothers who are my kinsmen according to the flesh. <note>Romans 9:2-3</note>

For writing to the Romans he also says:
> I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil. <note>Romans 16:19</note>

David the Prophet also says of fear:
> The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever. <note>Psalm 19:9</note>

Likewise, he says: "Fear the Lord, all you his saints." Regarding sorrow, he says:
> I was troubled in my exercise. <note>Psalm 55:2</note>

The same man says of desire:
> My soul has desired to long for your justifications at all times, and I have desired your salvation, O Lord. <note>Psalm 119:20; 119:174</note>

And concerning joy, the same Psalmist, exhorting the saints of God, says:
> Be glad in the Lord and exult, you righteous; rejoice, all you righteous in the Lord. <note>Psalm 32:11; 33:1</note>

Therefore, whoever wishes to find fault with this fear or sorrow, this desire or this joy, finds fault with the Apostle and the Prophet themselves. For they not only pleased God through such affections, but even exhorted others to do the same; and those who were devoid of them were blamed among the criminal for being "without affection." We do not sin, therefore, by having these affections, but by using them poorly; for the nature of human affections belongs to man...

### III. Figure. Concerning the nine orders of Angels, and concerning their names arranged in the figure of a Cross.

->**[A Grid Poem: The Cross and the Heavenly Host]**<-

<note>This page features a "carmen figuratum" or pattern poem. The letters are arranged in a perfect grid so that while the main text is read horizontally, a secondary "hidden" text is formed by the letters inside the red-outlined shape of a Cross. In this figure, the vertical and horizontal beams of the Cross contain the word **SALVS** (Salvation) and **CRVX** (Cross). The names of the Archangels Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael are woven into the background grid.</note>

Hail, holy salvation of Christ, O you joyful passion!
Venerable Cross of God, teacher, wisdom, and light!
Dear praise of truth, virtue, and clear philosophy for those
Whom the fields of heaven give, O Creator of the high sky <note>original: "olympi," using the name of the Greek mountain to signify the Christian heaven</note>!
And the starry choirs, the bright scepters of the day.
For you are the salvation of men, the beautiful renewal of all things.
The whole world blesses you; save us indeed, O renowned one of the heavens!
Every knee in heaven bows and surrounds you,
And those on earth and below, according to their known bonds.
Scepters, leaders, and kingdoms bow at the name of Jesus.
But Michael the prince, leader of those dwelling on high,
Remembers you; by your virtue, the entire heavens are revealed.
To rule and to protect is the task of the nourishing altar of the Spirit <note>The poet identifies the Cross as an "ara" or altar</note>.
With which shield he <note>Michael</note> exults, and with which sword the strong man enters
The horrid wars of the dragon, triumphing with unsullied purity.
And the victor shall seek your praises as his rewards.
For by right He established this Cross suspended, and in this manner
Fate destined such a cross, this true altar for all,
So that the very path of life, testifying to these things, may bring forth virtues.
Good deeds justly rise up in the cross of life.
Christ <note>original: "Xps," a Greek abbreviation for Christ</note>, the holy Rock of faith, greatly increased,
Came down humble from the heavenly citadel and led us.
He taught with words and left lessons through His deeds.
And on the holy, pious cross, the Creator fulfilled all things.
Here swift Gabriel, bringing the clear word to the ear
Of the Virgin, you prayed as Archangel and bridal attendant <term>paranymphus: an ancient term for a best man or bridal attendant; here it refers to Gabriel's role in the Annunciation</term>.
Now touching the news of Jesus the Savior, let him praise the triumph.
O Raphael, "Medicine of God," has not this cross granted you <note>The name Raphael means "God heals" in Hebrew</note>
To be able to restore the radiance of the figure which then
You showed to the blind man, which restored light to the world? <note>A reference to the Archangel Raphael healing the eyes of Tobit in the Apocrypha</note>
Therefore, we believe the ancient praises of the cross remain,
When the new song of those singing psalms sounded praise together.
The Angels were in their office, and the ministers came by right.
Hence I ask, O heavenly host, bless Christ,
Who saved the world by the cross, giving kingdoms to the blessed,
And fulfilled your number in the heights of the heavens.

### PAGE VII.

Hail holy salvation, O you joyful passion of Christ!
Venerable Cross of God, teacher, wisdom, and light!
Praise of truth, dear virtue, and clear philosophy for those
Whom the fields of the earth provide, or for whom the peak of heaven <note>original: "olympi," using the classical name for the home of the gods to signify the Christian heaven</note> conceals
The starry choirs and the bright scepters of the day.
For you are the salvation of humanity, the beautiful renewal of all things:
The whole world blesses you, as does the renowned wing of the heavens.
Through you, every knee of the celestial beings is bowed,
As well as those of the earthly and those below <note>referring to the inhabitants of the underworld or purgatory</note> according to their known bonds.
Scepters, leaders, and kingdoms bow at the name of Jesus.

But Michael the prince, leader of those dwelling on high,
Remembers you; by the virtue of God, he declares that all the heavens
Are both ruled and protected by you, for you stand as the nourishing altar of the Deity.
With this shield he exults; with this spear he, the strong one, will enter
The horrid wars of the dragon <note>the biblical dragon, representing Satan</note>, triumphing with thousands of holy angels.
And as a victor, he will seek your praises as his reward.
For by right, action, manner, and destiny, he established
This Cross as such an altar, so that for every truth
Life itself, as a witness, might bring forth its high council of virtues.
Good writings justly rise up in the life found in the Cross.

Christ, bowing humbly, led himself to the Rock of faith and the twelve <note>original: "senos," literally 'sixes', referring to the twelve apostles as two groups of six</note>;
Then He came from the citadel of heaven and taught with words,
He left proofs through His deeds,
And as the Creator, He completed all things by the holy and pious Cross.
This is what you, eager Gabriel, the Archangel and <term>paranymphus</term> <note>original: "paranymphus," a term for a best man or bridal attendant, here referring to Gabriel’s role as the messenger of the "marriage" between divinity and humanity at the Annunciation</note>,
Prayed when giving the clear word to the ear of the Virgin,
Already touching upon the triumph of Jesus the Savior with praise.

O Raphael, "Medicine of God" <note>the name Raphael literally means "God heals" in Hebrew</note>, did not this Cross grant you
The power to restore radiance? For you then rightly showed its form
To the blind man <note>a reference to the Archangel Raphael healing the eyes of Tobit in the Apocrypha</note>, which restored light to his world.
Therefore, we believe that the Cross is found in ancient praises:
When the new song of those singing psalms sounded its praise,
And the angels came by right into their service as ministers.
Hence, I ask the army of the heavens: bless Christ,
Who saved the world by the Cross, giving kingdoms to the blessed,
And completed your number in the citadel of the heavens.

Praise of the Truth, dear virtue, and clear philosophy for those
Whom the fields of the earth bring forth, or for whom the peak of heaven <note>original: "olympi," the classical name for the home of the gods used here to mean the Christian heaven</note> conceals
The starry choirs and the bright scepters of the day.

# Book I. EXPLANATION.

It is only right that the orders of the holy Angels and the armies of the heavenly host should harmonize with the name and number of the Holy Cross. They do so to praise the victory of the eternal King and to proclaim the greatness of their joy through their honorable service. We know this because the sacred text of the Gospel records that they not only offered praise at the hour of Christ’s birth and later served Him in the desert, but clearly narrates that they were present to perform their duties during the time of His passion and resurrection. One must believe they are especially devoted to this mystery; for the more worthily they serve in His army, the more devotedly they praise His triumph.

There are, therefore, nine orders of Angels, as the Holy Scripture commends to us: these are, **Angels**, **Archangels**, **Virtues**, **Principalities**, **Powers**, **Dominions**, **Thrones**, **Cherubim**, and **Seraphim**. To explain these, let us set down the words of the blessed Pope Gregory <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604), also known as Gregory the Great, whose "Homilies on the Gospels" defined the standard medieval hierarchy of angels</note>: "Almost all pages of the sacred word testify that there are Angels and Archangels. The books of the Prophets often speak of Cherubim and Seraphim, as is well known. The Apostle Paul also enumerates the names of four orders when writing to the Ephesians, saying:
> Above all principality and power and virtue and dominion.

Writing again to the Colossians, he says:
> Whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers.

Now, he had already described the dominions, principalities, and powers when speaking to the Ephesians, but when he was about to speak to the Colossians, he placed 'thrones' first, about which he had said nothing to the Ephesians. Therefore, when 'thrones' are joined to those four he mentioned to the Ephesians—that is, principalities, powers, virtues, and dominions—there are five orders specifically named. When Angels, Archangels, Cherubim, and Seraphim are added to these, the orders of Angels are beyond doubt found to be nine." Hence it is said to that very Angel who was created first <note>This refers to the "Anointed Cherub" from Ezekiel 28, traditionally interpreted as Lucifer before his fall, whose original beauty represented the perfection of all nine orders</note> through the Prophet:
> You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty, you were in the delights of the paradise of God.

In this, it should be noted that the first Angel is not said to be made *to* the likeness of God, but is called the "seal of likeness," so that the more subtle his nature is, the more expressively the image is instilled within him. In that same passage, it is immediately added:
> Every precious stone was your covering: the Sard, Topaz, and Jasper, Chrysolite, Onyx, and Beryl, Sapphire, Carbuncle, and Emerald.

Behold, he named nine types of stones, because there are surely nine orders of Angels. That first Angel stood adorned and covered by these orders for a reason: because while he was set above all the ranks of Angels, he was more brilliant in comparison to them. 

But what sacred mystery does this arrangement of the nine orders of Angels on the Cross suggest to us? Let us follow the thought. This form of the Holy Cross holds in its lower part two orders, that is, Angels and Archangels; in the right arm two, that is, virtues and powers; in the left arm likewise two, that is, principalities and dominions; in the middle one, that is, thrones; and in the upper part again two, that is, Cherubim and Seraphim. These names are quite fitting for proclaiming the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ and are appropriately suited for telling of His magnificence and power. For whom do the Angels and Archangels placed in the lowest part of the Cross announce, if not Him who descended from heaven to earth—namely, the "Angel of Great Counsel" <note>original: "magni consilij Angelum," a title for Christ derived from the Septuagint version of Isaiah 9:6</note>, sent to announce to the gentle, so that the Stronger might bind the strong man and plunder his goods? And whom else do the Virtues, Powers, Principalities, and Dominions proclaim, placed as they are in the arms of the Cross, if not Him of whom it is written:
> The right hand of the Lord has worked virtue. <note>original: "Dextera Domini fecit virtutem," quoting Psalm 117:16 (Vulgate). In this context, "virtue" implies both moral excellence and miraculous power.</note>

<summary>This page explains the symbolic relationship between the nine orders of angels and the physical structure of the Cross, using biblical citations and the authority of Pope Gregory the Great. It maps the celestial hierarchy onto the Cross's shape, identifying Christ as the central figure praised by these various ranks.</summary>

# BOOK ONE. FOLIO VIII.

-> b ii <-

<meta>Fourth Figure.</meta>

And likewise: *All power is given to me in heaven and on earth.* <note>original: "Data est mihi omnis potestas in cælo & in terra" — Matthew 28:18</note> And again: *And the government is placed upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God the Mighty, Father of the world to come, Prince of Peace.* <note>original: "Et factus est principatus super humerum eius..." — Isaiah 9:6</note> And again: *And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.* <note>Psalm 72:8</note> Therefore, as the **Thrones** are placed in the middle of the cross, whom else do they signify sitting within them? Save for Him to whom it was said, as the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> witnesses: *Thy throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of rectitude is the scepter of thy kingdom.* <note>Hebrews 1:8</note> And the Psalmist says: *You sit upon your throne, you who judge with equity.* <note>Psalm 9:4</note> And whom do the **Cherubim** and **Seraphim** signify, placed at the summit of the Cross? Save for Him of whom the Apostle says: *In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.* <note>Colossians 2:3</note> And again: *Our God is a consuming fire.* <note>Hebrews 12:29</note> Indeed, **Cherubim** is interpreted as "fullness of knowledge," and **Seraphim** as "those who are burning" or "setting on fire." <note>These etymologies were standard in medieval theology, derived from Jerome and Isidore of Seville to explain the nature of these high-ranking angels</note>

But we do not proclaim these things concerning the orders of Angels as if we were making them equal to the Only-Begotten Son; rather, through the offices and names of the subordinate creation, we venerate the <term>sacraments</term> <note>In this context, "sacramenta" refers to the hidden "mysteries" or "sacred signs" of God's plan</note> of His divine <term>dispensation</term> <note>The "divine economy" or the way God manages the world and salvation history</note>. For He Himself is the God and Lord of the Angels: begotten of God the Father before all ages—that is, from the substance of the Father—who in the final age of the world was born of a Virgin Mother. He took human nature upon Himself, sent specifically to conquer the prince of this world <note>Satan</note>, so that He might despoil the principalities and powers, triumphing over them openly in Himself. The Father raised Him from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavens, above every principality and power and virtue and dominion, and every name that is named not only in this age, but also in the one to come. He has put all things under His feet, and gave Him to be the head over all things for the Church, which is His body. 

Therefore, the nine larger letters which form the shape of a Cross on this page sound out this phrase: **THE CROSS IS SALVATION** <note>original: "CRVX SALVS"</note>. Each individual letter contains one of the nine orders of Angels; this will be easily clear to anyone who knows their letters and is not ignorant of the names of the nine orders.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of the Cross's form, transitioning from the poetic verses of the previous page to a prose "Declaration" or explanation. ### ->DECLARATION<- <note>original: "DECLARATIO"</note>

In this page, therefore, the Cross of the Lord is seen depicted and described, together with the figures of the Seraphim and Cherubim placed around it. These are introduced here into this work to show with what great providence and dispensation divine mercy has always provided for the salvation of the human race. For through prophetic revelation, He willed that the form of our redemption be seen beforehand even among the angelic spirits themselves; and through prophetic works constructed in the entrances of the Tabernacle and the Temple—that is, in those very Cherubim placed next to the Ark beyond the veil—He decreed to make known the eternal atonement <note>original: "propitiationem"</note> to the world.

Furthermore, although many authors have interpreted many things regarding the appearance and position of these living beings, and have written various things in different styles but not with different faith: yet it seems not unfitting to me (saving the tradition of our elders) that these living beings, by their very posture, form a pattern of the holy Cross. This is because they maintain its intervals in space and similarly extend themselves upward and downward, and to the right and to the left in their position.

Finally, the Prophet Isaiah relates this among other things, saying: *I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and the things that were under Him filled the temple. Seraphim stood above it; one had six wings and the other had six wings; with two they covered his face, and with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew; and one cried to the other, saying: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God of hosts; all the earth is full of His glory.*

What then does this position of the six wings of the Seraphim prefigure, if not the image of the Cross of Christ? Indeed, those wings which covered the upper part of their body—that is, the face—must necessarily be raised upward toward the head, and for this reason, it is manifest that they demonstrate the upper part of the Cross. Those, however, which covered the lowest part—that is, the feet—how else can they be believed to be positioned except sent downward, and for this reason they signify the lower part of the Cross. Those other two wings which are extended for flying—what else do they signify but the transverse wood of the Lord's Cross, upon which His arms and hands were extended?

And therefore, in the positioning of the six wings of the Seraphim, no wise person doubts that the sign of the whole Cross of Christ is clearly expressed. They are also well-interpreted as "the moving ones" or "the burning ones": because they demonstrate that form in which all opposing powers were overcome, and the sins of the whole world were consumed and blotted out. Indeed, they commend to the elect of God that fire which the Lord testified He willed to send upon the earth so that it might burn. And they rightly encouraged all the elect with a threefold voice to the praise of the Holy Trinity—that is, those who lived before the coming of the Savior, those who lived in the presence of His incarnation, and those who are still to be converted to the faith until the end of the world after His ascension into heaven: because the one passion of Christ redeemed all together, namely from the Jews and from the Gentiles.

As for the rest, those Cherubim which were fashioned in the Tabernacle or the Temple, what else did they display by the extension of their wings but the image of the Cross of Christ? Of these, it is well-narrated in the Book of Kings that they were made ten cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</note> in height, and they had ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other wing. According to this likeness, the form of the human body can also be compared, whose width in the extension of the arms—from the tip of the fingers of one hand to the tip of the fingers of the other hand—is almost as great as its height or length from the sole of the foot to the top of the head. These, therefore, stood next to the Ark and the Mercy Seat <note>original: "propitiatorium", the golden lid of the Ark of the Covenant where God's presence rested</note>, because they demonstrated the true atonement for the human race in the incarnation of the Savior. These also [held] their wings extended in the manner of a Cross...

<summary>This page provides a theological explanation (Declaratio) of why Seraphim and Cherubim are depicted flanking the Cross, arguing that their six wings and temple dimensions geometrically prefigure the Cross and the proportions of the human body.</summary>

### V. Figure. Concerning the four Square Figures placed around the Cross, and the Spiritual Building of the House of God.

> I pray, O sacred Cross of God, mark my breast with your name:
> So that I may rightly sing of your bright trophies with praises,
> How you lead covenants from the heavens to earthly things,
> Confirm the pact, and break the chains of death <note>original: "laeti," likely a variant of "leti," meaning death</note>.
> O you, apostolic host, and the order of martyrs as well,
> Whom the height has rightly placed within the house of Christ itself;

> Grafted and constructed, fixed by the strength of the Crucified,
> Which has truly dedicated the human race to life.
> And the guardian <note>original: "philax," from the Greek "phylax"</note> goes forth to show the firm pillar

# BOOK ONE

### FO. XL

I pray, O sacred Cross of God, let your power mark my breast,
So that I may rightly sing of your bright trophies with praises:
How you lead covenants from the heavens to earthly things,
Confirm the pact, and break the chains of death <note>original: "lethi," a variant of "leti," death</note>.
O you, apostolic host, and you, the order of martyrs,
Whom the summit of the house of Christ has rightly placed;
You have built upon Him; the nourishing people are found by your voice.
Holy and salvific Cross, grafted and constructed
Upon the highest foundation, fixed by the strength of the Crucified:
Which has truly dedicated the human race to life.
The guardian <note>original: "philax," from the Greek "phylax" meaning a watchman or protector</note> goes forth to show a firm pillar,
That an eternal form rises through itself toward paradise,
As well as the hall of the covering, of the bridegroom, and of the just king.
O Christ, you raise up new trophies in the world soon by right,
By blood, and by the Way, so that it may preserve the covenants of the just:
May it despise the damned and conquer the deceitful one with piety:
To whom you are the favor and the fear, the virtue, the palm, and the crown.
Illustrious Cross of the Lord, foundation of Christ and of His hall,
You are more beautiful than any field blooming with flowers:
Taller than the Cedar, and more precious than white Parian marble,
You join the squared stones in a firm path:
And the law of the patriarchs and the common people rightly draw
Their first foundations from the floor of the entire house:
Which well knows how to bind devout hearts first with doctrine.
The words of the Prophet had rained down upon the one ruling correctly,
So that a living hall might be piously ruled for the King by His commands:
As they had already formed for Christ in the worn arena <note>original: "scāmate," from the Greek "skamma," referring to a wrestling pit or arena, symbolizing spiritual struggle</note>:
For everyone together climbs toward the stars because of His name.
This hall of Jesus flourishes toward the joyful North <note>original: "Arcton," the constellation of the Bear, used here to signify the North</note>,
And the good structure of life grows strong, confirmed by His voice:
The joining signifies this, and by His command, this omen grants the way to travel:
By which the Leader leads us to hold the scepters of light:
Those whom the joyful, good dwelling <note>original: "mansio," a place of staying or a station</note> of Christ dedicates in the temple:
And He increases the Cross with these four rocks:
The Cornerstone himself leading the way to the perfect house.

-># DECLARATION<-

->### Page 10<-

In this page, therefore, the Holy Cross stretches through the middle, having four quadrangular forms placed around its sides: this is to show the structure of the celestial building—namely, the **Church of the living God**, which is both His house and the *pillar and ground of truth*. To this house belong the chosen Angels, whose likeness is promised to us in the future life, as the Lord says: *But those who are accounted worthy of that world and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they can no longer die: for they are equal to the Angels, and are the sons of God, being sons of the resurrection* <note>original: "Illi autem qui digni habentur..." quoting Luke 20:35-36</note>. To this house also belongs the mediator between God and men himself, the man **Christ Jesus**, as He himself testified when He said: *Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.* The Evangelist, explaining this, added: *But He spoke of the temple of His body.* Furthermore, the Apostle says of us: *Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?*

If, therefore, He was made the temple of God through His assumed humanity, and we are made the temple of God through His indwelling Spirit, it is certain that that material temple which **King Solomon** built in **Jerusalem** held the figure <note>A "figure" in this context is a prophetic symbol or "type" that points to a later reality.</note> of all of us—of the Lord himself and of His members, which we are. But He is uniquely the **Cornerstone** <note>original: "lapidis Angularis"</note>, chosen and precious, set in the foundation; whereas we are like **living stones** built up upon the *foundation of the Apostles and Prophets*, that is, upon the Lord himself. This the Apostle shows, saying: *For no one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus.* He is rightly called the foundation of the house of the Lord because, as Peter says: *There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.* And likewise: *Coming to Him,* he says, *as to a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God and honored, you yourselves as living stones are built up into a spiritual house, into a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.*

Therefore, the **Patriarchs and Prophets, Apostles and Martyrs**, can be fittingly understood as the first stones of this foundation, suitable for the groundwork. Whether by preaching, by working, or by suffering, they laid the foundations of faith for us; the rest of the multitude of the faithful follows their authority in doctrine, their examples in deeds, and imitates them in endurance. For just as the Apostles and Martyrs, after the Savior's incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, constructed the spiritual building of the house of God throughout the whole world by preaching Christ or even by dying for Christ; so before His coming in the flesh, the Patriarchs and Prophets among the former people <note>Referring to the Israelites of the Old Testament.</note>, and in those regions where they lived, always strove to turn the lives of others toward the better by word and example. They did this so that they might deserve to have God as an inhabitant through worthy conduct, and might feel that God was favorable to them, under whose dominion they recognized the Almighty.

It is well written, then, in the Book of Kings concerning the building of that symbolic temple, that the king commanded that they should bring **great stones, precious stones**, for the foundation of the temple, and **square them**. The precious stones are holy men, illustrious in merit, who are commanded to be well squared, and thus placed in the foundation. For everything **squared** <note>original: "Quadratum," referring to a cube or a perfectly hewn block.</note> is accustomed to stand firm no matter which way it is turned. To this shape, surely, the hearts of the chosen are likened: they have learned to stand so firm in the strength of faith that they cannot be turned from the uprightness of their state by any adversity they encounter, nor even by death itself; such as...

# BOOK ONE. FOLIO XII.

...that is to say, it has received many Teachers of the Church <term>Ecclesia; the assembly of believers</term> not only from Judea, but also from the Gentiles. This construction is rightly demonstrated in the Holy Cross, because in it—that is, in the passion of Christ—the entire universal Church was founded, perfectly built, and dedicated. Nor would this building ever have come to fruition unless the human race were liberated through the Cross, nor would the office of the priest himself be worthily fulfilled unless the Priest himself became the sacrifice upon the Cross. Within the Cross itself, this written verse is contained: **The glorious Cross of the Lord is the foundation of Christ’s palace.** <note>original: "Inclyta Crux Domini Christi fundamēta aulæ." Here, "palace" or "hall" refers to the celestial Church.</note>

In the four-sided shapes <note>original: "tetragonis"; the 6x6 squares in the grid</note> placed around the Cross, the verses are written so that they do not circle all the way around—that is, they do not return from the final letters to the starting letters through a curve. Instead, they all begin in their upper right corner and descend through the upper left to the lower left in nineteen letters. Then, starting again from the twentieth letter in the upper right corner and descending through the lower right, they reach the lower left in seventeen letters. Thus, each verse of the four squares contains 36 letters. This is the number of a plane square <note>A square number in mathematics.</note> and of the number six multiplied by itself, as we shall demonstrate in what follows.

This is the verse of the square placed below the right arm: **The praiseworthy action of the Patriarchs signifies you.** <note>original: "Te Patriarcharum laudabilis actio signat."</note> The verse of the square placed below the left arm is this: **And the people of the Prophets, commanded by divine speech.** <note>original: "Plebsq; Prophetarum diuino famine iussa."</note> Furthermore, the verse of the square placed above the right arm of the Cross is: **The Apostolic host duly makes known your trophies.** <note>original: "Agmen Apostolicum pandit tua rite trophæa."</note> Finally, above the left arm is this: **And the choir of Martyrs itself, by the rightful shedding of blood.** <note>original: "Martyrum & ipse chorus effuso iure cruore."</note>

Almighty power, highest wisdom, O Christ,
pious Lord who adorns the whole world from the height of the Cross,
and distributes the holy gifts of salvation to Your saints:
For this four-horse chariot <note>A traditional metaphor for the four Cardinal Virtues (Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance) or the four Gospels.</note>, well-fitted with four holy corners,
reveals the sequence of the virtues. Through the consecrating triumph
of the Victor King's blood, it shows that all types of goodness
flourish in the world through the fruit of piety.
Virtue is a habit of the soul and the sum of all moral beauty,
the nobility of life, the reason and the moderation of the tongue.
These things, O nourishing Cross, you grant to the faithful as things to be proven with rightful praise;
you bring forth all things at once and each thing individually through a pleasing vow.
Your holy <term>Prudence</term> <note>The virtue of wisdom and discerning the right course of action.</note> has taught the fledgling world;
from You, <term>Justice</term> <note>The virtue of giving each person their due and acting with moral rightness.</note>, burning brightly, rejoices to despise
the terror of the Devil <note>original: "zabuli," a medieval variant of "diaboli."</note>. Blessed love climbs
toward holy counsels and rescues the mind consumed by deceit.
From this, one can remove carnal power and the struggle of the flesh
with all one's might and strong effort; from here too, one gazes
toward things glorious to see. Bearing up under adversity, Virtue goes along,
forbidding pestilential things and the harmful guilt of crimes and slaughter,
showing that happy times can now sing out.
To know the signs of God, to explain His commandments, and
to seek the light through hope and deed; in this way, the saints’
ears, pricked up, may worthily gather the best of heavenly things—
just as the gifts of the countryside and the sprouts of the field prepare
fruit from the leaves, and as dry, rough branches are properly gathered
to build a fire and bring forth royal dishes.
Therefore, most sacred Piety has sown these fruits,
Grace has purified them, and strict <term>Patience</term> <note>The virtue of enduring hardship with composure.</note> has proven them.
The Covenant has joined them, and the nourishing law of the Father has watered them;
Goodness has brought them forth, for they are the living grasses of Christ.
Devotion has hallowed them, and <term>Constancy</term> <note>The virtue of remaining firm and steady in purpose.</note> with praise
supported every stalk. Now humble Virtue
stores new grain throughout, and <term>Modesty</term> <note>The virtue of moderation in behavior and speech.</note> nourishes the full
crop in the ear of grain. <term>Perseverance</term> <note>The virtue of continuing in a state of grace until the end of life.</note> gives the fruit,
and at the right time, Christ quickly makes it mature and shining.
Then, O Cross, through you and through Justice—as the Divine Presence <note>original: "numine"</note> is nearly seen—
He, now putting forth the sickle, will gather the harvest into the granaries.

-># EXPLANATION.<-
<meta>catchword: joined,</meta>

It is worthy, therefore, to commemorate in this sacred poem how great and what kind of fruits the wood of the holy Cross brings forth by its budding. Its fruit is eternal and its root is perpetual; its scent fills the world, and its flavor nourishes <note>original: "faginat," likely a variant of "saginat," meaning to fatten or feed.</note> the faithful. Its splendor surpasses the sun, and its brightness outshines the snow; its summit exceeds the heavens, and its base penetrates the depths of the underworld. Its firmness exalts the humble with joy, and its exalted power humbles the proud. Indeed, the sequence of all virtues was bestowed upon the world through it and in it, because in it the perfection of all things was completed. In it, <term>Prudence</term> <note>The ability to govern and discipline oneself by the use of reason.</note> demonstrates its height; in it, <term>Justice</term> <note>The moral virtue that consists in the constant and firm will to give their due to God and neighbor.</note> reveals its solidity; in it, <term>Fortitude</term> <note>Courage in facing difficulties and constancy in the pursuit of the good.</note> seals its power; in it, <term>Temperance</term> <note>The virtue that moderates the attraction of pleasures and provides balance in the use of created goods.</note> praises its own restraints. Here also, Prudence more devotedly grants the acquisition of wisdom and the understanding of truth; and from here, every faithful person perceives the gifts of providence, intelligence, and memory. Here, Justice has placed the foundation of faith, and from here distributes the equity of piety and religion, as well as grace and retribution, to each one. Here, Fortitude most magnificently despises both charms and adversities, and from here proposes examples of confidence, patience, and perseverance. Here, Temperance casts the reins of discipline upon the insolent impulses of lust and stubbornness, and from here bestows the manifold gifts of modesty and continence, as well as clemency and sobriety, upon those who desire them. This, clearly, is the tree planted by God Himself, of whom the Prophet says, making a comparison to a tree:

> And he shall be like a tree that is planted near the running waters, which shall bring forth its fruit in its due season, and its leaf shall not fall off, and all whatsoever he shall do shall prosper. <note>original: Psalm 1:3.</note>

The "running waters" <note>original: "decursus aquarum."</note> are therefore the daily transitions of failing peoples. And concerning Himself, Truth <note>A common medieval title for Christ, based on John 14:6.</note> says:

> If they do these things in the green wood, what shall be done in the dry? <note>original: Luke 23:31.</note>

The wood near the running waters, then, is with leaves and fruit because the Creator, appearing in the flesh, brought forth the shelter of His protection for us. Through His resurrection, He raised the human race to life—a race that, through its failings, was daily heading toward death. For truly this wood gave fruit in its season, when our Savior, having completed His passion and resurrection, made the Church (as the true vine united in Himself) abound with all virtues throughout the breadth of the world, He himself testifying to this:

> I am, He said, the vine and you are the branches. He who abides in me, and I in him, the same bears much fruit, for without me you can do nothing. <note>original: John 15:5.</note>

For spiritual fruits are born here, which the Apostle enumerates, saying:

> But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, benignity, faith, modesty, continence, chastity. <note>original: Galatians 5:22–23.</note>

Rightly, then, is spiritual fruit attributed to the holy Cross, because the Author of all good things was crucified upon it. For on the part of the flesh, while Christ willed to die upon it, the human race perceived total salvation. The grain of wheat fell into the earth and brought forth a glorious harvest of martyrs. One post <note>original: "stips," referring to the upright stake of the Cross.</note> carried a suspended man, and the whole world was dedicated to the heavenly kingdom. The insolent Judean nation did not fear to destroy the King, and the nations of the entire orb received Him as their Redeemer, because in the seed of Abraham all the families of the earth shall be blessed. Therefore, these four figures, arranged into one form of the Cross, contain the names of the four principal virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance, from which the whole sequence of virtues proceeds, and in which the reason for a good life consists. These mentioned figures are therefore joined according to the appearance of a triangle <note>The text here begins to explain the visual/geometric layout of the accompanying carmina (picture-poems), where the words for virtues are often arranged in shapes like triangles or squares.</note>,

All things now shine with the true light of Christ
Illuminated, and made blessed by the works of the holy Cross.
They celebrate together, so that they may pay their owed vows
To the celestial victor, the kingdoms singing devotedly
That all things keep their measure under the great divinity of Jesus.
Whatever moves in the world, whatever exists everywhere—
That which is, which tastes and feels, which lives and preserves the laws:
The earth, the sea, the stars, the grasses, the winds,
Shall be subject to this command; they are now, as they were before:
Rain, cloud, hail, ice, snow and frost,
Springs and rivers, dust and dew, and the sunbeam; without this,
The regions of the North <note>original: "Cretæ, arcton". This refers to the constellations of the North (Ursa Major/Minor), though "Creta" here may be a variant of "creata" (created things).</note>, the stars and all the airs [would not be].
Behold the nourishing [light], and do not wander <note>original: "vaaharo". Likely a variant or OCR error for "vagare" (to wander/stray).</note>; again, speak the truths,
And let the just man also sing rhythms, songs, and odes:
May the Cross draw all things, and piously crown them with holy law:
Let it not discord with the praise of God, but let His work
Speak honorable things in joy: the fish and the fearsome dragons <note>In medieval natural history, "dracones" often referred to large serpents or whales as well as mythical beasts.</note>,
The hills and groves, mountains, flocks, the tree, and the sand,
Along with wild beasts, wasps, worms, and the gaping-mouthed beast:
And the birds, whether peaceful in appearance or savage in mind.
<term>Followers of Christ</term> <note>original: "Xpicolæ". This uses the Greek "Xp" (Chi-Rho) for "Christ" combined with the Latin "cola" (worshipper/cultivator).</note> to whom the hall of heaven and the earth are granted:
For you, virtue is a light leading from everywhere against the enemies.
It brings news, whether in prayer or in the water [of baptism]; but one skilled in speech
Casts away such fame; here the palm [of victory] is known to the seized,
It gives to the happy, it gives these tidings to all the just:
Sparingly treating the enemy by right, it grants life by its word,
But by law it damns many whom the wicked growth has hedged in.
Thence it is fitting that mouths likewise hymn praises
And declare vows of thanks; behold, your crowd of the heavens,
The host, and you, the people whom the earth brings forth everywhere:
A shared reason has guided you equally to these odes:
The joys of heaven, the celestial kingdoms and good things
Now perhaps they take hold of, and greatly seek with vows:
Behold, your Savior gave this to you, and He himself
Is your own King, leader, and joyful creator, Jesus.

-># EXPLANATION<-

Rightly, therefore, almost no one is ignorant that the number four <term>quaternarius: the number four, often considered a "perfect" number in medieval numerology because it represents stability and the physical world</term> is consecrated with perfection, and thus the whole world venerates that number as it is transfigured into the shape of the Cross of Christ. Indeed, it is manifest that the world consists of four elements—namely, fire, air, water, and earth. It is also well known that the whole world is bounded by four parts or corners: the East, the West, the North, and the South. There are also four successions of the seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. And there are four quadrants of the natural day—that is, four sets of six hours—which are distinguished by these starting points: morning, noon, evening, and the dead of night.

But it must be explained how this arrangement can be suitably fitted to the Cross. If we wish to look upon the upright Cross, let us place fire, which is the highest of the elements, at its summit. Air and water, which are the middle elements, we assign to the transverse beam of the Cross (the horizontal arm) which is drawn through the middle of the upright post. Earth, however, which is the heaviest and holds the lowest place among created things, we assign to the lower part of the Cross. Just as all these elements are mixed together by a certain natural proximity to complete the integrity of the world, so they are also joined to the four parts of the Cross to demonstrate its perfect form. 

If, however, we wish to assign the Cross to the four regions of the world, we must measure it lying flat in this way: so that we assign its first part (the top) to the East, the far end (the bottom) to the West, the right to the North, and the left to the South. Similarly, the four successions of the seasons and the natural day can be united in the Cross by the same arrangement, so that a single image of the year or the day may be appropriately shown within them. 

For Spring and the dawn bring forth the rising of light and the budding seeds in the earth in their proper order, and for this reason, they are well assigned to the East. Summer and noon are fitted to the South because of the heat; for while the sun is raised in those parts of the sky, it scorches the world with a more burning heat. Autumn and evening are rightly assigned to the West, because then the harvest of all the fruits of the earth is finished, and the entire span of the day ends. Winter and the dead of night are likened to the North; because then the earth is numb with cold, and it is a time more suitable for rest than for any work. 

Therefore, since it is certain that all things are restored through the Cross, and reborn and improved through the passion of Christ, all things rightly agree to His praise. For He Himself is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to whom alone those blessings belong which the three boys <note>This refers to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the Book of Daniel, who sang a hymn of praise while in a fiery furnace.</note> in the furnace of burning fire sang together while exhorting all creatures to the praise of the Creator, saying: *Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord, and so forth.* <note>original: "Benedicite omnia opera Domini Dominum & cætera."</note> Concerning which the Psalmist also says: *Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and everything that is in them* <note>original: "Laudent eum cæli & terra, mare & omnia quæ in eis sunt"</note>: because, according to the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul in Romans 11:36.</note>, *from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be honor and glory forever and ever.* <note>original: "ex ipso & per ipsum & in ipso sunt omnia, ipsi honor & gloria in sæcula sæculorum."</note> 

As for why I have depicted the four elements, or the four seasons, or the four regions of the world within wheels, this is the reason: because the entire machine of the world is temporal, and is variable or changeable by a certain mixing of elements and the succession of times. Solomon attests to this, saying: *All things have their time, and all things under heaven pass away in their appointed spaces.* <note>original: "Omnia tempus habent, & suis spacijs transeunt vniuersa sub cælo." From Ecclesiastes 3:1.</note> Now fire dries the air, now water makes it wetter; now the earth is affected by the flooding of waters, now it is dried by the heat of the sun. Indeed, water is mobile by nature and completes a certain circle in its course. All rivers, says Ecclesiasticus <note>The author attributes this to Ecclesiasticus, though the quote "All rivers run into the sea..." is famously from Ecclesiastes 1:7.</note>, *enter into the sea, and the sea does not overflow; to the place from where the rivers come, they return, so that they may flow again.* Fire also similarly has a natural motion,
