# EXPLANATION.

It is rightly understood by almost everyone that the number four is hallowed by perfection, and therefore the entire world venerates that number as it is transformed into the shape of the Cross of Christ. Indeed, it is manifest that the world consists of four <term>elements: the fundamental building blocks of matter in ancient science</term>, namely: fire, air, water, and earth. It is also well known that the whole world is bounded by four parts or corners: the east, the west, the north, and the south. There are also four changes of the seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Furthermore, there are four quarters of the natural day—that is, four sets of six hours—which are distinguished by these starting points: morning, midday, evening, and the dead of night.

However, we must explain how this arrangement can be appropriately fitted together. If we wish to look upon the Cross standing upright, let us place fire, which is the highest of the elements, at its summit. Let us assign air and water, which are the middle elements, to the cross-beam of the Cross, which is drawn through the middle of the upright post. Finally, let us assign earth, which is the heaviest and holds the lowest place among created things, to the lower part of the Cross. Just as all these elements are mixed together by a certain natural kinship to complete the integrity of the world, so too are they joined to the four parts of the Cross to demonstrate its perfect form. 

If, however, we wish to assign the Cross to the four regions of the world, we must measure it lying flat: so that we assign its first part to the east, its furthest part to the west, the right side to the north, and the left side to the south. Similarly, the four changes of the seasons and the natural day can be united in the Cross in the same arrangement, so that one image of the year or the day can be suitably shown in them. For spring and the dawn bring forth the rising of light and the budding growth in the earth in their proper order, and for this reason, they are well assigned to the east. Summer and midday are fitted to the south because of their heat; for while the sun is raised up in those parts of the sky, it scorches the world with a more flaming heat. Autumn and evening are rightly delivered to the west, because then the harvest of all the fruits of the earth is finished, and the entire span of the day is ended. Winter and the dead of night are likened to the north, because then the earth is numb with cold, and the time is more suited for rest than for any work. 

Therefore, since it is established that all things are recovered through the Cross and reborn and improved through the passion of Christ, all things rightly come together in his praise. For he himself is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to whom alone those blessings belong which the three boys in the furnace of burning fire sang together and spoke, exhorting all creatures to the praise of the Creator:

> Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord, and so forth. <note>A reference to the "Song of the Three Holy Children" from the Book of Daniel</note>

Concerning which the <term>Psalmist: King David, traditionally credited with writing the Psalms</term> says:

> Let the heavens and the earth praise him, the sea and everything that is in them. <note>original: "Laudent eum cæli & terra, mare & omnia quæ in eis sunt"</note> For, according to the <term>Apostle: St. Paul</term>, from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be honor and glory forever and ever. <note>original: "ex ipso & per ipsum & in ipso sunt omnia, ipsi honor & gloria in sæcula sæculorum"</note>

Now, the reason why I have depicted the four elements, the four seasons, or the four regions of the world in wheels is this: because the entire machine of the world is temporal, and is variable or changeable by a certain mixing of elements and the succession of time, as <term>Solomon</term> bears witness, saying:

> All things have their time, and all things under heaven pass away in their own spans. <note>A paraphrase of Ecclesiastes 3:1</note>

Now fire dries the air, now water makes it wetter; now the earth is affected by the flooding of waters, now it is dried by the heat of the sun. Indeed, water is by nature mobile and completes a certain circle in its course. All rivers, says <term>Ecclesiasticus: Though the text cites Ecclesiasticus, this quote is from Ecclesiastes 1:7</term>, enter into the sea, yet the sea does not overflow; to the place from which the rivers come, they return so that they may flow again. [Fire] possesses this quality, from which it always raises itself higher when ignited and seeks a place for itself above the air. Lightnings flash across, and the ether <note>original: "æther"; the highest, purest part of the atmosphere in ancient cosmology</note> glitters with frequent fires. For the seasons pass by in cycles, and the successions of the four seasons—each comprised of three months—proceed in rounds. The year also received its name <note>The author likely connects "annus" (year) to "annulus" (ring or circuit)</note> from the fact that it always turns and returns into itself. The spirit <note>or "the wind," referencing Ecclesiastes 1:6</note> goes about turning and turning, and returns into its own circuits. Five zones hold the sky, where the slanted order of the signs <note>the zodiac</note> turns itself. There are also verses written within wheels based on a spherical or circular number <term>spherical number: a number which, when multiplied by itself, ends in the same digit, such as 6 x 6 = 36</term>: that is, 36, which results from multiplying six by six and terminates in a six. The first verse, located in the topmost circle, is this: **Spring, the rising sun, fire, and the dawn shine in this part.** In the lowest part, however, is this: **Autumn, the west wind, the earth, and evening happen here.** On the right side indeed: **Behold, the North <note>original: "Arcton," referring to the constellation of the Bear</note>, winter, water, and midnight are located here.** And on the left is this verse: **Air, summer, the south wind <note>original: "auster"</note>, and midday belong to this arc.**

<meta>This page continues the theological and cosmological justification for the number four, which the previous page introduced through mathematical concepts like the "spherical number." It moves from abstract geometry to the physical composition of the universe (the four elements) and how they are symbolically mapped onto the physical structure of the Cross.</meta>

-># EXPLANATION.<-

Almost no one is unaware that the number four <note>original: "quaternarium numerum"</note> is hallowed by its perfection, and therefore the entire world rightly venerates that number as it is transformed into the shape of the Cross of Christ. Indeed, it is manifest that the world consists of four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. It is also well known that the whole globe is bounded by four parts or corners: the East, the West, the North <note>original: "aquilone"; literally the North Wind</note>, and the South. There are likewise four turnings of the seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Furthermore, there are four quarters of the natural day—the twenty-four hours—which are distinguished by these starting points: morning, midday, evening, and the dead of night <note>original: "intempesto"; the "unseasonable" time when humans are inactive and deep in sleep</note>.

We must now explain how this arrangement can be appropriately fitted to the Cross. If we wish to look at the upright Cross, let us place fire—the highest of the elements—at its peak. Air and water, which are the middle elements, we assign to the transverse wood of the Cross <note>the horizontal crossbeam</note> which is drawn through the middle of the upright post. Earth, however, which is the heaviest and holds the lowest place among created things, we assign to the lower part of the Cross. Just as all these elements are mixed together by a certain natural proximity to complete the integrity of the world, they are also joined to the four parts of the Cross to demonstrate its perfect form.

If, however, we wish to assign the Cross to the four regions of the world, we must measure it lying down in this way: assign its first part to the East, the furthest part to the West, the right side to the North, and the left side to the South. Similarly, the four turnings of the seasons and of the natural day can be united in the Cross by the same arrangement, so that one image of the year or the day can be suitably shown in them.

For spring and the dawn bring forth the rising of light and the budding seeds in the earth in their proper order, and for this reason, they are rightly assigned to the East. Summer and midday are fitted to the South because of their heat; for while the sun is raised in those parts of the sky, it scorches the world with a more flaming heat. Autumn and evening are justly claimed by the West, because at that time the harvest of all the fruits of the earth is finished, and the entire span of the day is ended. Winter and the dead of night are likened to the North, because the earth then grows numb with cold, and the time is more suitable for rest than for any labor.

Therefore, since it is established that all things are recovered through the Cross, and reborn and improved through the passion of Christ, all things rightly come together for his praise. For he himself is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to whom alone those blessings belong which the three youths <note>the biblical Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the Book of Daniel</note> sang together while in the furnace of burning fire, exhorting all creatures to the praise of the Creator, saying: "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord," and so forth. Of this the Psalmist also says: "Let the heavens and earth praise him, the sea and everything that moves in them" <note>Psalm 69:34</note>; because, according to the Apostle <note>St. Paul, in Romans 11:36</note>, "from him and through him and in him are all things, to him be honor and glory forever and ever."

The reason why I have depicted the four elements, or the four seasons, or the four regions of the world within wheels <note>referring to the circular diagrams typical of this manuscript</note> is this: the entire machine of the world is temporal and—by a certain mixing of elements and the succession of time—variable or changeable. This is attested by Solomon, who says: "Everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass away in their own spaces" <note>Ecclesiastes 3:1</note>. Now fire dries the air; water makes it more humid; now the earth is affected by the flooding of waters; now it is dried by the heat of the sun. Indeed, water is mobile by nature and completes a certain circle in its course. As the book of Ecclesiasticus <note>The author quotes Ecclesiastes 1:7 here, though he attributes it to Ecclesiasticus (Sirach)</note> says: "All rivers enter the sea, yet the sea does not overflow; to the place from which the rivers come, they return to flow again." Fire also similarly has a natural motion,

### BOOK ONE. FOLIO XVII. ###

->**BOOK ONE. FOLIO XVII.**<-

Christ the Savior, Christ the King, serene in the heavenly heights,
Counsel, great power and blessing, the light,
The divine offspring of the Father: surely from this source
Every law draws its origin, the workmanship of the Creator, and pure custom its honor.
From here comes whatever good, true, and wondrous is seen,
Whatever of justice remains in the heavens or on the earth.
Whatever the world rightly approves and brings forth in order,
And the good angel, as well as those things which even the wicked must endure,
All are from here; and that law which God had cast down as vain,
He recalls from this age: behold, Christ as Lord embraces
All things with honor, and seals his gifts with a nod.
Hence it is fitting that the human race, though exiled from the light,
Should know these rays: which this blessed, saving Cross
Raises up, restoring that dawn of light which the first man once held,
But from which the fallen <term>Adam</term><note>The author refers to Adam not just as a historical figure, but as the representative of humanity's "exile" from divine light through the Fall.</note> had departed.
Indeed, as many as truly celebrate those rays
Shine with the perpetual light that frequently flashes forth.
By this brightness, the weapons of the <term>Prophets</term><note>original: "Prophetæ"; referring to the Old Testament seers whose foresight was seen as "armed" by divine truth.</note> shone sufficiently,
And the Apostolic flock is decorated with shimmering light.
By this the faith of Christ glows white; by this sun
The hearts of men shine brightly, and by this light the vows
Of the powerful and just flourish through mystical signs; they shall cast
A good ray of light to believe in the commands for His sake,
And they grant to the people the ability to mark the heavenly laws.
They record that Christ leads the fellowships of life:
Christ the King, the divine Lord, supreme in his gift,
Ascending the mighty wood of the Cross—behold, in this very act,
By planting that form, He delivered the opening of the heavens,
And willed that the grateful should be sought there.
Therefore, he blessed the twelve <note>original: "quater ternos" (four times three)</note> winds from the waters and the boundaries
Of the world in this path of the Cross; He himself,
As Prince, governs by encompassing the twelve signs <note>original: "signaq; bissena"; likely referring to the twelve signs of the Zodiac or the twelve Apostles as cosmic pillars.</note>,
And the rising region receives the twelvefold spaces of God
Drawn upon its shores—behold, the whole creation labors in these divisions,
For the Cross, the glory of Christ, releases all boundaries,
And standing there, it offers, marks, praises, and approves
The holy joys of the sky and the laws of the earth, and gives them as a gift.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of sacred geometry and numerology, specifically focusing on the number twelve as a bridge between the physical cosmos (the zodiac, seasons, and winds) and divine history (the Patriarchs, Apostles, and the New Jerusalem). ### EXPLANATION ###

->**EXPLANATION**<-

Therefore, why the <term>twelvefold</term><note>original: "Duodenarius"; referring to the symbolic and mathematical properties of the number twelve.</note> number so well and aptly fits the Holy Cross is of no small importance to understand. For there are twelve winds that blow through the world, and twelve signs of the <term>zodiac</term><note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, used here to show how the physical universe reflects divine order.</note>, in which the seven planets proceed in their circles in an orderly and arranged manner; and twelve months, by which the year's course is completed; and twelve hours of the daylight, by which the Sun illuminates the entire surface of the earth. There are also twelve <term>Patriarchs</term><note>The biblical ancestors of the Israelites, from whom the twelve tribes descended.</note>, from whom the entire multitude of the children of Israel was propagated, which possessed the promised land according to the lots of the twelve tribes, and from whom arose the Prophets, the heralds of the divine birth. From this lineage, the Savior himself deigned to take on flesh and be born among men. He, the light coming into this world, the <term>Sun of Justice</term><note>original: "Sol iustitiæ"; a common title for Christ, signifying him as the source of spiritual light and truth.</note>, chose twelve Apostles from that same nation, illuminating them like the hours of the day, and sent them through every region of the world to preach the faith of the Holy Trinity. And in the building of the heavenly Jerusalem, the mystery of this same number is suggested in many ways, as the <term>Apocalypse</term><note>The Book of Revelation.</note> shows, where it is written:

> And he showed me the holy city Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God, having the glory of God: and her light was like unto a stone most precious, even like a jasper stone, clear as crystal; and it had a wall great and high, and had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written thereon, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel. On the east three gates; on the north three gates; on the south three gates; and on the west three gates. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and in them the twelve names of the twelve Apostles of the Lamb, and so forth.

For the Holy Church is signified in this spiritual building, which is namely the heavenly Jerusalem and the city of the great king, whose architect and founder is God. He is both its foundation and its completion, who also deigned to become our <term>high priest</term><note>original: "pontifex"; literally a "bridge-builder," here referring to Christ's role as the intermediary between God and humanity.</note>, so that by the sacrifice of his own blood he might wash and likewise dedicate the walls of that city. He possesses all things that are his own in peace; wherefore, on the breast of the high priest, twelve precious stones were seen to be placed, arranged in four rows and inscribed with the names of the twelve Patriarchs. This was done so that by a most beautiful mystery it might be revealed that all spiritual gifts—which each of the saints achieved individually and in part—were fulfilled together and perfectly in the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. John also testifies to this in his Gospel:

> And the Word, he said, was made flesh, and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.

And a little later:

> And of his fullness have we all received, and grace for grace. For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.

Therefore, this form of the Holy Cross has three lines on its tips <note>original: "cornibus"; literally "horns," referring to the ends of the cross-arms.</note> to demonstrate that, just as the cross itself has neighboring and adhering lines on its right and left in its direct path, so the four principal cardinal winds associate other winds with them by their position on the right and left. In the same way, the four seasons, each having three months, are divided—whether centered on the equinoxes or the solstices—according to certain calculations. This will be clear to anyone who diligently cares to learn the systems of time used by the Greeks or Egyptians. There are, however...

<meta>Continuing the mathematical meditation on the Holy Cross from Folio XIX. The previous page introduced a grid poem calculating the days of the year; this page, titled "Declaration," provides the mathematical and theological proof for how the Cross governs the solar calendar and the leap year cycle.</meta>

->**DECLARATION**<-

Therefore, this figure of the holy Cross—composed of four hexagons and a single unit <note>original: "monadem," referring to the central point of the cross</note> placed in their midst—encompasses all the days of the year. For the solar year contains 365 days and a quarter-day. If you divide these by four, you get four times 91, which equals 364, leaving a remainder of one day and a quarter. If you then divide that one remaining day by four, you get four times six hours, which equals 24—the length of a full day from one sunrise to the next. Furthermore, if you divide that quarter-day itself, you find that four times an hour and a half completes six hours; this represents the annual increment of the Leap Year <term>Bissextus; the extra day added every four years to keep the calendar aligned with the sun</term>. From this, it follows that if you divide the entire year into four parts, each part contains 91 days and seven and a half hours. This constitutes the true division of the four seasons—Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter—so that each possesses 91 days and seven and a half hours.

It should be noted, however, that in this figure, the demonstration of the quarter-day is only revealed through the understanding and examination of the six angles <note>referring to the points of the hexagons in the visual poem</note>, so that each individual hour is assigned to an individual angle. If you look closely at the angles of the four hexagons, you will count 24 hours within them; it is by this fullness of hours that the leap-year day is completed. This mathematical ratio is most fittingly applied to this subject. For if, over four years, the quarter-portions reach the sum of one full day, the Cross rightly demonstrates both the rule and the pattern of "four times six hours" through its four hexagons.

The hexagon was rightly and divinely ordained for this arrangement because the number six <term>senarius numerus; the number six was considered a "perfect number" in medieval mathematics because its factors (1, 2, and 3) sum to itself</term> is of the greatest importance in the entire series of the year. To demonstrate this, let us include a passage from the fourth book of Saint Augustine's *On the Holy Trinity*:

"Even a single year, if we consider twelve full months of thirty days each (for the ancients observed such a month based on the lunar cycle), excels through the number six. For whatever the value of six is in the first order of numbers (the ones, which go up to ten), that same value is held by sixty in the second order (the tens, which go up to a hundred). Therefore, a sixty-day period is the sixth part of a year. Accordingly, the sixes of the first row are multiplied by the sixes of the second row, resulting in six times sixty: 360 days, which constitute twelve full months. But just as the lunar cycle reveals the month to mankind, the solar cycle reveals the year. There remain, however, five days and a quarter-day for the sun to complete its course and conclude the year. For four quarters make one day, which must be intercalated <note>inserted into the calendar</note> after four years have passed—which they call a Leap Year—so that the order of time is not disturbed. Even if we consider those five days and the quarter-day, the number six remains most powerful within them. First, as is common when a whole is calculated by its part, we may count six days rather than five, treating that quarter-day as a whole. Furthermore, because within those five days is the sixth part of a month, and the quarter-day itself consists of six hours. For a full day and night consists of 24 hours, of which the fourth part—the quarter-day—is found to be six hours. Thus, in the course of the year, the number six is of the highest importance."

It is with good reason, then, that the series of days has been adapted to the holy Cross, for through the Cross the hearts of men are illuminated. The joining of the hexagons is suited to it because in the Cross resides the perfection of all things. The order of temporal light <note>the sun and the calendar</note> agrees with it, because through the Cross man finds eternal light. The number ninety [90] and the single unit [1] <note>making 91, the number of days in a season calculated earlier</note> concur with it, because through the Cross the angelic order reaches the fullness of its number. To the center of the Cross, the hexagons directed from the four sides are joined by unity: because through...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Folio XIX regarding the mathematical and symbolic properties of the Cross. # BOOK ONE. FOLIO XX #

To His majesty all nations from the four quarters of the world are joined in the unity of faith; and by His completed work, celestial and earthly creatures are joined in one charity. To Him be honor and majesty: through whose mercy all these things were accomplished, praise and glory forever and ever.

Indeed, this form of the holy Cross contains, along its vertical length through two hexagons, a Sapphic meter, which is a pentameter <note>a line consisting of five metrical feet</note> and a hendecasyllable <note>a line of eleven syllables</note>, and there are three such equal verses. Each of these receives four feet of two syllables—a trochee <term>a metrical foot consisting of a long syllable followed by a short one</term>, a spondee <term>two long syllables</term>, another trochee, and an iamb <term>a short syllable followed by a long one</term>—and a final three-syllable bacchius <term>one short syllable followed by two long ones</term>. After these three verses, a dactylic dicolos <note>a short verse of two units, also known as an Adonic line</note> is added, which consists of a dactyl <term>one long syllable followed by two short ones</term> and a spondee. 

In the uppermost hexagon are these verses: 
**Three times a hundred, six times ten, and five once—the whole of time contains this many. The annual circuit is within the Cross. Behold the day here.** 
In the second hexagon are these as well: 
**But placed within the regions of the hexagon, four show ten times nine. Each reveals the whole, piously with the unit. And one more besides.** 
It must be noted, however, that the upper verses have **92** letters, because they draw to themselves the letter 'C' which is in the middle of the hexagons, while the following verses have **91**.

Those two hexagons, however, which form the transverse part <note>the horizontal crossbeam</note> of the Cross, are composed in elegiac meter <term>a poetic form consisting of alternating lines of hexameter and pentameter</term>. The first of these contains these verses: 
**The holy stem of the Cross also completes the scepter in a certain order. This is the beauty of the world and this the great salvation of men.** 
The latter hexagon has these: 
**Christ holds all things: the abyss, the world, and the high heavens. For He rules the stars of the sky and all the gates of the day.**

# XIX. O. EXPLANATION #

Therefore, this figure of the holy Cross, through four hexagons and through a monad <term>a single unit or the number one</term> placed in their midst, encompasses all the days of the year. For indeed, the solar year has 365 days and a quadrant <note>a quarter of a day, or six hours</note>. Divide these by four: four times 91 makes 364, and there remains one day and a quadrant. Divide that one day by four: four times six hours makes 24, which is a complete day from one sunrise to the next. Divide the quadrant itself: for four times one hour and a half completes six hours <note>1.5 hours x 4 = 6 hours</note>, which is the increment of the bissextile <term>the leap year day</term> for each individual year. 

From this, it follows that if you divide the whole year into four parts, each part contains 91 days and seven and a half hours. This becomes the true partition of the four seasons—that is, spring, summer, autumn, and winter—so that each has 91 days and seven and a half hours. It should be noted, however, that in this figure, the demonstration of the quadrant <note>the six-hour remainder</note> is only made possible through the understanding and examination of the six angles, so that each hour is assigned to an individual angle. For if you look closely at the four hexagons in their angles, you will notice 24 hours in them: by which fullness of hours the leap day is completed. This logic is not absurdly applied to this matter. For if in four years the portion of the quadrant reaches the sum of one day, the Cross rightly shows the rule and measure of four times six hours in the four hexagons. 

Rightly, therefore, the hexagon was divinely ordained for this arrangement, because the number six <note>original: "senarius numerus"</note> is of great value in the entire series of the year. To demonstrate this, let us include a passage from a chapter of the book of **Saint Augustine**, the fourth volume of *On the Holy Trinity*: 

"Even a single year, if the twelve complete months are considered, which thirty days each fulfill (for the ancients observed such a month, which the lunar cycle <note>original: "circuitus lunaris"</note> reveals), excels by the number six. For what six is worth in the first order of numbers, which consists of units to reach ten, sixty is worth in the second order, which consists of tens to reach a hundred. Therefore, the number sixty is the sixth part of the year. Accordingly, they are multiplied by the six of the first row, as if by the six of the second row, and they become six times sixty, which is 360 days, comprising twelve full months. But because just as the cycle of the moon shows the month to men, so the year is perceived by the cycle of the sun. There remain five days and a quadrant of a day for the sun to complete its course and conclude the year. For four quadrants make one day, which must be intercalated <note>inserted into the calendar</note> after four years have passed (which they call the bissextum <term>leap year</term>) so that the order of seasons is not disturbed. Even if we consider those five days and the quadrant, the number six is of great value in them. First, as is customary for the whole to be calculated by the part, there are not just five days but rather six, if that quadrant is accepted as one day. Secondly, because within those five days is the sixth part of a month <note>5 days is 1/6 of a 30-day month</note>, and the quadrant itself has six hours. For a whole day—that is, with its night—is 24 hours, of which the fourth part, which is the quadrant of the day, is found to be six hours. Thus, in the course of the year, the number six is of great value."

Meritedly, therefore, the series of days has been fitted to the holy Cross, because through the Cross the hearts of men are illuminated. The joining of the hexagons is appropriate to it, because in the Cross consists the perfection of things. The order of temporal light conforms to it, because through the Cross man finds eternal light. To the Cross, the number ninety <note>the 91 days minus the central monad</note> concurs with the monad, because through the Cross the angelic order <note>historically associated with the number 9 or 99</note> reaches the fullness of its number. To its center point, from four directions, the hexagons are joined by unity...

<page-num>FOLIO XX</page-num>
<header>BOOK ONE</header>

Through His majesty, all nations from the four quarters <note>original: "plagis," referring to the চার cardinal directions</note> of the world are joined in the unity of faith; and with His work completed, heavenly and earthly creatures are joined by a single charity. To Him be honor and majesty; through whose mercy all these things were accomplished, praise and glory forever and ever.

Indeed, this form of the holy Cross contains, along its length through two hexagons, a Sapphic meter <note>A complex verse form named after the Greek poet Sappho</note>, which is a pentameter <term>a line consisting of five poetic feet</term>, hendecasyllabic <term>having eleven syllables</term>, and its three lines are equal. Each of these lines receives these four feet of two syllables: a trochee <note>a long syllable followed by a short one</note>, a spondee <note>two long syllables</note>, a trochee, an iamb <note>a short syllable followed by a long one</note>, and finally a three-syllable bacchius <note>a short syllable followed by two long ones</note>. After these three verses, a dactylic dicolos <note>a two-part line; specifically an Adonic line</note> is added, which consists of a dactyl <note>one long and two short syllables</note> and a spondee.

In the topmost hexagon are these verses:
> Three times a hundred, ten times six, and once five, the universe has.
> The time: the yearly circuit upon the Cross. 
> Behold the day here. 
<note>The Latin verse "Terq; centenos deciefq; fenos, & femel quinos" mathematically describes the 365 days of the year: (3x100) + (10x6) + 5 = 365.</note>

And in the second [hexagon] are these:
> But the hexagons placed sufficiently in the regions.
> Four show ten times nine. 
> Each shows all piously with the monad <term>the unit of one</term>.
> And one above.
<note>The math here refers to the four hexagons representing 90 days each, plus the central unit, totaling 361, with further units added to reach the solar total described on the previous page.</note>

It should be noted that the upper verses, because they draw to themselves the letter **C** <note>The letter C often represented the number 100 in Roman numerals, or served as a central "hub" letter in the poem's grid</note> which is in the middle of the hexagons, have 92 letters, whereas the following verses have 91. 

However, those two hexagons which form the transverse <note>horizontal</note> part of the Cross are composed in elegiac meter <note>Alternating lines of dactylic hexameter and pentameter, often used for mournful or memorial inscriptions</note>, of which the first has these verses:
> The holy lineage of the Cross also completes the scepter in a fixed order.
> This is the glory of the world and this is the great salvation of men.

And the latter has these:
> Christ holds all things: the abyss, the world, and the high heavens.
> For He rules the stars of the pole and all the barriers of the day.

->### FOLIO XXI.<-

Behold what brings life, what corruption fears,
What looses our debts, and what causes clinging chains to yield;
Now it is fitting that the truthful Muse, cheerful with hope,
Should bring forth in this blessed song the steep heights and deeds of the Cross.
Rightly let every voice from the throat ring out with this art:
Mouth, fingers, quill, vows, heart, tongue, and speech.
For the grim dragon <note>A reference to Satan as the serpent from Revelation</note> fell in war—that savage, harmful one
Who by poisoned art expelled man from Eden.
And falling from the citadel of heaven, Lucifer <note>The name "Lucifer" literally means "light-bringer," referring to the fallen angel</note>
Dragged with him a third part of the stars to the
Sulfurous smoking pools of hell; because, guilty and proud through deceit,
He tried to make himself like the Supreme Being above,
Establishing his throne in the cold seat of the North. <note>original: "Aquilonis." In biblical tradition, the North was often associated with the seat of evil or the dwelling of a vainglorious power (Isaiah 14:13).</note>
And the Lamb overcame this wolf; by powerful right
He snatched away the prey and suppressed his fierce efforts.
Nay, he even converted the nations by his will to the sacred tidings,
Marking better things and granting heavenly gifts.
Lest a fable now harm this chaste birth in its white rising,
Let him who perceived open dogmas <term>dogmata: established religious principles or doctrines</term> rise in strength;
Lest the mouth dry up from singing, the King refills the parched and drained places,
And the Author of the seed makes them fertile in sacred praise.
Behold, the generous power of the Cross drives out treachery
Through its gift, releasing the world's debts.
Finally, this number signifies to the whole world
That redemption was manifest: the seventy weeks of Daniel <note>original: "Danielis septuaginta ebdomadæ." This refers to the prophecy in Daniel 9:24-27 regarding the timing of the Messiah’s arrival.</note>
Mark this, so that transgression might receive a certain end,
Along with sin, guilt, and iniquity;
And that the Creator himself might bring in everlasting justice.
Jeremiah wrote of ten-times-seven years, <note>The 70 years of Babylonian exile predicted in Jeremiah 25:11.</note>
After which the Author himself would loose his people from their chains.
And Moses himself, by his warning, distinguished the healthy ones,
Those seventy elders whom he patiently taught.
You, O Cross, bringing peace to the ages, purify everything
With the blessed word of the Gospel, the Decalogue, <note>original: "decalogi." The Ten Commandments.</note> and the bright covenant.
Nor will you, I think, be a powerless figure inscribed here,
If you grant to the five senses <note>original: "quinis sensus"</note> that everyone might piously,
Magnificently, and pleasingly favor you by just right.

<meta>This page transitions from the poetic verses of the previous folio to a prose "Explanation" (Declaratio). It provides a theological commentary on the numerical symbolism within the cross's design, specifically focusing on the number seventy as it relates to the prophecies of Jeremiah and Daniel.</meta>

-># EXPLANATION.<-
<meta>catchword: years</meta>

Indeed, the present form of the holy cross, written with scattered letters, demonstrates the number seventy <note>original: "Septuagenarium... numerum"</note>. This suggests to us that all the mysteries contained within that same number are most fittingly suited to the honor of the holy cross. For what else do the seventy years of captivity, which the Prophet Jeremiah foretold would come upon the sacrilegious people, signify? They represent the entire span of this life, which runs through the seven-day cycle of the week. In this time, we are condemned because of the sin of the first man; we are afflicted by punishments and hardships, and we are daily affected by various tribulations and anxieties. 

But because the same Prophet announced the end of the captivity after seventy years, this implies—if I am not mistaken—that at the end of the world, our captivity will be perfectly dissolved. This is when the last enemy, death, shall be destroyed; when we shall rejoice without end with Christ, both in the beauty of the soul and the immortality of the body. Therefore, it was fitting for this reasoning to be shown in the form of the holy cross, because the cross itself, through the passion of Christ, bestowed upon us the effect of this grace. The very words of the Prophet agree with this, saying: "Thus says the Lord: When the seventy years begin to be fulfilled in Babylon, I will visit you, and I will rouse my good word over you, and bring you back to this place. For I know the thoughts of peace and not of affliction that I think toward you, to give you a good end and patience. And you shall call upon me, and you shall go and adore me, and I will hear you. You shall seek me and you shall not find me <note>The text here follows a variation of Jeremiah 29:13; usually "you shall find me when you seek with your whole heart."</note> until you have sought me with all your heart; then I will be found by you, says the Lord, and I will bring back your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations and all the places to which I drove you, and I will make you return to the place from which I caused you to be moved," and so forth. 

For what does the Prophet mean when he says, "When the seventy years begin to be fulfilled in Babylon, I will visit you, and rouse my good word over you," if not what the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note> says: "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive the adoption of sons"? And likewise: "In these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the worlds." 

He said, "when they begin to be fulfilled," not "when they have been completed," because Christ was incarnated not at the very consummation of the world, but in the final age of the world <note>Early Christian scholars often divided history into six or seven "ages"; Christ's arrival marked the beginning of the final era.</note>. Through the word of the Gospel, he enlightened the believers, and through his passion and resurrection, he restored the human race. The fact that he predicts a "return" twice in this passage—first when he says, "And I will bring you back to this place," and a little later adding, "And I will make you return to the place from which I caused you to be moved"—can be understood such that the first sentence suggests the soul's return to rest, and the second suggests the resurrection of bodies to glory. Therefore, after death, the souls of the saints now go into paradise, and at the end of the world, receiving their bodies back, they shall enter the eternal kingdom. 

Furthermore, Daniel counted seventy weeks <term>weeks: "hebdomadas," refers here to the "Seventy Weeks" prophecy in Daniel 9, where each "week" is interpreted as seven years, totaling 490 years.</term> until Christ, when transgression and sin would receive an end, and everlasting justice would be brought in. Truly, so that these things may shine more clearly, let us look at the very words of the angel to the Prophet. "Seventy weeks," he said, "are shortened upon your people and upon your holy city, that transgression may be finished, and sin may receive an end, and iniquity may be abolished, and everlasting justice may be brought in, and vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed," and so forth. There is no doubt that these words designate the incarnation of Christ, who took away the sins of the world, fulfilled the law and the prophets, and was anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows. Therefore, let these weeks be counted by sevens...

-># EXPLANATION. FOLIO 22.<-

...years, distinguished from the twentieth year of the reign of King Artaxerxes, when Nehemiah his cupbearer <note>Nehemiah 2:1 describes Nehemiah serving wine to the Persian King Artaxerxes I.</note> obtained permission from him to restore the walls of Jerusalem—the temple having been built much earlier by the permission of Cyrus—which are described as being "shortened," that is, according to the lunar calculation of twelve lunar months. From this come four hundred and ninety years <note>The "seventy weeks" of Daniel 9:24 are interpreted as 490 years (70 x 7).</note>, which, when reduced to the solar cycle, make 475 years. Indeed, up to his baptism, when the "Holy of Holies" <note>original: "sanctus sanctorum"</note> was anointed as the Holy Spirit descended upon him like a dove, not only were the 7 and 62 weeks completed, but also a part of the seventieth week had begun.

And "after the sixty-two weeks," it says, "Christ shall be put to death, and the people who denied him shall no longer be his." <note>A paraphrase of Daniel 9:26.</note> Christ was not put to death immediately after the sixty-two weeks, but at the end of the seventieth week, which he set apart from the others—as far as we can surmise—because he was going to relate more concerning it. For Christ was crucified in that week, and he was denied by a faithless people, not only during his passion but continuously from the moment he began to be preached by John. "He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week," <note>Daniel 9:27.</note> namely, that very last one, in which either John the Baptist or the Lord and the Apostles converted many to the faith through their preaching. 

"And in the middle of the week, the victim and the sacrifice shall fail" <note>Daniel 9:27.</note>—that is, in the 15th year of Tiberius Caesar, when, after Christ’s baptism had begun, the purification by animal sacrifices began to lose value little by little among the faithful in Christ. And rightly so, because the more the Truth approached, the more the shadow receded. It was also fitting that when the Savior himself willed to become the sacrifice required by law <term>legalis hostia: a sacrifice fulfilling the requirements of the Old Testament Law</term> upon the Cross, the victim of cattle should cease; and when the true Lamb of God, Christ, was sacrificed for the sins of the whole world, that symbolic <note>original: "typicus"</note> lamb should fail, which had been slain as a witness for the liberation of only one nation. 

Likewise, Moses placed seventy elders over the people by the Lord’s command, to show that only those who spiritually understand the Law through the grace of the Holy Spirit are fit to provide leadership. And it was fitting for this to be shown in the number of the holy Cross, because no one was found, "neither in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth, who could open the book and loosen its seven seals, or look upon it," except for the Lamb who stands in the midst of the throne as if slain, "having seven horns and seven eyes." <note>References to the Book of Revelation (Apocalypse) 5:3-6.</note> Indeed, he is the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, who "holds the key, and when he shuts no one opens, and when he opens no one shuts"; <note>Revelation 3:7 and Isaiah 22:22.</note> who was given as "a light to the nations, that he might open the eyes of the blind, and bring out the prisoner from confinement, from the prison house, those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death." <note>Isaiah 42:6-7.</note>

There are, indeed, five little circles <note>original: "sperulae" (little spheres); these are the circular clusters of letters in the visual poem.</note> arranged here in the figure of the holy cross, which together contain the number seventy; individually, however, each contains fourteen letters. Three of these form one verse in length, beginning from the top and ending at the bottom, thus: 

**The pious cross constructed here, you have overcome the bonds of death.** 

Likewise, in width, three of the totals form another verse, thus: 

**Great, good, and holy, here you have overcome the crimes of the age.** 

The middle of the cross is also common to both verses.

# FIGURE XI. An explanation of the five books of Moses and how they are renewed through the Cross.

<note>This page features a "carmen figuratum" or "grid poem," where the text is laid out in a perfect square of letters. You, nurturing Father, teacher of the heavens, in this song
and Ruler I call upon; look with favor on these happy beginnings.

so that I might be able to reveal what your first Law signifies.

giving the true gifts of light with the Cross to the ages.
For <insert>Genesis</insert> <note>Genesis is the first book of the Bible, meaning "Origin."</note> praises this wonderful tree of life,
which was planted among all things in Paradise,
a life-giving wood, offering the gifts of fruit.
This wood the father <note>Abraham</note> and Isaac, who was to be sacrificed, carried to the altar.

carried it [the cluster of grapes] which the shoulder of the priest sings of.

it wets with its passage; the enemy sings because of the great wonders.
And the people sing a song to Him; the pure one excellently admires the trophies.
In praise and love of God, he sings psalms of the Triumph of God.

But this wood <note>The Cross, prefigured by the wood Moses threw into the bitter water.</note> sweetened the ancient abyss of the Law.
Twice it strikes the rock and brought forth living water.

the sign of this Cross likewise deleted his name and that one's.
Both scouts carried back this holy cluster of grapes on a pole <note>A famous image from the Book of Numbers: two men carrying a massive cluster of grapes on a pole, often seen as a symbol of Christ on the Cross.</note>.
With the prayers and triumphs of the carriers, they praise all things,
the gifts of God to these lands, the ineffable joys of the banquets.

# XIIII

-> DECLARATION. <-

Whoever desires to have full knowledge of the first law <note>The "first law" refers to the Torah or Pentateuch.</note> must be mindful of this figure <note>The author is referring to a diagram or "figure" (likely a cross-shaped arrangement of text) that this text accompanies.</note> in all its parts, and should frequently revolve its construction in their mind. Comparing what comes before with what follows, they should recall what is written: *All these things happened to them in figures <note>original: "in figura"; this refers to "typology," the idea that Old Testament events foreshadowed New Testament truths.</note>, but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come;* and that *they serve as a copy and shadow of heavenly things;* and likewise, *for the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things.* For a shadow does not exist without a true body; yet the shadow itself does not express the true and complete appearance of the body. Therefore, it is necessary that whoever is a lover of truth, if they first see the shadow, should quickly turn their eyes toward the true body of which that shadow is a part; lest, while they remain stuck gazing deeply into the shadow, they neglect and lose the fruit of the truth.

The Law, therefore, offered a drink to the thirsty, but without the wood <note>The "wood" is a constant metaphor for the Cross of Christ.</note> it was not fit to drink. Indeed, the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood which, when he threw it into the water, took away all its bitterness; and that which previously attracted the thirsty people with a false appearance, once the wood was put in, refreshed them all with a most sweet drink <note>This refers to the miracle at Marah in Exodus 15:23–25, where bitter water was made sweet.</note>. Thus, according to the Apostle <note>The "Apostle" almost always refers to St. Paul.</note>, the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good; but the law is Spiritual, as the same Apostle says, and it must be understood not in the oldness of the letter, but in the newness of the Spirit. *For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.* Therefore, the Law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set us free from the law of sin and death. For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. 

For it is written in the law: *Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all things written in the book of the law to do them.* But since no one is justified before God by the law, and whoever relies on the works of the law is under a curse, Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: *Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree <note>original: "ligno," literally "wood," referring to the Cross.</note>;* so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith. 

Therefore, since the curse of the law has been destroyed through the Cross, and its bitterness turned into sweetness through the same, it is fitting that the books of the law be arranged in the image of the Cross, so that the harmony of the work may be known in this, and the sacrament of the mystery may appear. Therefore, at the head—that is, at the summit of the holy Cross—let the book of <insert>Genesis</insert> be placed, because it is the head and the first of all books, telling how in the beginning God made heaven and earth; specifically, God the Father through his Son, co-eternal with himself—that is, through his Word. Of this the Psalmist says: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth.* Hence the Evangelist John also says: *All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.* 

At the bottom part of the Cross, however—that is, at the foot—let the last of the five books of the law be placed, which is <insert>Deuteronomy</insert>, which is interpreted as the "renewal of the law"; certainly signifying the Gospel, in which all things that the law brought forth figuratively and typically are truly and Spiritually explained, and opened by the mouth of our Savior. Rightly, then, Genesis stands at the head of the Cross and Deuteronomy at the end; because the one whom the law describes as having created all things with the Father at the beginning of time, the Gospel records as having renewed all things through the Cross at the end of time. <insert>Exodus</insert>, however, is well placed on the right, in which the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt is recorded, and in the same place many miracles performed by the Lord are told, according to that 

<meta>catchword: Psalm.</meta>

# XXIII.

-> DECLARATION. PAGE XXIII. <-

The Psalmist says: *The right hand of the Lord has shown strength.* <note>original: "Dextera Domini fecit virtutem"; Psalm 118:16.</note> And likewise: *He who struck Egypt with their firstborn, and led Israel out from their midst, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm.* <note>Psalm 136:10-12.</note> On the left, the book of **Numbers** is placed: because it describes how the "left-handed" <note>In medieval symbolism, the "left" often represented dissent or those who strayed from the path.</note> congregations of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram raised contentions against Moses and Aaron, and were quickly suppressed through the power of the Lord.

But **Leviticus**, standing in the middle of them all, holds the center of the cross: because it signifies that High Priest in the many rites of sacrifice, who offered himself on the altar of the Cross as an immaculate victim to God, to drain away the sins of many; and praying for transgressors, he was heard because of his reverence. <note>This draws a parallel between the priestly laws of Leviticus and Christ's sacrifice as described in the Book of Hebrews.</note>

Therefore, in five squares <note><term>tetragonis</term>: four-sided figures or squares used in the visual layout of the manuscript.</note>, the five books of the Law are noted here through five verses. These are located in the sixth position according to the order of the squares, and by the number six multiplied by itself. For six times six makes the sixth square in a flat figure, which totals thirty-six. <note>The author is explaining the mathematical structure of the grid used to create the visual poem.</note>

The verse of the square placed at the summit of the Cross is this:
*Nurturing Cross, Genesis blesses you and praises your gifts.* <note>original: "Te Genesis Crux alma beat tua munera laudat."</note>

The second verse, which is placed here in the corner of the right arm of the square:
*And Exodus sings a song of the passage with love.* <note>original: "Exodus atq; canit transitus carmen amore."</note>

For the third is situated here in the middle of the Cross:
*Leviticus sings most excellently of the laws of the priest.* <note>original: "Iura sacerdotis Leuiticus optimè psallit."</note>

The fourth indeed is written thus in the left arm:
*But Numbers sings the wondrous miracles of triumph.* <note>original: "Ast Numerus cantat magnalia mira triumphi."</note>

The last also, which is described in the final square—that is, at the base of the Cross—sounds thus:
*For Deuteronomy speaks of the joys of the one who renews.* <note>original: "Nam Deuteronomium renouantis guadia dicit."</note>

# XII. Figure. Regarding the name of Adam the first-formed, how it signifies the Second Adam, and demonstrates His Passion.

-> **THE POEM IN THE GRID** <-

Proceed, Muse, to tell in beautiful verse the soul-saving
praises of the Lord’s Cross, the solace and the deed
in which death was conquered and all sins forgiven;
light has returned to the world and comes with the gift of mercy.
For the first Adam <note>The "first-formed" (protoplastus) man of Genesis.</note> took away all that was worthy of beauty
from his entire offspring when he ate the harmful food.
All beautiful and dear, blessed things lacked substance
until Jesus, the holy **Second Adam** <note>A theological title for Jesus Christ, who undoes the fall of the first Adam (see 1 Corinthians 15:45).</note>, came into the fields.
Through the crime of one man, all descendants suffered
such great losses, perishing in all things and under death;
but by the gift of one man, all believers everywhere are saved,
destined to enjoy the supernal light.
Finally, through the wood <note>The Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil.</note> harmful death reigned,
ruling over the world; and through the wood <note>The Wood of the Cross.</note> it strongly
lost its hold on the blessed kingdom and lost it all.
Once, the wicked one took away many through a harmful tree;
behold, Christ granted so much that from here there is a gate
for the whole world; for here the Pious One established the whole form,
removing the dire altars within,
and had given light to the heart and established a covenant.
The first man was of the earth and fathered only earthly
children, leaving behind the debts of death.
The later one, however, was the true heavenly Adam,
and He remains heavenly, whose generation is a wheel.
He, the Lord of the world, reigns forever over the land,
the sea, and the heavens, and gives gifts to the blessed with His reign.
The Creator himself, the Adam of the whole world,
[established] four regions of the world by right, as if named after him;
His light and virtue bear witness to the Lord everywhere.
Behold: **Anatole**, **Dysis**, **Arctos**, and **Mesembria** <note>original: "Anatol, Dysis, Arcton, Mesembria." These are the Greek names for the four cardinal directions: East (Anatole), West (Dysis), North (Arktos), and South (Mesembria). In the manuscript's grid, the first letters of these four words—A, D, A, M—spell the name of the first man.</note>
thus designate the Father by skill, so that all might piously
recognize the Lord as their author with blessed praise,
and let them celebrate Christ, because he is truly the Son
of the Highest Father and the true right hand of the Thunderer <note>original: "Tonantis." A classical epithet for a high god, here applied to God the Father.</note>,
whose care is good and who has made the medicine of salvation.

<summary>This page explores the symbolic connection between the name 'Adam' and the four cardinal directions in Greek, arguing that the first man's name prefigured Christ's universal redemption on the Cross. It contrasts the 'earthly' first Adam, who brought death through a tree, with the 'heavenly' second Adam (Christ), who brought life through the wood of the Cross.</summary>

Proceed, Muse, to tell in beautiful verse of the soul-saving
Praise of the Lord’s Cross, its solace and its deed,
In which death was conquered, all sins forgiven,
Light returned to the world, and came with the gift of mercy.
For the first Adam <note>The first man, through whom sin entered the world.</note> took away all that was worthy of honor
From his whole progeny, when he ate the harmful food:
All lovely and good things returned, dear and blessed,
When Jesus, the holy **Second Adam**, came into the fields.
From the crime of one man, all descendants suffered so many losses
In all things, and being lesser, were destined to perish in death:
But by the gift of one man, all believers are saved everywhere,
And shall enjoy the light from above.
Finally, through the wood <note>The Tree of Knowledge in Eden.</note>, harmful death reigned
Even over the whole world; and by the wood <note>The Wood of the Cross.</note> it strongly
Lost its captive kingdom and lost it all:
And the wicked one had once lost many harmful things.
Behold, Christ granted that from here there is a door to the whole
Circle, to the world: for here this Pious One
Established the whole form, removing the dread altars within,
And gave light to the heart, and struck a covenant.
The first man was of the earth, and all his children
He sired for the earth, leaving them the debts of death:
The latter Adam <note>Christ.</note> was the true and heavenly one,
And His whole generation remains heavenly,
He is the Lord of the world, of earth, sea, and sky,
He reigns forever and grants kingdoms to the blessed.
The Creator himself will give the four regions of the whole world
Rightly to Adam, as if they were named from his name:
Whose light and virtue testify to the Lord everywhere.
Behold <term>East</term> <note>original: "anatol"</note>, <term>West</term> <note>original: "dysis"</note>, <term>North</term> <note>original: "arcton"</note>, <term>South</term> <note>original: "mezembria"</note>; these thus
He designates with the art of song; behold, it is fitting that all things
Holy should know their Author and Lord with blessed praise:
And let them celebrate Christ, for He is truly the Son
Of the Most High Father, and the true right hand of the **Thunderer** <note>A classical epithet for God (originally Jupiter), here used to emphasize Christ's divine power.</note>:
Whose care is good, and whose touch is the medicine of salvation.

->### EXPLANATION.<-

<meta>catchword: who</meta>

What therefore this figure and this writing mean must be understood. For the name of the first man, that is, **Adam**, is arranged in the figure and form of the holy cross: from him all nations have arisen, and the entire human race has drawn its origin. He, according to the Apostle <note>St. Paul.</note>, is a "type of the one who was to come," namely **Christ**, about whom the same Apostle says: *“The first Adam was made into a living soul, the last Adam into a life-giving spirit.”* And a little later: *“The first man,”* he says, *“is of the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly man, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly man, so also are the heavenly. Therefore, just as we carry the image of the earthly, let us also carry the image of the heavenly.”* And why he said this, he immediately added the reason: *“Now this I say, brothers, because flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, nor shall corruption possess incorruption.”* For the name **Adam** is rightly placed, shaped into a cross, in which the entire human race is known to have been set free through Christ; nor is the appearance of our redemption more suitably held in any other form than in that one, where the wounds of the whole world could be encompassed. This is indeed the holy Cross, which, as it lies, measures the entire globe, of which the Poet <note>original: "Poëta"; likely referring to the Christian poet Sedulius or Arator.</note> says: *“From there it gathers the four quarters of the squared world. The brilliant Dawn shines from the summit of the Creator. The sacred feet are licked by the setting star. The right hand holds the North, the left raises the central axis. And all of nature lives from the limbs of the Creator.”* And the Lord, fixed to the cross, rules the world from every side.

This same thing was also designated long ago in the name of the <term>Protoplast</term> <note>From Greek "protoplastos," meaning the first-formed or first-created man (Adam).</note>, namely **Adam**. In his name of four letters, the four parts of the world are shown through Greek names. For if East, West, North, and South are spoken in Greek—as holy scripture mentions them in many places—you will find **Adam** in the first letters of the words. For the four mentioned parts of the world are called in Greek: *Anatole* <note>East</note>, *Dysis* <note>West</note>, *Arctos* <note>North</note>, *Mezembria* <note>South</note>. These four names, if you write them under one another like four lines of verse, **Adam** is read in their first letters: and from this it is given to be understood that he was created as the lord of the world, and to signify him who, on the squared cross, was to be the redeemer and restorer of the entire world. 

Whence he is also called the **Second Adam**. This same name also contains within itself the mystery of the Incarnation of Christ, if the number in the letters of the same name is considered according to the Greek rule <note>This refers to <term>Gematria</term>, a system where letters represent numbers.</note>, for those who calculate their numbers by letters. For **A** in numbers among the Greeks signifies one (1). **Δ** (Delta) signifies four (4). The other **A** signifies one (1). **M** signifies forty (40). Combine these four numbers and they become forty-six (46). And this is what the Jews are read to have answered in the Gospel: *“This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?”* Understanding this, the Evangelist said: *“But he was saying this about the temple of his body,”* because our Lord Jesus Christ took his body from Adam, but did not draw sin from Adam; he took his bodily temple from there, but not the iniquity which is to be driven out of the temple. Moreover, the Jews crucified that very flesh which he drew from Adam (for Mary is from Adam, and the Lord’s flesh is from Mary), and he was going to raise up that same flesh in three days, which they were going to kill on the Cross. Thus they destroyed the temple built in forty-six years, and he raised it up in three days. Let us therefore bless God the Father Almighty, who formed us through his Word co-eternal with himself. Let us also bless our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who through the mystery of his incarnation reformed us on the cross. Let us also bless the Holy Spirit,

-># EXPLANATION.<-
<meta>catchword: who</meta>

What this figure and this writing might mean, therefore, must be understood. For the name of the first man, that is, **Adam**, is arranged in the figure and form of the holy cross: from him all nations arose, and the entire human race drew its origin. He, according to the Apostle <note>Paul the Apostle, in 1 Corinthians 15:45–49.</note>, is the "pattern of the one to come," namely Christ, of whom the same Apostle says: *The first Adam was made into a living soul, the last Adam into a life-giving spirit.* And a little later: *The first man, he says, was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly man, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly man, so also are the heavenly. Therefore, just as we carry the image of the earthly, let us also carry the image of the heavenly.* And why he said this, he immediately added the reason: *Now I say this, brothers, because flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God, nor shall corruption possess incorruption.*

For it is rightly done that the name **Adam** is placed in the configuration of a cross, in which the entire human race is known to have been set free through Christ. Nor is it fitting for the beauty of our redemption to be held in any other form more than in that one, where the wounds of the whole world could be encompassed. This is surely the holy Cross, which, in its reach, measures the whole world, and of which the Poet <note>original: "Poëta." Likely referring to the Christian poet Sedulius or a similar Late Antique source.</note> says:

->From there he gathers the four regions of the square world.<-
->The dawn shines splendidly from the head of the Creator.<-
->The sacred soles of his feet are touched by the setting star.<-
->The right hand holds the North, the left raises the southern axis.<-
->And all nature lives from the limbs of the Creator.<-
->And fixed to the cross, the Lord rules the world from every side.<-

This same meaning was also signified long ago in the name of the First-Formed <note>term: "Protoplast" (Protoplasti) — a traditional term for Adam as the first created being.</note>, namely **Adam**. In his name of four letters, the four parts of the world are demonstrated through their Greek names. For if the East, West, North, and South are spoken in Greek—as holy scripture mentions them in many places—you will find the name **Adam** in the first letters of those words. For the four mentioned parts of the world are called in Greek: **Anatole**, **Dysis**, **Arctos**, **Mesembria**. <note>original: "Anatole, dysis, arctos, mezembria." These represent East, West, North, and South respectively. The first letters (A-D-A-M) form the name Adam.</note> If you write these four names one under the other like four lines of verse, **Adam** is read in their starting letters. From this, it is given to be understood that he was created as the lord of the world, and that he signifies the One who, upon the four-sided cross, was to be the redeemer and restorer of the whole world.

For this reason, Christ is called the "Second Adam." This same name also contains within itself the mystery of the incarnation of Christ, if one considers the number in the letters of the name according to the Greek rule, where they calculate their numbers by letters. For **A** (Alpha) in numbers among the Greeks signifies one. **$\Delta$** (Delta) signifies four. The second **A** signifies one. **M** (Mu) signifies forty. Join these four numbers together, and they make forty-six. This is what the Jews are read to have answered in the Gospel: *This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?* But the Evangelist, understanding this, said: *But he was speaking of the temple of his body.* <note>John 2:19–21. This is an example of "gematria," a system where letters represent numbers to reveal hidden meanings.</note> This is because our Lord Jesus Christ took his body from Adam, though he did not draw sin from Adam; he took the bodily temple from there, but not the iniquity which must be driven out of the temple. The very flesh which he drew from Adam (for Mary was descended from Adam, and the Lord’s flesh was from Mary), the Jews crucified; and he was to raise up that same flesh in three days which they were to kill on the Cross. And so they destroyed the temple built in forty-six years, and he raised it up in three days.

Let us therefore bless God the Father Almighty, who through his Word co-eternal with himself formed us. Let us also bless our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who through the mystery of his incarnation reformed us on the cross. Let us also bless the Holy Spirit,

FOLIO XXVII.

### BOOK ONE.

A tree powerful in scent, broad with a leafy peak,
Where the highest abundance <note>original: "ubertas"</note> flows in truly sacred order,
Enriched at its birth, and none in the world is equal to it,
Rich in flowers and leaves, wealthy with a thousandfold sprout,
Exceeding all high forests in its grandeur:
When great honor and grace turn it entirely with piety,
True honor surrounds it; the man standing there speaks these things 
With a joyful vow. The horrendous envy of the black demon 
Denies this to the nations: to know the truth, or to be moved by praise.
This tree alone holds various colors by its virtue,
Shining dewy under the purple touch of the King <note>A reference to the blood of Christ staining the wood of the Cross</note>,
You are an eternal ray, for in you stand, piously bound,
The turreted houses; from this is it not so that the very 
Mechanism of God is blessed? The altar, and the hearth that visits 
Supreme things; this is the hearth and the wondrous lamp. 
The Lamb established all this peace, marking the way rightly 
By his journey. This is true salvation, which the true fountain 
Of goodness is the blessing that consecrated it: love, and piety,
The holy light of salvation, and life, true redemption.
And in the house, the Prince gives the gift of peace to the world,
And from here he strengthened the laws of friendship, and set aside 
The efforts summoned of old, which the winter of death covered, when
With seductive play around the fire—harmful indeed—the deceiver 
Thus tricks, and when he has seen the sluggish man 
With a disturbed vow, smiling now, he openly bound him.
O you beautiful Cross, O lovelier pine, you who conquer 
All forests, O taller than the cedars themselves,
Showing from a radiant number <note>Refers to the numerological patterns, specifically the 276 days of gestation, woven into the poem's grid</note> the blessed gifts 
Which the upright Jesus brought within to peace by his nod;
He granted that we might go blessedly when he piously came 
Coming forth from the womb here, and with his gentle divinity 
Marked himself, to found the heavens and earthly kingdoms,
As long ago the tongues of the holy Prophets sang.
This teacher made the high things while he founded the low,
And let there be power upon his shoulders <note>A reference to Isaiah 9:6, "and the government shall be upon his shoulder," traditionally applied to Christ carrying the Cross</note> for such a pious king.

### XIII. Figure. Concerning the days of Christ's conception in the womb of the Virgin, demonstrated by four Crosses: that is, 276, and the significance of the same number.

<note>The number 276 was significant to medieval scholars like Rabanus Maurus. Following the calculations of St. Augustine, they believed Christ was in the womb for 276 days, a number that also corresponds to the traditional time taken to build the Temple in Jerusalem. Here, Rabanus uses a "grid poem" where the letters forming the shapes of crosses within the grid create additional hidden messages related to this theme.</note>

A tree powerful in scent, broad with a leafy peak,
Where the truly highest abundance flows in sacred order,
Enriched at its birth, and none in the world is equal to it,
Rich in flowers and leaves, wealthy with a thousandfold sprout,
Exceeding all high forests in its grandeur:
When great honor and grace clothe it entirely with piety,
True honor surrounds it; the man standing there speaks these things 
With a joyful vow. The horrendous envy of the black demon 
Denies this to the nations: to know the truth, or to be moved by praise.
This tree alone holds various colors by its virtue,
Shining dewy under the purple touch of the King <note>original: "purpureo regis subtractu" — This refers to the blood of Christ staining the wood of the Cross, a common motif in medieval poetry where the Cross is "ennobled" by the color of royalty and sacrifice.</note>,
You are an eternal ray, for in you stand, piously bound,
The turreted houses; from this is it not so that the very

The Lamb established all this peace, marking the way rightly 
By his journey. This is true salvation, which the true fountain 
Of goodness is the blessing that consecrated it: love, and piety,
The holy light of salvation, and life, true redemption.
And in the house, the Prince gives the gift of peace to the world,

Thus tricks, and when he has seen the sluggish heart where he disquiets it,
Now smiling, he has bound it openly with his vow.
O you beautiful Cross, more lovely than all riches,
You who surpass the groves, O taller than the cedars themselves,
Showing on your shoulder <note>The horizontal beam of the cross was often referred to as its "shoulders" (humeri)</note> radiant, blessed gifts,
For the coming of Jesus, which the upright man enjoys within as peace by His will,
He brought it, and gave it to those who were blessed when He came piously.
Emerging from the womb, He marked Himself with a charming divinity,
He marked the heavens and established earthly kingdoms,
As the tongues of the holy prophets sang long ago:
This high Teacher did so while He established the lowest things,
And the empire is placed upon His shoulders, which belongs to the pious King.

# BOOK ONE. FOLIO XXVII.

A tree powerful in scent, broad with a leafy peak,
Where truly the highest abundance flows in sacred order,
Enriched at its birth, and one to which none in the world is equal
In flowers and leaves, wealthy with a thousandfold sprout,
Surpassing all high forests in its majesty:
When great honor and grace piously clothe it entirely,
True honor surrounds it; the man standing there speaks these things
With a joyful vow. The horrendous envy of the dark demon
Denies this to the nations: for the truth to be known, or to be moved by praise.
