# DECLARATION.

These four crosses, inscribed in a triple path, show within themselves through the sequence of letters the number of days in which the body of the Lord, according to the faith of the Church, was formed and compacted in the virginal womb. This is clearly that temple which the Savior himself predicted would be destroyed by the Jews and raised by him in three days. To make this more manifest, let us place a chapter from the fourth book of Saint Augustine’s *On the Holy Trinity*, in which this is written:

"Not without reason," he says, "in the building of the Lord's body—in the figure of which he said the temple destroyed by the Jews would be raised by him in three days—is the number six itself understood as standing for a year. For they said the temple was built in forty-six years <note>original: "XLVI. annis"</note>; and forty-six times six makes 276 <note>original: "CC. LXXVI."</note>. This number of days completes nine months and six days, which are accounted as ten months for child-bearing women; not because all reach the birth day after nine months, but because the very perfection of the Lord's body is found to have been brought to birth in that many days, as the authority of the Church maintains, receiving it from the tradition of the elders. For he is believed to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April <note>March 25, the Feast of the Annunciation. In the medieval calendar, this was also the traditional date of the Crucifixion.</note>, on which day he also suffered. Thus, the new tomb in which he was buried, where no dead person had been placed either before or after, corresponds to the womb of the virgin in which he was conceived, where no mortal was ever sown. He is said to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January <note>December 25, Christmas.</note>. Therefore, counting from that day to this, 276 days are found, which contain the number six forty-six times. In this number of years the temple was built, because in that number the sixfold body of the Lord was perfected, which, destroyed by the suffering of death, he raised in three days. For he said this concerning the temple of his body, as is declared by the most evident and robust testimony of the Gospels." This is what Augustine says.

Furthermore, we must observe how appropriately this same number suits the form of the Holy Cross, upon which the temple of the Lord’s body was unfastened by the Jews and prepared to be raised by the Lord himself. For Christ came for this purpose: to die in the flesh which he had taken up for the redemption of the world; he died for this purpose: to rise again in that same flesh. Therefore, it is pleasing to see how the mentioned number, that is, 276, when divided into four parts, universally expresses the horns <note>In medieval architectural and symbolic language, the "horns" of the cross refer to its four extremities—the head, the foot, and the two arms.</note> of the Holy Cross, and brings forth the image of the Cross through each part. For sixty-nine <note>original: "LX. enim & IX."</note> consist in each horn, which also does not differ from the likeness of the previous reasoning, where it was said that the number 276 completes nine months and six days.

Just as the numbers nine and six excelled in the whole, and according to their dominance the entire sum was calculated, so also in the parts, that same denomination shines forth no less alongside the mystery. For what is suggested in the number nine but the nine orders of Angels, and what in the number six but man, who was created on the sixth day? For both creatures are denoted in the figure of the Cross, because both are restored by the Savior on the Cross, and by both the mystery of the Lord's incarnation was honored; because on the day of his birth, both were moved to praise and joy. Hence Luke says: "And suddenly there was with the Angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying:

->**Glory to God in the highest: and on earth peace to men of good will.**<-

And a little later: "And the shepherds returned," he says, "praising and glorifying God for all the things they had heard and seen, just as it was told to them." # ->DECLARATION.<-

These four crosses, written with a triple path, show within themselves through the sequence of letters the number of days in which the Lord’s body was constructed and joined together in the Virgin’s womb according to the faith of the Church: namely, that temple which the Savior himself predicted would be destroyed by the Jews and raised up by him in three days. To make this clearer, let us set down a chapter from the fourth book of Saint Augustine’s *On the Trinity*, in which this is written:

> Not without reason, he says, in the building of the Lord's body—in whose figure he said the temple destroyed by the Jews would be raised by him in three days—the number six itself is understood to stand for a year. For they said the temple was built in 46 years; and forty-six times six makes 276. This number of days completes nine months and six days, which are counted as ten months for pregnant women; not because all reach the sixth day after nine months, but because the very perfection of the Lord's body is found to have been brought to birth in that many days: as the authority of the Church maintains, receiving it as a tradition from the elders.

For he is believed to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April <note>original: "Octauo Kalendas Aprilis"; March 25th</note>, the same day on which he also suffered. Thus the virgin womb in which he was conceived, where none of the mortals was sown, corresponds to the new tomb in which he was buried, where no dead person had been placed, neither before nor after. He is said to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January <note>original: "octauo Kalendas Ianuarias"; December 25th</note>. Therefore, counting from that day to this, 276 days are found, which contain the number six forty-six times: the number of years in which the temple was built. This is because the Lord’s body was perfected by that six-fold number <note>In medieval numerology, 6 was considered a "perfect number" because it is the sum of its divisors (1, 2, and 3).</note>, and though destroyed by the passion of death, he raised it in three days. For he said this concerning the temple of his body, as is declared by the most evident and powerful testimony of the Gospels. Thus far Augustine.

Furthermore, one must observe how fittingly the same number corresponds to the form of the Holy Cross, upon which the temple of the Lord's body was unfastened by the Jews, and prepared to be raised up by the Lord himself. For Christ came for this purpose: that he might die in the flesh which he had taken up for the redemption of the world; he died for this purpose: that he might rise again in that same flesh. Therefore, it is pleasing to observe how the aforementioned number—that is, 276—when divided into four parts, expresses the "horns" <note>The four points or arms of the cross were often called "cornua" (horns) in medieval literature.</note> of the Holy Cross universally, and brings forth the image of the Cross through each individual part. For 69 <note>276 divided by 4 equals 69.</note> consists in each "horn," which also does not differ from the logic of the previous comparison, where it was said that the number 276 completes nine months and six days.

For just as the numbers nine and six stood out in the whole, and the entire sum was calculated according to their dominance, so too in the parts the same designation shines forth together with the mystery. For what is suggested by the nine, if not the nine orders of Angels? And what by the six, if not man, who was created on the sixth day? # BOOK ONE.
## FOLIO XXIX.

It is a worthy and noble work to sing of the victorious King’s
Standard, the noble triumph of the Ruler with praise;
By which He rescued the world, and by which He destroyed the scepters
Of the harmful tyrant, rejecting the false reigns of that [wicked] ruler:
By which He well sustains the heaven, the sea, and the earth.
For His sacred exaltation was accomplished in this world, when
The series of years of the age, meeting in mystery
From the beginning of the world’s birth, brought this forth, and from here,
By the right of holy faith, He made the believing peoples
Run to the scriptures; the honest Creator establishing all
Times, harmonizing all things with the sacred number.
Because the Lord renewed all the ancient ages,
For, restoring them with His blood, He perfected all things with His gore,
Which He, the Good One, then fashioned in those first days.
As the beginning of Genesis reveals in holy doctrine,
That the Creator, making man, completed His works:
And thus on the sixth day, the Redeemer, in restoring man,
Showing the Sabbath, truly celebrated the Sabbath.
Behold, this commanded number accomplishes that the Passion—though by falsehood—
May meet [death]; then may it press down upon this essence <note>original: "vsiam," a Latinization of the Greek *ousia* (substance or being)</note> tempting the skill [of the enemy],
So that the part of cares that is bound may succumb to the dire fate.
Which the faction of the deceitful people shall never again
Show; but let the honest virtue of piety spread
The true dogmas of God through all these times of the world.
To sanctify the Cross and to bless the future kingdoms
Which the Savior would be—the blessed power of the Father:
For Christ is about to give new rewards in the highest to those
Whom He turned with His warnings, whom He taught the words of salvation,
Whom a pious faith in the heart clothes, and whom the sacred headband <note>original: "infula," a ribbon or headband worn by priests or used to mark a person or object as sacred</note> of work clothes:
But this appearance of the Cross grants the comforts of faith,
The material for praise, to know from this the goodness of the Creator:
Who, the pious and almighty, gave a healthy life before,
When He willed man to hold paradise as his lot:
And after the fall and flight, He, pitying, did not want him
To perish by the fraud of the wolf; the Creator [established] this citadel especially:
But by a vow He had dedicated it to the world for the life of the Cross, hence
So that He might carry them up to the heavenly scepters by the number of virtues.
Hope, love, and faith—all whom He has ordained from eternity
As worthy of Christ’s venerable sight here,

-># DECLARATION.<-

**O**n this page is contained the number of years from the beginning of the world until the year of the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord: specifically expressed in Greek letters, which are arranged in the figure of a cross, totaling 5,231 years <note>The text uses "v. cc. xxxi." In this system, 'v' represents 5,000, 'cc' is 200, and 'xxxi' is 31.</note> according to the faithful chronicles of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian who created a famous chronological table of world history.</note> and Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), who translated the Bible into Latin and expanded Eusebius's chronicles.</note>. Indeed, according to their calculation, there are 2,242 years from Adam until the Flood; from the Flood until Abraham, 942 years; and from Abraham until the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar <note>Tiberius reigned from 14–37 AD; his 15th year is traditionally associated with the start of John the Baptist's ministry.</note>, in which the Lord was baptized by John in the Jordan and announced the way of salvation to the people, proving His words true with signs and wonders, there are 2,044 years. All of these joined together make 5,228 years. Add three years, when in the eighteenth year of Tiberius Caesar the Lord came to His Passion, was crucified by the Jews, and rose on the third day, and the total becomes 5,231 years.

If these years are divided according to the letters written above in the cross, a mystery worthy of our veneration is suggested. There are, therefore, four letters that make up the image of the cross: namely **Γ** (Gamma), **Ζ** (Zeta), **Τ** (Tau), and **Χ** (Chi). The three latter letters are placed four times—that is, once on each arm of the cross. **Γ** is placed once, in the middle of the cross. If the numerical value <note>original: "potestas," referring to the value of Greek letters used as numerals (isopsephy).</note> of these letters is considered, their arrangement demonstrates to us the gifts of heavenly grace.

For **Γ** among the Greeks signifies the number three <note>original: "ternarium"</note>; **Ζ** signifies seven <note>original: "septenarium"</note>; **Τ** signifies three hundred <note>original: "tricenarium"</note>; and **Χ** signifies one thousand <note>original: "millenarium"</note>.

But what is suggested to us by **Γ** if not faith in the Trinity? What by **Ζ** if not the hope of the faithful? And what by **Τ** if not charity? And what is signified by **Χ** if not eternal bliss? Rightly indeed is Faith shown through **Γ**, which is the first of these letters and placed in the middle of the cross, because right faith is the foundation of good works and the beginning of our salvation. For "it is impossible to please God without faith" <note>Hebrews 11:6</note>, because "the just man lives by faith" <note>Romans 1:17</note>.

By **Ζ**, hope is well-intimated, because the whole intention of the faithful pants for that eternal rest which is signified by the number seven <note>Referring to the Sabbath, the seventh day of rest.</note>, saying with the Prophet: "My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?" <note>Psalm 42:2</note>.

Charity is also properly expressed by **Τ**, which holds the very image of the holy cross <note>The letter T (Tau) was anciently viewed as a symbol of the cross.</note>. For in the work of the cross, the great charity of God the Father was shown, "who did not spare His own Son, but delivered Him up for us all" <note>Romans 8:32</note>, just as the Savior Himself said of Himself in the Gospel: "For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life" <note>John 3:16</note>. And the Apostle says: "But God commends His love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us; much more then, being now justified by His blood, shall we be saved from wrath through Him" <note>Romans 5:8-9</note>. **Τ** therefore signifies the number 300, which is six times fifty. In these numbers, what else is suggested but the perfection of charity? For the number fifty, because of the Pentecost of the Holy Spirit, demonstrates grace. And the number six is a perfect number <note>In ancient mathematics, a perfect number equals the sum of its divisors (1+2+3=6).</note>. "The charity of God," as the Apostle says, "is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us" <note>Romans 5:5</note>.

Finally, by the letter **Χ**, which expresses the number one thousand, eternal bliss is aptly signified. For the number one thousand is often used in the Scriptures to signify perfection, because it makes a solid square number <note>A "solid square" refers to a cube ($10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000$).</note>. Indeed, ten led ten times makes one hundred. This figure is already square, but it is still flat; but let it rise into height, and it is made solid. Multiply 100 by 10, and it becomes 1,000. By this perfect number, the stable, inseparable, and, as it were, "squared" life of the just in heaven is designated, because it is perfect in every part, since they enjoy both the infinite joy of souls and the immortality of bodies. Then they possess a perfect state of being: in length, eternity; in breadth, charity; in height, divine contemplat-

->### FIRST BOOK. FOLIO 30.<-

...salvation. Finally, I would like to say something regarding the meaning of the characters of the letters themselves, which mark the aforementioned numbers and demonstrate the image of the cross by their very placement. Indeed, the **Γ** <note>Gamma, the third letter of the Greek alphabet</note>, which is erected upward and is flat at the top, well signifies the **faith** which ought to be raised upward to the Lord and strengthen the state of the mind; yet it must be preserved with the great guardianship of humility, lest by wandering uncertainly here and there, it fall into error. The Apostle <note>Paul</note> shows both of these things, saying: *Brothers, stand firm in faith, act manfully, and be strengthened.* <note>original: "Fratres state in fide, viriliter agite & confortamini" — 1 Corinthians 16:13</note> Likewise elsewhere: *Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly, according as God has dealt to every man the measure of faith.* <note>original: "Non plus sapere quàm oportet sapere..." — Romans 12:3</note>

The **Ζ** <note>Zeta</note>, therefore, well suggests **hope**, which curves its ends in the manner of an anchor; showing that we ought to cling immovably to heavenly things by hope, lest the storm of persecutions, the whirlwind of temptations, or the allurements of pleasures be able to tear us away from the desire for eternal life. Concerning this, the Apostle wrote to the Hebrews: *That we may have a very strong comfort,* he says, *who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us, which we have as an anchor of the soul, sure and firm, and which enters even into the inner parts of the veil, where the forerunner Jesus has entered for us, made a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.* <note>Hebrews 6:18-20</note>

The letter **Τ** <note>Tau</note>, therefore, which has the likeness of a cross and is joined by a double form, well suggests to us the two precepts of **charity** <note>In this context, "charity" refers to "Caritas" or divine love.</note>. For one part of it ascends upward, and another part goes across; but that part which is erected upward commends divine love to us, that we may love God our Creator with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind. That part, however, which is led through the middle—yet in such a way that it rests upon the upright part—suggests to us our love for one another, which ought to be ordered by divine love, so that we love our friends in God and our enemies for the sake of God. Regarding this matter, the Apostle John instructs us: *In this,* he says, *we have known the charity of God, because He laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.* <note>1 John 3:16</note> And likewise: *This commandment we have from God, that he who loves God should love his brother also.* <note>1 John 4:21</note>

The **Χ** <note>Chi</note>, which in Greek means *chilioi* <note>original: "chile"</note> and in Latin means "a thousand," is written not with straight lines but with encircling ones when it signifies a thousand. So too is the **Ω** <note>Omega</note>, which indicates another number <note>800</note>, written with direct lines. Therefore, we have said this signifies the perfection of the saints in heaven, which is written with rounded lines to show that there is no end to celestial joy, where the praise of the saints will remain without end. Of them the Prophet says: *Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord, they will praise you forever and ever,* <note>Psalm 84:4</note> when, according to the Prophet Isaiah, the seed of the saints shall stand before God like a new heaven and a new earth, and when there shall be month after month and sabbath after sabbath. 

Moreover, **Χ** is the first letter of the name of **Christ**, and this fits this reasoning well. For He Himself is our joy, to whom we say with the Prophet: *You will make us glad with joy with your countenance,* <note>Psalm 21:6</note> upon whom even the angels desire to look. Therefore, the series of these letters, beginning from **Γ**—that is, from the center of the cross—is led through the four regions of the world. This signifies something marvelous: that after the Passion of Christ, His disciples, beginning from Jerusalem, began to preach the Gospel in the whole world and distribute divine gifts to all nations; so that from all parts of the earth, the faithful might deserve to reach eternal rewards through the gifts of faith, hope, and charity. 

There are also two verses of the Holy Cross written here in the aforementioned numbers, the first of which is to be read downward in length from the summit of the cross, thus:
**Lo, this form of the cross well shows the honor of Jesus.**
The other, however, is to be recited across its horizontal path, thus:
**Jesus calculates this number in the world where He suffered.**
The name of Jesus, which the central mark of the cross contains, is common to both verses, as is clearly shown.

<meta>This page continues the "Declaration" or explanation of the symbolic figures accompanying the Cross, moving from the poetic verses of the previous page into a detailed prose analysis of the four Evangelists as the "four living creatures" from the visions of Ezekiel and the Apostle John.</meta>

### EXPLANATION.

Here also, those four prophetic living creatures standing around the Lamb express the likeness of a cross; this is the vision that Ezekiel and the Apocalypse of John <note>The Book of Revelation</note> recount. Ezekiel writes that they are in the midst of fire or electrum <term>electrum: A precious alloy of gold and silver, or a glowing amber-colored substance mentioned in biblical visions to describe divine radiance.</term>, and John describes them in the midst of the throne and around the throne. But let us first look at Ezekiel’s words concerning them, who wrote among other things: "As for the likeness of their faces, each of the four had the face of a man and the face of a lion on the right side; and the four had the face of an ox on the left side; and the four had the face of an eagle above," and so forth. John, however, wrote thus: "And in the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures <note>original: "animalia"</note> full of eyes before and behind: and the first living creature was like a lion, and the second living creature like a calf, and the third living creature had a face like a man, and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle." And a little later he introduced another vision, saying: "And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as if it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven Spirits of God sent forth into all the earth." Although the Prophet and the Apostle agree on the four living creatures and their four faces, they differ in some details which there is no time to discuss individually now. Let us see what the placement of these four living creatures signifies, which John wrote were around the throne and the Lamb who stands in the middle of the throne. Does it not signify the Cross of the Lord? Therefore, when it is said that there are four around the throne, I believe he means nothing else than that they are in four parts—that is, in front and behind, to the right and to the left—as far as physical position is concerned; otherwise, something of this sort cannot be defined in a non-spatial way. These four parts, therefore, what else do they signify but the four horns <note>original: "cornua crucis," referring to the four ends or arms of the cross</note> of the cross, if we wish to consider it lying flat? And the Lamb who is in the middle of the throne, what else do we understand Him to hold but the center of the cross? For He Himself was fixed upon it, He who took away the sins of the world. Indeed, these four living creatures signify the four Evangelists, as the authority of the Church hands down: that is, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. They are rightly depicted in the form of the holy cross because they all harmoniously testify to the passion and resurrection of the Lord in the books of the Holy Gospel. Matthew is rightly placed at the bottom and holds the likeness of a man, because in the beginning of his Gospel, describing the genealogy of the Savior, he indicated that He took on flesh from earthly parents. Mark and Luke, however, placed as if higher up, signify the royal power and priestly dignity in Him. The first of these, Mark, has the likeness of a lion, in whom the voice of a lion roaring in the wilderness is heard. "The voice of one crying," he says, "in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight." For Amos says: "The Lord will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem." The lion is the king of beasts, whence Solomon says: "As the roaring of a lion, so is the wrath of a king." And in Genesis, the Patriarch Jacob said of Judah (from whom the kings and from whom Christ took His flesh): "Judah is a lion's whelp; to the prey, my son, you have gone up; resting, you couched as a lion and as a lioness. Who shall rouse him? The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent: and he shall be the expectation of the nations." The other, that is, Luke, holds the likeness of a calf <note>The "vitulus" or calf/ox symbolizes sacrifice and the priesthood.</note>. Starting from the priest Zechariah, he testifies that the Lord Himself was born according to the human nature from the kindred of priests, when he relates that the Angel said to Mary His mother: "And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has conceived a son in her old age." And by tracing the genealogy of the Savior from David through Nathan, he suggests that He is a priest. John, however...

FO. XXXII.

### BOOK ONE.

...shows in himself the appearance of an eagle: who rightly stands at the summit <note>original: "arce," meaning a citadel or high point</note> of the cross, who flying to the heights, explores the more secret mysteries of Christ's divinity. As if fixing the eyes of his mind upon the sun of the Deity itself, he immediately began his Gospel with the divinity of Christ, thus: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word." Therefore, the four Gospels written by the four Evangelists signify the four rivers of paradise proceeding from one fountain; for just as those rivers, proceeding from one source-matrix <note>original: "matrice"</note> of a fountain, watered the whole earth, so the four Gospels—emanating from the one true fountain, which is Christ, from whom whoever drinks once shall not thirst forever—stream through the mouths of preachers to irrigate the whole world for the germinating of the fruits of virtues. These are the divine chariot, the four wheels that followed the four living creatures, having four faces and four wings. 

Now, what the Prophet says—"That one wheel appeared upon the earth beside the living creatures having four faces," and immediately adds in the plural number, "And their appearance was like the vision of the sea <note>This refers to the beryl or chrysolite color mentioned in Ezekiel 1:16; the Latin "maris" implies the color of the sea</note>, and the likeness of the four was one," and so forth—can be applied to the understanding of this logic. For in one wheel, four types of wheels appeared, because the four Gospels agreed in the one passion of the Savior. For so great was the likeness of the four wheels following the four living creatures that they might most truly be believed to be one wheel; and so great is the likeness in the narration of the evangelists that it is very easily seen to be dictated by one Spirit. As for the fact that the wheels went through their four parts and did not turn back when they walked, this is because the Gospels run through the four regions of the world by teaching, nor shall they return to deny what they teach: because truth observes the course of rectitude and is not turned aside into the crooked paths of falsehood. 

Indeed, upon the four living creatures themselves are inscriptions appropriate to them, signifying their right and authority and what they preach concerning the Lord Savior. For in the form of the man, this verse is written below: 

**Matthew marked this man in the order of his lineage.** 

The lion truly has these words: 

**Mark marks the king.** 

The image of the calf also contains this: 

**Luke gives the priest.** 

But the eagle, standing at the summit of the cross, sounds this verse: 

**John, the high-flying eagle, also drank the Word at the summit.** 

These same living creatures also hold four scrolls <note>original: "chartas"</note> in which their principal sentences are noted, from which the first parts of the four Gospels are shown. 

The Lamb indeed, who stands in the center, has written upon his head and horns: **The seven Spirits of God.** This signifies the same as the seven horns and seven eyes. On the rest of his body, he also holds the sentence of John the Baptist concerning himself: **Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world.** Upon the Cross, which he carries on his head, he shows the Greek name written: **YOS** <note>original: "YOS", a Latinization of the Greek word for "Son", Υιός (Huios)</note>. This is interpreted as "Son," signifying that this image does not demonstrate any common lamb, but the Son of God.

<meta>This page provides a prose explanation (Declaratio) of the poetic themes introduced on the previous page, specifically focusing on the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit as prophesied by Isaiah and their manifestation in the person of Christ.</meta>

# EXPLANATION.

It is written in Isaiah: *A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his shoot: and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and fortitude, the Spirit of knowledge and piety: and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.* <note>original: "Egredietur virga de radice Iesse..." Isaiah 11:1-3. This is a foundational prophecy for the "Tree of Jesse," a common artistic motif showing the genealogy of Jesus.</note> Thus, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is numbered by the Prophet, which is said to rest most pleasantly upon that flower, who says to his bride in the Song of Songs: *I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.* <note>Song of Songs 2:1.</note> Regarding the rod <note>original: "virgam"</note> and the flower of which the Prophet spoke, the Jews say these refer to the Lord himself, representing the power of his reign and his beauty. We, however, say that the rod is Holy Mary, born from the stock of Jesse; she had no other "shrubbery" attached to her, because she had no husband in carnal union. The flower, truly, is the Lord Jesus, who burst forth most brilliantly from the "bark" of human nature, because he proceeded from the virginal womb born without the stain of sins. In the chastity of his flesh, he demonstrated the whiteness of the lily, and in the blood of his passion, he showed the redness of the rose.

Therefore, the Spirit of the Lord "rests" upon him, which is to say, it remains in him as an eternal dwelling place: for in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily. <note>A reference to Colossians 2:9.</note> For God does not give the Spirit by measure, but God the Father anointed him with the oil of gladness above his companions: and from his fullness we have all received. How then is it written of Christ that he received the Holy Spirit from the Father, and gave it himself? Both natures were demonstrated in him—namely, the human and the divine. He received it as a man; he gave it as God. We, however, are certainly able to receive this gift according to our small measure, but we are by no means able to pour it out upon others; rather, so that it may happen, we call upon the Lord to effect this within them.

But it may be asked why the Prophet began counting from the Spirit of Wisdom <note>original: "sapientia"</note> and ended with the Spirit of Fear, when the Psalmist says: *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.* <note>Psalm 111:10.</note> This can be resolved in this way: When the Prophet prophesied concerning the flower of the rod which was to come forth from the root of Jesse—that is, Christ—he understood him to be co-eternal with the Father in his divinity. He recognized him as the author of all goodness, holiness, and indeed of all things. To signify that Christ descended to us from the heavens with such a fullness of holiness, and to show that he poured grace into our nature (that is, human nature), the Prophet begins from the very summit of spiritual gifts and proceeds down to the lowest. For what grace is greater than to fully and perfectly behold, according to our small measure, the omnipotent Creator himself—from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist—and eternal Wisdom itself, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things are illuminated? Or what grace is lesser than for a man to restrain himself from sins simply for fear of the punishment of hell <note>original: "gehennæ"</note>? For one who is moved by punishment has not yet ascended to the higher steps: because fear involves punishment. He who fears is not perfected in charity <note>or "love"</note>.

Yet, it is only through this [fear] that human weakness is able to climb to higher things. And for this reason, the Psalmist says: *The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom*, because a person must first restrain himself from sins through fear, knowing it is written that God renders to each according to his works, and that the wicked shall go into eternal punishment, but the just into eternal life. Thus, through the love of an eternal reward, one ascends to the other steps. That is, to the second step: that he might be pious and mild, keeping a right faith, returning evil to no one for evil but always returning what is good, not cursing back at the one who curses him, but on the contrary, blessing him. To the third step as well: that he might have the knowledge to choose good things and reject bad ones, to turn away from evil and do good, to follow peace and spurn hatred. To the fourth: that he might be strong, walking with the firm step of justice, and not

<meta>catchword: may suffer [patiatur]</meta>

<summary>This page explains the "Tree of Jesse" prophecy from Isaiah, identifying the 'rod' as Mary and the 'flower' as Christ. It reconciles why Isaiah lists the seven gifts of the Spirit starting with Wisdom, while the Psalms start with Fear, by distinguishing between Christ's divine descent and humanity's spiritual ascent.</summary>

FO. XXXIIII.

### BOOK ONE.

f iiij

[...he does not] allow himself to be corrupted by any prosperity or afflicted by any adversity. In the fifth step, indeed, he acts in all things with true counsel, and according to what the divine scripture teaches, he acts obediently; that is, he forgives the debts of his neighbors, so that God may forgive him his own sins: he has mercy on another, so that God may have mercy on him: he makes friends for himself from the mammon of iniquity <note>original: "mammona iniquitatis," referring to worldly wealth (Luke 16:9)</note>, so that when he fails they may receive him into eternal tabernacles: he sows earthly things, so that he may reap heavenly things: he loses his soul for a time in this world, so that he may keep it for eternal life, and other such things. In the sixth step, that he may understand God, that is, that he may seek Him with the whole intention of his heart, consider Him, and look upon Him, and hasten to suddenly uproot all evil thoughts coming into his heart, and dash his "little ones" <note>original: "parvulos," an allegorical reference to Psalm 137:9; here, the "infants" represent the first stirrings of sinful thoughts which should be crushed against the rock of Christ before they grow.</note> against the rock, which is Christ. 

When, however, he has ascended into the seventh step, that is, into wisdom, he will now show the man himself to be perfect, and he passes from the condition of a servant into a son: and he has no need for anyone to teach him, but, as it is written, his anointing teaches him about all things <note>1 John 2:27</note>: and having been delighted by the perfect love of God, he is made certain with the Apostle, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate him from the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. <note>Romans 8:38-39.</note>

However, the fact that these same seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are numbered twice here signifies, without doubt, the two precepts of charity <note>Love of God and love of neighbor.</note> which are poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit: or the two testaments <note>The Old and New Testaments.</note>, which were dictated and written down by the same Spirit: which are joined and united in the one Cross, that is, in the one passion of Christ. In the Cross of Christ, therefore, two things are achieved: one, because every separation and enmity is dissolved in it, and all things are made peaceful in it, both those which are in heaven and those which are on earth. 

Therefore, I have described here a **flowering Cross** in four principal colors—namely, hyacinth <note>original: "hiacinthino," a deep blue or violet color.</note>, purple, fine linen <note>original: "byssino," representing white.</note>, and scarlet—so that I might demonstrate the beauty of that most pleasant flower, which prophetic speech tells us rose from the royal stock: he who, being beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, wonderfully showed the beauty of all virtues in himself beyond all others. For it is not right to believe that any of the saints could have reached the excellence of his charity: because it is certain that he alone was born without the stain of sin: and what grace bestowed upon others in part, nature provided to him in its entirety. Indeed, in the **hyacinth** [blue] we understand his heavenly conversation among men; in the **purple**, the blood of the passion; in the **brightness and fine linen**, the most inviolate chastity of his body; and in the **scarlet**, his extraordinary and perfect charity [love]. Truly, in all these things the man Christ Jesus, born among men, shone serenely, because he was full of the beauty of all adornment both within and without. Therefore, the boy Jesus increased in wisdom, and age, and grace before God and men: and having become a man, he was praised by the testimony of the people saying: *He has done all things well: he has made the deaf to hear, and the mute to speak.* <note>Mark 7:37.</note> He, illuminating the world with his doctrine and healing its sick, destroyed death through death: and triumphing, he rose again in glory, ascended into the heavens, and sits at the right hand of God the Father, from whence he shall come to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire.

### Figure XVII. On the eight Gospel Beatitudes.

<note>This page features a "carmen figuratum" or pattern poem. In the original manuscript, the text is arranged in a perfect grid of letters. Overlaid on this grid are eight hexagonal shapes (visible in the image description) which highlight specific letters forming the text of the Eight Beatitudes from the Gospel of Matthew. The poem itself praises the Cross as the framework for these virtues.</note>

Holy, blessed, powerful praise of life, the glory of Christ,
Venerable Cross of God, you are the prosperous fulfillment of the age,
Worthy, good, and pious, because you affected the members of Christ.
Hung from the wooden stake, those afflicted under the shadow of the prison
You snatch away, a people placed into the sublime kingdom.
To whom you had given, since the long-awaited vision of the heavens
Is returned by right to the pious, once making them worthy of the crown.
For the good things which the pious Arbiter <note>The "Arbiter" refers to Christ as Judge.</note> with serene countenance
Scattered as sacred seeds on earth, he multiplied and loved.
And which the Master, sitting on the summit of the mountain, prayed,
Bestowing upon the disciples the pact and the pious covenants of the law.
For he began then, in life-giving order, to reveal to the saints
The pious sayings of the Lord with these titles of virtues,
So that he might mark the blessed things of the Father with this teaching of the Son.
Because the Cross embraces all good things and is best in itself,
It gives, teaches, nourishes, and binds the blessed to those who love it.
Thus happy, with the fervor of a divine mind, press the heart,
He who ceases from sin seeking justice, the cold becomes warm by the pious enemy.
Those weeping, who are desirous; for to them a sign is given from above.
For whom the eternal Counsel and mercy will see;
Consolation and that refreshment, the bountiful feeding, remains in the citadel.
Not from on high, the action competes, and the heavenly reward is paid.
Help is now strong here, and this is enough within,
They are far off from the humble ground which he, prostrate, adores.
When the Word seeks not only the meek, but morals in order,
The All-Holder <note>original: "Omnitenens," a title for God as the sustainer of all things.</note> demands this always and at all times.
Therefore it is the desire of the blessed to dwell in the light, and
In this eightfold number <note>Refers to the eight Beatitudes.</note> so that they might seek the gifts above the heights.
And those rising again seek this kingdom, because thus they will go by the Cross.
The Cross is the way, the ladder, the wheel, the homeland, the leader, the gate, the triumph.
The blessed life of men and the greatest reward of merits.
The pious formula of the kingdom, placed twice four times <note>Meaning eight times.</note>, reveals
That the holy deserve by good gifts to climb the heavens.
And the Lord of the All-powerful God is of this Omnipotent.
The Spirit himself wishes to climb the seat of peace in these ways,
And he had raised seven steps to the stars above, where
From here, the high things of the heaven can piously open to the kind,
Whom love, reason, light, praise, good virtue accompany.
Glory, the crown, and the throne are added in the citadel of the heavens.

-> Holy, blessed, powerful praise of life, and glory of Christ, <-

Afflicted under the shadow of the prison, and you give them

Blessed at last and worthy of the crown <note>original: "stemmate," referring to a wreath or garland of victory</note>.

Scattered sacred seeds upon the earth; he multiplied and loved them.

So, happy soul, trembling with fervor, press the divine string <note>A metaphor for the heart or the "chord" of the soul in harmony with God</note>—

And in that high citadel, no action is bound by a proud mouth. 
Suddenly, heavenly help is present; it prevails here and is sufficient, 
When internal troubles are far away, or when one is on the humble ground 
Which the prostrate man adores. For the All-holding One <note>original: "Omnitenens," a title for God</note>
Demands not only words, but mild manners in their proper order,
Always and at every time.
Therefore, it is the nature of those wishing to dwell in the light of the blessed
To seek the gifts above the heights by this number of eight,
Rising toward this kingdom; because thus they shall journey by the Cross.
The Cross is the way, the ladder, the wheel <note>A symbol of the divine engine of the universe or the cycle of time</note>, the fatherland, the leader, the gate, the triumph,
The blessed life of human merits, and the greatest reward.
Behold, the pious formula of the kingdom, placed "twice four" <note>original: "bina quater," meaning eight</note> times,
Reveals that the holy gifts earn the heavens for the good as they climb.
And the All-powerful Lord, the Spirit of the Almighty God himself,
Wishes us to climb to the seat of peace by these ways.
He had erected these steps above the seven celestial stars <note>A reference to the seven gifts of the Spirit mentioned on the previous page</note>,
So that from here, he might reveal to the kind that they can piously go 
To the heights of heaven, accompanied by love, reason, light, praise, 
Good virtue, glory, the crown, and the throne, all of which are added 
In the citadel of the heavens.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion of Figure XVII, where the Cross was presented as a framework for the Beatitudes. # EXPLANATION

Therefore, the series of eight beatitudes is noted here in the form of the holy Cross, so that it may become known to the whole people of the faithful where their salvation had its beginning and where they will find the fulfillment of their perfection. This occurs when, through the passion of Christ, they have received the remission of sins, and through His resurrection, they hope for eternal life and immortality; and when they seek the wholeness of heavenly bliss from no one else but Him, from whom they have once again obtained redemption. Rightly, therefore, do all these sacred mysteries <note>original: "sacramenta," referring here to sacred signs or truths</note> belong to the holy Cross, because those liberated through it enter into a covenant of faith and a fellowship of unity. There, redemption from death is introduced; there, a holy way of life <note>original: "morum conversatio," a term often used for the dedicated lifestyle of a monk or devout Christian</note> is demonstrated; there, the perfection of all virtues is made known; there, the resurrection to eternal life is promised; and there, the attainment of eternal life and the acquisition of true happiness is hoped for. For since we were pleased yesterday, after our enumeration of the figures, to move to a treatise on the spiritual gifts of the eight beatitudes, let us see how these two things agree with one another, and if the form of the holy Cross can demonstrate this agreement within itself. For the blessed father Augustine, in the book he chose to name *On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount*, makes such a commemoration of this agreement, saying:

> It seems to me, therefore, that the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, of which Isaiah speaks <note>Isaiah 11:2-3, listing the Seven Gifts of the Spirit</note>, also corresponds to these steps and sayings; but the order is different. For there, the numbering begins from the most excellent things; but here, it begins from the lower. For there, it begins with the wisdom of God and ends with the fear of God; but "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom." Therefore, if we count step-by-step as if ascending, the first is the **fear of God**, the second is **piety**, the third is **knowledge**, the fourth is **fortitude**, the fifth is **counsel**, the sixth is **understanding**, and the seventh is **wisdom**.
>
> **Fear of God** corresponds to the humble, of whom it is said here: *Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven*—that is, those who are not puffed up or proud. Of these, the Apostle says: *Do not be high-minded, but fear*—that is, do not be exalted.
>
> **Piety** corresponds to the **meek**; for he who seeks piously honors the Holy Scripture, and does not criticize what he does not yet understand; therefore he does not resist, which is what it means to be meek. Hence it is said here: *Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.*
>
> **Knowledge** corresponds to **those who mourn**, who have now learned from the Scriptures by what evils they are held bound—evils which they previously sought as if they were good and useful. Of these, it is said here: *Blessed are those who mourn now, for they shall be comforted.*
>
> **Fortitude** corresponds to **those who hunger and thirst**. For they labor, desiring joy from true goods, and wishing to turn their love away from earthly and bodily things. Of these, it is said here: *Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be satisfied.*
>
> **Counsel** corresponds to the **merciful**. For this is the one remedy for escaping such great evils: that we forgive, just as we wish to be forgiven; and that we help others in what we can, just as we desire to be helped in what we cannot do. Of these, it is said here: *Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.*
>
> **Understanding of the heart** corresponds to the **pure in heart**, as if the eye were purged so that it might be able to perceive what the physical eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man. Of these, it is said here: *Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.*
>
> **Wisdom** corresponds to the **peacemakers**, in whom all things are now ordered, and no rebellious motion exists; but all things obey the spirit of man, just as the man himself obeys God. Of these, it is said here: *Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.*
>
> And a little later he added: And these things indeed can be fulfilled in this life, as we believe they were fulfilled in the Apostles. For that absolute transformation into angelic form, which is promised after this life, cannot be explained in any words. *Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice...*

# BOOK ONE. FOLIO XXXVI.

...because theirs is the kingdom of heaven. This eighth sentence, which returns to the head <note>The "head" refers back to the first beatitude, as both promise the "kingdom of heaven."</note> and declares the perfect man, perhaps signifies both the circumcision on the eighth day in the Old Testament and the Lord’s resurrection after the Sabbath, which is surely the eighth day, and likewise the first. Rightly, therefore, is the entire series of virtues distributed into steps: because the whole life of the faithful is raised to higher things through growth and increase, until it reaches the height of perfection—that is, love <note>original: "charitatem"</note>—specifically that perfect love which "casts out fear," through which one earns the right to have God dwelling within; for God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God in him. This occurs when, the storm of temptations having been calmed, the soul is entirely fixed upon the contemplation of God. Hence the Psalm says: *They shall go from virtue to virtue: the God of gods shall be seen in Zion*; and elsewhere: *His place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion.* And this becomes known rightly through spiritual gifts <term>charismata: spiritual graces or gifts granted by the Holy Spirit</term>: because through the grace of the Holy Spirit every best gift and every perfect gift is granted to us.

Rightly indeed are these steps arranged in the form of the holy Cross: because through the Cross one truly ascends to the heavenly kingdom. But because there are two parts of the holy Cross—one which stands upright, and another which goes across—the eight steps of the beatitudes have been arranged by us upon it in such a way that they ascend from the bottom to the middle on its upright part, and then the order of ascent is led through its transverse part. Finally, on its upright part, in that section which rises above the crossbar, that ascent is finished; this will be easily apparent to anyone who rightly understands what we have written upon it. Indeed, the fitting arrangement of these parts can be recognized in the very division of the sections. For on the upright post at the bottom, the "poor in spirit" are placed; and at the very top, those "who suffer persecution for the sake of justice." To both of these the kingdom of heaven is promised: because only through true humility does one rightly arrive at the palm of martyrdom and the heavenly kingdom; and for the sake of justice, which is Christ, all adversities are most patiently endured. 

In the transverse part, however, the path stretches from the blessed "who mourn now" all the way to the blessed "who are pure in heart." To the former, consolation is promised; to the latter, the vision of the Lord—which is rightly understood to be one and the same. For they are truly comforted who enjoy the vision of the eternal King without end. Therefore, holy men in this present life, the more they cast themselves down by despising themselves outwardly, the more they are fed inwardly by the revelation of contemplation. For those whom the valley of humility holds in weeping outwardly, the ascent of contemplation raises up inwardly. Therefore, these eight octagons <note>Referring to the geometric shapes containing the letters in the visual poem</note> composed of odd numbers contain eight verses of thirty-seven letters, containing the eight beatitudes. The first of these, which is placed at the base of the Cross, has this verse: **The Lord wills the kingdoms of heaven to belong to the blessed poor man.** The second after this is: **And that the meek shall always inhabit the celestial soil.** The third octagon in order is that which is first on the transverse path of the cross, holding this verse: **Happy are those who weep, for whom there is consolation on high.** The fourth, which is next to it, has this verse: **For eternal refreshment fills those who long for justice.** Next to it is the fifth with this: **Generous mercy rewards the pious in mind from above.** The sixth is that which closes the transverse path: **Serene hearts shall see God even in the heavenly citadel.** The seventh, which stands in the section rising above the cross, is this: **The Lord embraces the peacemakers with the love of a son.** The highest octagon of all is inscribed with this verse: **The one afflicted for Christ now looks upon the kingdom of heaven.** <note>original: "olympi," a poetic term for heaven.</note>

<meta>This page provides the prose "Declaratio" (Declaration) for Figure 18 of Rabanus Maurus's work. It continues the theological exploration of the number forty, transitioning from the poetic grid to a detailed symbolic explanation of why this number represents both the Cross and the span of human life.</meta>

# DECLARATION.

The number forty <note>original: "Quadragenarius".</note> therefore forms the shape of a cross in this manner, and declares the sacred mystery <term>sacramentum</term> through a fitting arrangement: for when divided into four sums, it clearly demonstrates the number ten <note>original: "denarium".</note> through each part in order. This pertains to the mystery because just as the fullness of the ten is found in four parts, so too the perfection of the Decalogue <note>The Ten Commandments.</note> is introduced to all the faithful in each of the four books of the Holy Gospel. Yet these joined decades <note>groups of ten</note> make a single shape of a cross: because the Decalogue of the Law and the majesty of the Gospel harmoniously establish the unity of faith and the fellowship of love.

Furthermore, the number ten itself is completed by the progression from one to four <note>A reference to the Pythagorean idea that 1+2+3+4 = 10.</note>, and likewise, it is multiplied by four to rise into the number forty; this undoubtedly signifies that the fulfillment of the Law does not happen without the Gospel, nor does the Gospel teaching lack the testimony of the Law. For Christ is the end and perfection of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. He is our peace, who made both one, dissolving the middle wall of partition—the enmity in his flesh—by abolishing the law of commandments in its decrees, so that he might create in himself one new man, making peace, to reconcile both in one body to God through the cross, killing the enmity in himself.

Because this number is the sacred mystery of this laborious time in which we fight against the devil under the discipline of Christ the King, it also declares what he consecrated by a forty-day fast and the humiliation of the soul. Both the Law and the Prophets—through Moses and Elijah, who fasted for forty days—and the Gospel—through the fast of the Lord himself, during which forty days he was also tempted by the devil—prefigure nothing other than that the entire duration of this world is our temptation in his flesh, which he deigned to take from our mortality. From the hour of his death until the dawn of his resurrection, there are also forty hours, if the ninth hour <note>3:00 PM, the traditional hour of Christ's death.</note> is counted; after the resurrection, too, he wished to be on this earth with his disciples for no more than forty days. From this point, still joined with them in human conversation and taking the food of mortals—though he was no longer to die—he signified through those forty days that he would fulfill by his hidden presence what he had promised when he said: *Behold, I am with you even to the end of the age.*

As for why this number signifies this temporal and earthly life, an immediate reason comes to mind (though there may be another more secret one): the seasons of the years run in fourfold cycles, and the world itself is bounded by four parts, which Scripture sometimes records by the names of the winds: from the east and west, from the north and south. Therefore, Matthew, receiving Christ the King as he came to this world, to this earthly and mortal life of men, and to rule us as we labor in temptation, began with Abraham and enumerated forty men <note>referring to the genealogy of Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew.</note>. For God separated Abraham from his own land and kindred so that the Hebrew people might be distinguished from the other nations. Christ came in the flesh, and from that very people, he brought the saving cross to the whole world. Within this term of years <note>referring to the number forty</note>, Isaac was joined to Rebecca, and through the mystery of this same number, the Church was joined to Christ. For this number of days, the twelve men who were sent scouted the land of promise, and for the same number of years, the unbelievers and detractors were punished in the sterility of the wilderness; for often through the labor of the present life, by which the chosen are tested, the rejected are tormented. Likewise, according to the half of this number—that is, from twenty years—the sons of Israel were chosen for military service— <note>The text ends mid-sentence. The catchword indicates the next word is "militiam" (military service or warfare).</note>

## FOLIO XXXVIII.

### BOOK ONE.

into the service of the Lord (as the history of the Pentateuch <note>The first five books of the Bible; here referring to the Israelites' forty years in the wilderness.</note> recounts), so it might be shown that as soon as the wars against vices began to arise for the holy ones, the great labor of struggle was immediately present. For those who belong to Christ, as the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, specifically in Galatians 5:24.</note> says, have crucified their flesh with its vices and lusts. Therefore, this number is measured according to the placement of the Holy Cross within the Holy of Holies <term>sancta sanctorum</term> of Solomon’s Temple—that is, twenty cubits in length and twenty cubits in breadth <note>Rabanus Maurus adds these two dimensions (20 + 20) to reach the symbolic number 40, the subject of this chapter.</note>—to show that He is the Holy of Holies himself, who was fixed to the trunk of the four-fold cross so that He might truly atone for the sins of the people and sanctify the nations of the entire world, dwelling among them and saving all who believe in Him. 

Deservedly, then, the cross itself can be called the "Holy of Holies," which is venerated and worshipped by all the saints on earth, and is also considered worthy of all honor (as we believe) by the holy angelic spirits themselves, who rejoice in our redemption. They remember that Christ was exalted because of His obedience to the Cross, and that the name which is above every name was given to Him, so that at the name of Jesus <note>original: "Hiesu", an archaic spelling.</note> every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth <note>A reference to Philippians 2:8–10.</note>. 

Moreover, the number forty itself is here enclosed within four triangles, following the power of geometric figures, containing a verse of forty letters in this manner: **Holy Cross, you are the victory of Christ the eternal King.** <note>original: "Crux sacra tu æterni es regis victoria Christi."</note>

# FIRST BOOK. FOLIO XXXIX.

The Cross shall be my song; lend your faithful ears,
Praise of the Cross flows from the mouth; lead forth your devoted minds,
You to whom Christ is dear, for whom wisdom is a care,
The eternal light of God, for whom incorruption <note>original: "incorruptio" — refers to the state of being free from decay or sin</note> becomes love.
Here sounds the virtue of the Creator, and of the blessed work;
Here beauty exults, here the glory of art is fashioned.
Your honor lives, because the vivid origin shines bright;
Your palm of victory remains by right immortal in the heavens.
Because bright victory is Christ for you everywhere.
He is your salvation, and he took vengeance in the dark abyss <note>original: "atro" — dark or gloomy place, referring to the underworld</note>
Dying for you, and he justly crushed the wicked one,
Killing death by death, while he conquered hell. <note>original: "tartara" — a classical term for the underworld, here used for the Christian Hell.</note>
Hither, hither, you who are sick, run with swift pace, behold:
Your physician shall be he whom the healing cross bore on the high 
Stake; he extended the arms of care, and 
Ask to be healed, and stretch out both your palms.
Therefore, by his touch, he is able quickly to restore the face, and that same
Pious right hand [is given] to the trembling one; here is the nourishing pinnacle of rest,
Whose virtue is greatest, the wise Art to apply health—
He who descended so that human nature <note>original: "physica" — literally "the physical" or "nature," referring to the healing of the human condition.</note> might recover by his art.
Let the losses of fear depart, let the blessed signs revive.
The fifty-fold <note>The Latin word "Quinquaginta" (fifty) is split across the line ("Quinqua... ginta") as a poetic device called tmesis.</note> number of salvation here
This blessed shape of the cross gives, full of divine gift:
Which signifies forgiveness, and the joyful sabbaths of rest,
Which is the indicator of the gifts of the ancient law after the feast of unleavened bread <note>original: "azima" — the Hebrew feast of Matzah or Passover.</note>,
And after the holy solemnities of Easter <note>original: "paschæ"</note>
It is itself full of the divinity of the Paraclete <term>Paraclete|A title for the Holy Spirit, meaning "advocate" or "helper."</term> sent from everywhere.
Upright through the love of peace, the cross brings forth the signs of peace,
Perfect in beauty, perfect in the form of honor.
It offers five crosses in its branches, and ten units <note>original: "monades" — units or ones.</note>
It counts as X <note>The Roman numeral X equals ten; its shape is also that of a cross (the decussis).</note>, a shape always fitting and friendly to the cross.
There are five books of the Law and ten commandments.
Indeed all things harmonize with the cross in the path of the word:
The Law, number, time, the mysteries performed, and the character <note>original: "character" — the literal shape or letter of the cross.</note>.
Therefore let us all together praise the cross exulting:
Let us pay our vows and debts here to the crucified King,
Who by his own blood released the world from its crimes.

# EXPLANATION.

<meta>catchword: Israel</meta>

This page, therefore, contains the number fifty, expressed in five of the letter X: which both denotes the sum of ten and expresses the figure of the cross, in whose honor the entire work is composed. This number maintains the observance of the **Jubilee** <note>In the Old Testament, a Jubilee year occurred every fifty years, marked by the release of slaves and the return of property.</note>, and it is an index of the true remission which is granted to the whole world through the cross. This is the witness to the most celebrated festival of the Law given on Mount Sinai after the celebration of the symbolic Passover, the solemnities of the slain lamb, and the passing over of the Lord in Egypt. And after the true Passover and the immolation of Christ the Lamb, it is the demonstrator of the **Paraclete** <note>original: "paracleti" — a title for the Holy Spirit, meaning "Comforter" or "Advocate," who descended fifty days after Easter at Pentecost.</note> sent upon the Apostles. This number designates the "Sabbath of Sabbaths" after the completion of seven weeks with a single unit added, and it demonstrates the joys of eternal rest, which is truly one, where the earth of our bodies shall truly celebrate its own Sabbath. For it shall feel no further losses of this present life or of its labors, but shall exercise its duty in the praises of the eternal Trinity; for it shall rejoice that its incorruption has no end.

For this reason, it is rightly asked how the number fifty arises from the number forty. The number forty is among those called **unevenly even numbers** <term>unevenly even</term> <note>original: "impariter pares" — a term from classical arithmetic (like Boethius) referring to numbers that can be halved, but those halves cannot be halved again down to unity in a symmetrical way.</note>, which is divided into equal parts, and whose parts can be divided into other equal parts, and even the parts of parts are divided, but it does not progress all the way to unity. That division is equal. Therefore, its half is 20, its fourth part is 10, its fifth part is 8, its eighth part is 5, its tenth part is 4, its twentieth part is 2, and its fortieth part is 1. For 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, and 20 make fifty. But what else does this growth from a smaller number into a larger one signify, if not our own progress? We have said before, therefore, that the number forty designates this temporal and present life; but the number fifty demonstrates the rest of the future fatherland and eternal joys.

What else is suggested to us through these two numbers, except that by leading this life in holy conversion, being instant in prayers, vigils, and fasts, and toiling in works of mercy and alms, we may hasten with full faith, integral hope, and perfect charity toward that fatherland which awaits us in the heavens? There, eternal rest is possessed without any labor; there, true joy is contained without any sadness; there, whatever good we perceived here in part shall be completed, whole and entire, without end. Furthermore, the number ten signifies the knowledge of the Creator and the creature. For the Trinity belongs to the Creator. The number seven, however, indicates the creature on account of life and the body. For in the former [the soul] there are three things, whence also God is to be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind; while in the body, four most manifest elements appear, of which it consists.

Rightly, therefore, the number signifying these things is expressed in the sign of the cross, because in it, through the mediator between God and men, we are reconciled and united to our Creator, and translated as adopted sons to the eternal Father. Correcty too is the number of the Jubilee expressed in the figure of the cross, because the whole logic of it is spiritually fitted to the Cross. For the unmerited servitude of the Israelites is relaxed in it, and through the cross, the captivity and servitude of the human race—by which it wickedly served sin and idols—is destroyed, and man, who was created in the image of God, is restored to the true liberty by which God alone is served. In the Jubilee also, a sold possession returns to its ancient owner; and in the passion of the Lord, the former possession—that is, Paradise—is restored to man, which he himself had poorly exchanged for the forbidden fruit, receiving food and losing life. There indeed it was commanded to the children of Israel that they should abstain from rural work; and here it is granted to the saints of God that they may be free from earthly greed. And the children [of Israel] sounded the trumpets...

### BOOK ONE. FOLIO 40.
g iiii

Israel, in the jubilee itself—on the tenth day of the seventh month, the time of atonement <note>The Day of Atonement, or Yom Kippur.</note> throughout all their land—sanctified the fiftieth year and proclaimed a release <note>original: "remissionem" — a debt-release or manumission of slaves.</note> to all the inhabitants of their land. Likewise, the Apostles and the other preachers of the Gospel sounded the trumpet of preaching, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. They interpreted the law spiritually and taught the whole world that all who believe in Christ may receive repentance and the remission of sins through his name. The Savior himself also revealed this time of true remission when, coming to Nazareth, he read the passage from the Prophet Isaiah pertaining to himself in the synagogue, saying: *The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor, to preach release to the captives and sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution.* 

You should understand "the acceptable year and the day of retribution" to mean the entire time of his preaching while he lived in the flesh. During this time, he opened the sight of the blind through his word and miracles to recognize the truth—that true light which enlightens every person coming into this world. By dying on the cross, he released the captives and the oppressed into freedom; for once the bonds of death were destroyed, he rose in glory and, ascending, *led captivity captive and gave gifts to men.* <note>A reference to Psalm 68:18 and Ephesians 4:8, signifying Christ’s victory over sin and death.</note> Luke the Evangelist testifies that these witnesses pertain to Christ himself when he adds that the Savior affirmed this very thing to his listeners, saying: *Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.* And everyone bore witness to him and wondered at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth. 

Furthermore, a single verse of fifty letters is contained here within five "X" marks: **"It is a joy to speak of sacred things in five points, for this too is of the cross,"** <note>original: "Quinq; iuuat apice ast sacra dicere, de cruce & hæc nam est"</note> with ten letters calculated for each mark. However, this is in the pronunciation. In the written form, nine letters are assigned to each mark. This is because the middle letter of each mark is common to both paths—both to the one that goes to the right and the one that goes to the left. <note>The author is describing a visual acrostic where the letter 'X' forms a grid. The central letter where the two lines of the 'X' intersect is counted twice when reading aloud, but written only once.</note>

### Figure XX: Concerning the numbers one hundred and twenty, and their mystical significance.

<note>This page features a "carmen figuratum" or figure-poem. The main text is written in a grid, and a secondary poem is formed by the red letters (here indicated in bold) which trace the shape of the Roman numeral CXX (120).</note>

Therefore, the pouring of sacred blood and water has washed us,
and Christ has wiped away all our filth and all
harmful stains; He here also, by erasing
the debt-bond <note>original: "cirographum" — a handwritten record of debt, referring to Colossians 2:14 where Christ nails our debt to the cross.</note> written against the world,
the Author established the **inimitable** light of the Gospel,
because he rejects all the vain things written in the **old** law.
Because he bestows life throughout the **entire world**,
the light of virtues **ascends**, and he rules everywhere.
The indicator **reveals the mystical** writings,
showing **how great the gifts of God** he offered to all with his voice.
For this praiseworthy character <note>original: "caracter" — referring to the Roman numeral CXX (120) formed by the grid.</note> contains ten times twelve.
Neither the letters nor this sign [signify] only once, but four times over,
noting the great mysteries of faith, and to the faithful
demonstrating the great and pleasing gifts of healing.
And the glory of the **Law**, which the **Author** of the Spirit in the mouth
gave as a burning **light**, with the gift of a harmonious tongue. <note>A reference to the "tongues of fire" at Pentecost.</note>
And hence the **wing** of the sacred assembly tosses [praises] everywhere,
expanding this name which the **Lamb** from the beginning
might draw back the full **altar** of the world and **hold** all safely.
With these reins **of the cross, so that Christ marks us** everywhere.
May he worthily commend to man the things which he **marks** with great **signs**.
Adding gifts in many things, he **bestows** the rewards of baptism.
**In** the world, the **Vicar** of the Lord establishes the **rewards** in the **Author**.
He multiplies [grace] for the worthy; He, the supreme ruler,
reigning with you, O Father, governing all by His authority.
He who had given the Paraclete <note>The Holy Spirit, the "Comforter" or "Advocate."</note> as a pledge of salvation by right,
so that he may rule and cherish and lead us to the fatherland of life; and
sing devotedly of **life**, sing well to Christ.
Nations and tongues, recognize the **true** King,
and the power of the Father, who **subdued** the dire power
and the sting of death; thus obey the Parent <note>God the Father.</note> in all things.
This [cross] has the highest peak, produced **from** the divine branch,
eternal rest; this is the order instilled in nature.
May it preserve us, and may it **bring** only such blessed gifts.
This glory is **virtue** and the highest cause of rest.
And may he **happily** preserve these laws; He is **free** here,
who rightly desires the highest goods and leads the way in moderation.

# EXPLANATION.
<meta>catchword: indeed</meta>
<sig>l</sig>

Finally, the Greek letter *lambda* <note>original: "lauda" — a medieval spelling for the Greek letter Λ (Lambda).</note> in this page expresses the form of the holy Cross, placed in four locations; among the Greeks, this letter also signifies the number thirty. Therefore, because it is placed here four times, it creates the number 120, the mystery <note>original: "sacramentum" — here meaning a sacred mystery or symbolic depth.</note> of which is great. For we read that before the flood, 120 years were decreed for humanity to repent; the height of Solomon’s temple was 120 cubits; and the Holy Spirit came upon 120 men on the day of Pentecost. Indeed, in the four marks that produce this same total, the four Gospels are signified, in each of which the number thirty is found: because the faith of the holy Trinity and the perfection of the commandments are most fully preached in each of the books of the Holy Gospel.

Furthermore, consider that when Noah's Ark was constructed by God's command—prepared for the salvation of the chosen in the likeness of the holy Cross, while the impious were to perish in the flood—the time for repentance decreed for humanity beforehand was calculated as 120 years. What else does this signify, except that we can only remain unharmed by the waves of this world if we obey the Gospel teachings with devoted minds, working worthily in the faith of the holy Trinity? 

The fact that the total height of the temple was 120 cubits looks toward the same mystery: that the primitive church in Jerusalem, after the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of the Lord into heaven, received the grace of the Holy Spirit in this same number of men. And so, following the progression of natural numbers from one up to fifteen, and collecting the sums of all those places together, they become 120. <note>The sum of all integers from 1 to 15 (1+2+3...+15) equals 120.</note> For the number fifteen, which consists of seven and eight, is sometimes used to signify the future life; this life is now conducted in the "Sabbath-rest" of faithful souls, but it will be perfected at the end of the age in the resurrection of immortal bodies. 

Therefore, the number one hundred and twenty aptly designates the great blessedness of the chosen in the future life. This "third upper room" <note>original: "cænaculum" — likely referring to the upper room of Pentecost or the levels of spiritual progression.</note> of the house of the Lord is aptly completed here, because after the present labors of the faithful, and after the rest of souls is received in the future, the full happiness of the entire Church will be fulfilled in the glory of the resurrection.

To this mystery it equally pertains, as we have said, that the Lord, rising from the dead and ascending to heaven, sent the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire to this number of men. Those who had been divided from one another by a diversity of languages, He suddenly caused to have a common speech in His praise through the thought of all tongues. For the Church, rising from death in its own time and ascending to heaven in incorruptible flesh, will be fully and perfectly illuminated by the gift of the Holy Spirit; then, according to the promise of the Apostle, God will be "all in all." Then there will be a full uniting of languages in all people to preach the greatness of God, because with a harmonious mind and voice, all shall together praise the glory of the Divine Majesty which they see present before them. 

Then that verse of the Psalm will be perfectly fulfilled, by which the Holy Spirit, through the Prophet, exhorts all nations to the praise of the Lord, saying: "Praise the Lord, all you nations, and praise Him together, all you peoples, for His mercy is confirmed upon us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever." <note>A translation of Psalm 117:1-2 (Psalm 116 in the Vulgate).</note> Then, as many from all nations as are predestined for eternal life—once all stumbling blocks have been cast out of Christ's Church by the service of Angels—all the members, united to their Head, will harmoniously and perpetually sing one song of praise. 

It should also be noted that not only does the letter *lambda*, placed here in four locations, show the number 120 in its own character (thirty for each one), but also the very verses which are written within it each contain thirty letters. There is,
