# BOOK ONE. FOLIO LIII.

Therefore, O Cross, the speech of the prophets honors you well,
It proclaims, exalts, and echoes your future deeds;
What the people, inspired by a sacred mouth, then brought forth,
And what the Holy Spirit had commanded them from within.
When they all speak of Christ restoring the world, and how, in you,
The Lord, fastened to the wood, grants kingdoms to the kind.
**David** <note>Traditionally the author of the Psalms; specifically referencing Psalm 22:16 and 69:21</note> spoke of his pierced palms and feet here,
And said that gall would be given for food, and vinegar for a drink;
And from your wood, he declares that he is the King of all. <note>original: "Deque tuo ligno regem"; a reference to a Latin variant of Psalm 96:10, "The Lord has reigned from the tree."</note>
**Isaiah** <note>Isaiah 9:6</note> prays that the empire be upon the shoulders of this boy,
With a blessed mouth, he spoke of the struck body and the hands extended,
Considering the spat-upon face, the death, and the cunning of enemies,
And that the dispersed of Israel run to you, who are raised up.
**Jeremiah** <note>Jeremiah 11:19</note> describes the lamb as if a burnt offering,
The pious one led silently, to be fed on wood; <note>original: "lignoque cibandum"; the Vulgate text "mittamus lignum in panem eius" (let us put wood in his bread) was widely interpreted as the Cross being applied to Christ’s body.</note>
**Ezekiel** sees in a vision the sign with the letter **Tau** <note>Ezekiel 9:4; the letter 'Tau' (T) was seen as a physical symbol of the Cross used to mark the faithful for salvation.</note>
To rescue the people, and in the likeness of the guiding Cross.
Thus you, holy salvation, were seen as power by the prophets:
You are pleasing to those above, O Cross, you are the navigator for this world.
For **Daniel** <note>Daniel 9:24-26</note> said that Christ here, by a wicked people,
Would be punished, and from then on all sin would have an end.
**Hosea** <note>Hosea 13:14</note> proclaims the people to be saved by the death of death,
And **Joel** <note>Joel 2:10</note> had foretold that at that hour
Both the sun and the stars would not pour light upon the lands:
The very same thing **Amos** <note>Amos 8:9</note> had foretold in the auspicious feasts:
**Obadiah** depicted the snares, and **Jonah** also the burials. <note>Jonah's three days in the whale were the primary symbol of Christ’s three days in the tomb.</note>
**Micah** announces the mountain of God; **Nahum** what vengeance is:
**Habakkuk** <note>Habakkuk 3:4</note> proclaims with his mouth the holy horns of the Cross: <note>original: "Cornua sancta Crucis"; the "rays" or "horns" coming from God's hand in Habakkuk were interpreted as the arms of the Cross.</note>
And **Zephaniah** long ago hears the bitter day of the Lord:
**Haggai** said that from here the heavens and the earth are moved.
**Zechariah** <note>Zechariah 3:3, 12:10</note> marks Jesus again through the filthy garment,
The wounds fixed in his hands, and that many would mourn:
**Malachi** sees the Highest ruling through the world,
And the world in a burning pyre and the ministers sweating.
Behold, the upright ancestors spoke of these your deeds with their mouths,
O nourishing Cross, the prophets spoke; the Author produced these things,
And in them you, O pious **Passion of Christ**, had fulfilled all these things.

# DECLARATION.
## PAGE 11
<meta>top-left: III. 01</meta>

Indeed, it has been pleasing to gather on this page certain testimonies from the sayings of the Prophets, which were prophesied concerning the passion of Christ and reach toward the glory of the holy Cross. Although many such testimonies can be found, we cannot denote them all here due to the brevity of this small work; however, we have introduced those which came more quickly to the mind of the writer and could be more easily found by a seeker. **David**, therefore, the Prophet and psalmist, holds many testimonies of this kind. Concerning the manner of the Lord’s passion, he speaks thus in Psalm 22 from the person of Christ:
> They pierced my hands and my feet, they numbered all my bones. Indeed, they considered and stared at me; they divided my garments among themselves, and for my vesture they cast lots.

And likewise in Psalm 69:
> And they gave, he says, gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.

And that he was to suffer upon the wood, he shows in Psalm 145 <note>The text cites Psalm 145, but the quote "The Lord reigned from the wood" is a famous early Christian addition to Psalm 96:10 (95 in the Vulgate). It was frequently used to prove the Cross was a throne.</note>, saying:
> Let the whole earth be moved before his face; say among the nations, the Lord has reigned from the wood, and so forth.

**Isaiah** also says of this:
> For a child is born to us, and a son is given to us, and the government is placed upon his shoulder, and so forth. <note>Isaiah 9:6. The "government on his shoulder" was interpreted as Christ carrying the crossbar of the Cross.</note>

And likewise:
> In that day there shall be a root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples; the nations shall pray to him, and his sepulcher shall be glorious.

And a little later:
> He shall raise, he says, a sign among the nations, and shall gather the fugitives of Israel, and shall collect the dispersed of Judah from the four quarters of the earth, and so forth.

And likewise:
> The Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all; he was offered up because he himself willed it, and he opened not his mouth; he shall be led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent, and shall not open his mouth.

And likewise, he speaks from the person of the Lord:
> I gave my body to the strikers and my cheeks to those plucking them; I did not turn my face away from those rebuking and spitting upon me, and so forth.

And again:
> I have spread out my hands all day to an unbelieving people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own thoughts.

**Jeremiah**, moreover, says from the person of the Lord:
> I am like a gentle lamb that is carried to the victim, and I did not know that they devised counsels against me, saying: "Let us put wood into his bread, and let us erase him from the land of the living, and let his name be remembered no more." <note>original: "Mittamus lignum in panem eius"; Jerome and other commentators saw the "wood in the bread" as the Cross (wood) being brought against Christ’s body (the bread of life).</note>

And likewise:
> The breath, he says, of our mouth, Christ the Lord, was captured in our sins.

**Ezekiel**, therefore, expressed the mark of the Cross in the figure of the letter **T** <note>The Hebrew letter 'Tau' was written like a cross in some ancient scripts. Ezekiel 9:4 was interpreted as a prophecy of the faithful being marked with the Cross for protection.</note>, saying:
> And he said to the man who was clothed in linen: "Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark a **Tau** upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and mourn over all the abominations that are done in the midst of it," and so forth.

And expressing that Good Shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep, he says: Thus says the Lord:
> Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, just as a shepherd visits his flock on the day when he is in the midst of his scattered sheep; so will I visit my sheep, and I will deliver them out of all the places where they had been dispersed in the day of cloud and darkness. And I will lead them out from the peoples, and gather them from the lands, and bring them into their own land, and I will feed them on the mountains of Israel.

And a little later:
> I, he says, will feed my sheep and I will make them lie down, says the Lord; that which was lost I will seek, and that which was cast away I will bring back, and that which was broken I will bind up, and that which was weak I will strengthen, and that which was fat and strong I will guard, and I will feed them in judgment.

**Daniel**, truly a most certain chronicler, faithfully indicated the time of the Lord’s incarnation and our redemption, with an Angel revealing this to him.

### BOOK ONE.

**Seventy weeks**, he says, **are shortened** <note>original: "hebdomadæ abbreviatæ sunt"; in the prophecy of Daniel, these "weeks" are interpreted by theologians as weeks of years (490 years total) leading to the Messiah.</note>, over your people and over your holy city, that transgression may be finished, and sin take an end, and iniquity be abolished, and everlasting justice be brought in, that vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Saint of Saints be anointed. Know therefore and take notice: from the going forth of the word that Jerusalem should be built again, until **Christ the leader**, there shall be **seven and sixty-two weeks**. And a little after he added this: And after sixty-two weeks **Christ shall be slain**, and he shall not be, and a people with their future leader shall destroy the city and the sanctuary. And so that it might be shown that this <term>week of years</term> <note>Referring to the final "week" of Daniel's prophecy.</note> excels the others—in which Christ preached the Gospel and performed miracles, and in which he suffered and rose from the dead—speaking of it separately he says: He shall confirm the covenant with many in **one week**, and in the half of the week the victim and the sacrifice shall fail, and in the temple there shall be the abomination of desolation, and the desolation shall persevere even until the consummation and the end.

**Hosea** also most clearly foretells the devotion of the nations and the gathering of the church assembled through Christ. And it shall be, he says, in the place where it is said, "you are not my people," it shall be said to them, "**children of the living God.**" And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves **one head**, and so forth. And concerning our rescue from the underworld and the slaying of death, he declares the promise of the Lord, saying: **From the hand of death I will free them**, and from death I will redeem them; **I will be your death, O death; your bite I will be, O hell.** <note>original: "morsus tuus ero inferne"; this famous verse was historically used in the Christian liturgy for Holy Saturday and Easter to describe Christ's "Harrowing of Hell."</note>

For **Joel** demonstrates the Lord’s passion and the salvation of the faithful, saying thus: The **Sun and Moon are darkened**, and the stars have withdrawn their light, and the Lord shall roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem, and the heavens and the earth shall be moved; and the Lord is the hope of his people, and the strength of the children of Israel, and you shall know that I am the Lord your God dwelling in my holy mountain, and Jerusalem shall be holy, and strangers shall pass through her no more, and so forth.

From here **Amos** says: And it shall be in that day, says the Lord, that **the sun shall go down at midday**, and I will make the earth dark in the day of light, and I will turn your festivities into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation, and so forth. <note>Medieval commentators interpreted this "darkness at noon" as a direct prophecy of the darkness that occurred during the Crucifixion.</note> And a little after: In that day, he says, I will raise up the **tabernacle of David** which has fallen, and I will rebuild the openings of the walls, and I will restore those things which had collapsed, and so forth.

**Obadiah**, however, expressing the deceits of the Jews against the Lord and the salvation of the church, says: All the men of your covenant have mocked you, the men of your peace have prevailed against you, and those who eat with you shall lay snares under you, and so forth. And a little after: On **Mount Zion** there shall be salvation, and it shall be holy, and the house of Jacob shall possess those who had possessed them. And likewise he added: And the Savior shall ascend onto Mount Zion to judge the mount of Esau, and the kingdom shall be the Lord's.

The Lord himself also showed the prophecy of **Jonah**, saying: As Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so shall the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth.

**Micah** indeed foretells the assembly of peoples to Christ, showing him to be the mountain of the Lord and the leader. In the last of days, he says, the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the peak of the mountains, and so forth. And likewise: **You, Bethlehem Ephrata**, are a little one among the thousands of Judah; out of you shall come forth to me the **leader who is to be the Ruler in Israel**, and so forth.

**Nahum** foretells the Lord as an avenger to his enemies, and good to the pious and his friends. God, he says, is jealous, and the Lord is revenging and having fury; the Lord is revenging on his adversaries and angry with his enemies, and so forth. And likewise, showing his piety, he says: The Lord is good...

# EXPLANATION.

...and **strengthening in the day of tribulation, and knowing those who hope in him.** <note>This opening quote is from the prophet Nahum 1:7, concluding a section likely begun on the preceding page.</note> **Habakkuk**, a strong and steadfast observer, stands upon his watchtower and sets his foot upon the fortification, that he might gaze upon Christ on the Cross and say: **His glory covered the heavens, and the earth is full of his praise. His brightness shall be as the light, horns are in his hands.** <note>original: "cornua sunt in manibus eius." In medieval exegesis, these "horns" or "rays" coming from the hands were interpreted as the nails of the Crucifixion.</note> **There his strength was hidden.**

**Zephaniah** tells that the coming of the day of the Lord is near, as well as the hour of his passion and resurrection. **The great day of the Lord is near,** he says, **near and exceeding swift. The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter, the strong man shall be troubled there.** And a little later: **I will afflict men,** he says, **and men shall walk like the blind, because they have sinned against the Lord.** And likewise: **Wherefore wait for me, says the Lord, in the day of my resurrection for the future,** and so forth.

**Haggai** announces the **Desired One** to all nations. **Yet a little while, says the Lord, and I will move heaven and earth and the sea and the dry land,** and so forth.

**Zechariah**, truly mindful of his Lord, sees **Jesus in filthy garments**, and the **stone of seven eyes**, and also the **golden lampstand**, and so forth. He speaks also in the person of the Lord: **They weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver.** And likewise: **I will pour out upon the house of David the spirit of grace and prayers, and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him with a mourning as if for an only son,** and so forth. And likewise: **Adam is my example from my youth,** <note>This follows the Latin Vulgate text of Zechariah 13:5, "Adam exemplum meum," which was traditionally interpreted as Christ (the New Adam) speaking of his humanity.</note> and it shall be said: **What are these wounds in the middle of your hands?** and he shall say: **With these I was wounded in the house of those who loved me. Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, and against the man who cleaves to me, says the Lord of hosts: Strike the shepherd and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered.** And likewise: **And the Lord shall be king over all the earth. In that day there shall be one Lord, and his name shall be one.**

**Malachi** tells of the salvific coming of the Lord: **And presently,** he says, **the ruler whom you seek shall come to his temple, and the Angel of the testament whom you desire; behold he comes, says the Lord of hosts, and who shall be able to think of the day of his coming, and who shall stand to see him? For he is like a refining fire and like the fuller’s herb,** <term>fuller’s herb</term> <note>Also known as soapwort; a plant used in the ancient world for cleaning and processing wool.</note> **and he shall sit refining and cleansing silver, and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and shall refine them as gold and as silver, and they shall offer sacrifices to the Lord in justice, and the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem shall please God,** and so forth.

There is also this verse written here upon the cross, consisting of 37 letters:
->*Es placida superis Crux huic es nauita mundo.*<-
<note>Translated: "You are pleasing to those above, O Cross; you are the navigator for this world."</note>
Which is a direct <term>hexameter</term> <note>A form of poetic meter consisting of six metrical feet, standard for Classical epic poetry.</note>, and when reversed, without removing a single syllable, it becomes a <term>pentameter</term> <note>A poetic line of five metrical feet.</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the abstract cryptographic tables seen previously into a specific "pattern poem" (carmen figuratum) by the Carolingian scholar Hrabanus Maurus. While the previous page dealt with the mechanics of a cipher, this page applies those visual grid principles to a theological poem. We are moving from the "how" of secret writing to a "what"—a sacred text where the image of the Cross is literally embedded within the letters of the New Testament's witnesses.</meta>

## XXVII. Figure. On the sayings of the Apostles concerning the same matter in the New Testament.

<note>This page features a "carmen figuratum" or pattern poem. In this artistic style, the letters are arranged in a perfect grid so that specific shapes—here, a cross—can be outlined to reveal further meanings or highlighted verses. The poem argues that the Apostles of the New Testament confirm the same truths about the Cross that the Prophets did in the Old Testament.</note>

->Figure XXVII<-

<note>The grid below is a 35x35 letter square. A cross shape is formed by the 18th row and the 18th column. The text below is a translation of the Latin verse contained within that grid.</note>

No less, therefore, does your sign <note>original: "caracter"—referring to the physical shape or "character" of the Cross</note> guard the laws of the New Testament rightly and reveal holy gifts, which God, the high man, brought down to the divine world. Through you, O sacred Cross, to be worshipped with frequent prayer, fulfilling the promise and the truthful teachings of the prophets; but testifying to the Lord of both the old and new law.

He who as Father made the twin abyss <note>this likely refers to the "waters above and below" or the heavens and the earth</note> for the world by his word, cheers us, satisfying the prayers of those who came before. He who used to console, truthful, good, and fair to all; whence the apostolic order praises your nurturing trophies everywhere in speech, O Cross. 

Peter, the leader, sounds out through the world from an exceptional heart, thus speaking praises in holy speech, saying excellently: "Behold, brothers, Christ has suffered for you upon the beam <note>original: "stipite"—referring to the wooden post or trunk of the Cross</note>, handing down a clear example so that you may follow his footsteps, whose sacred wounds heal." 

From here, I believe Jesus receives the words of the one who prays. If the Lord is with him, let honor be given; because he himself is gentle, these gifts do not seem base to him. But James from here exhorts us with pure speech, setting Christ as an example concerning the end of labors. And from here John, the leader, warns in writing with his mouth: "May chaste love remain and bring forth sober prayers; as Jesus suffered devotedly because of love, so let us suffer with a holy mind and shared love here." 

Jude <note>original: "Iudas"—referring to the Apostle Jude Thaddeus</note> testifies to the leader, both for the faithful and the wicked. Not a little did Paul pray to you with his mouth, O sacred Cross, when he said he no longer knew how to speak anything without you, nor did he know how to give any praise from his throat. 

A great name in the heavens, on the lands, and through the underworld <note>original: "tartara"—the classical term for the depths of the afterlife, used here to show the Cross's power over all realms</note>; because of you, Christ promises that it is rightly powerful. Thus also the apostolic order praises in harmony; you join all things to the ancient prophets. O holy Passion of Jesus, Christ through the ages.

<header>DECLARATION.</header>

## DECLARATION.

The writings of the New Testament offer such abundant examples regarding the life-giving passion and resurrection of our Lord that one cannot easily select the most evident testimonies from such a vast multitude. One would hardly know which to choose first, as they are so numerous they cannot be gathered into a single small book; and all are of such great dignity that even the learned cannot worthily estimate which are more manifest or proven. But just as we excerpted some things from the Old Testament—that is, from the books of the Prophets—which were omens <note>original: "p̃ſagio"—a presage or foreshadowing</note> of the future and not yet completed passion of the Lord, so also from the New we shall excerpt only those things which suit the proclamation of the magnificence and praise of the Holy Cross, and which pertain to glorifying the goodness of the Creator and the mercy of our Redeemer for our liberation. For those things which the former [Prophets] predicted as future, the latter [Apostles] preach as already done and completed. It is fitting that the acts of the Holy Cross be preached from both Testaments, because Christ is the administrator and mediator of both. He Himself, therefore, who invisibly ruled the minds of the Prophets through the inspiration of His Spirit, assuming a visible body, taught the Apostles by words and examples—He who through the Patriarchs and Prophets promised salvation and life to His people. Having been made man, He fulfilled the promise through the power of His cross, He who said through the Prophet:

> Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees; say to the faint-hearted: take courage, do not fear; behold, your God will bring the vengeance of retribution; God Himself will come and save us, and so forth. <note>A reference to Isaiah 35:3-4</note>

He showed through the Apostle that this has now been done, when the Apostle Peter says:

> You know, brethren, what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism which John preached: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with Him. And we are witnesses of all that He did in the region of the Jews and in Jerusalem; Him they killed by hanging Him on a tree <note>original: "ligno"—literally 'wood' or 'timber', a common biblical term for the Cross</note>. This man God raised on the third day and allowed Him to be made manifest, not to all the people, but to witnesses preordained by God, to us who ate and drank with Him after He rose from the dead; and He commanded us to preach and testify that He is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. <note>Acts 10:37-42</note>

To Him all the Prophets bear witness that all who believe in Him receive remission of sins through His name. Peter says something similar in his epistle:

> Christ died once <note>original: "sel'"—abbreviation for "semel" (once/for all)</note> for our sins, the just for the unjust, that He might offer us to God, put to death indeed in the flesh, but brought to life by the Spirit.

And likewise:

> Christ, he says, suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow His footsteps.

And a little later he added:

> He handed Himself over to Him who judges justly, who Himself bore our sins in His body upon the tree <note>original: "lignũ"—the wood of the Cross</note>, so that, dead to sins, we might live for justice; by whose wounds <note>original: "liuore"—literally the 'livid' marks or welts of a beating</note> you have been healed.

James also, the brother of the Lord, exhorts us to the same example, saying:

> Take the Prophets as an example of labor and patience, who spoke in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Behold, we call blessed those who endured; you have heard of the patience of Job and have seen the end of the Lord, for the Lord is compassionate and merciful.

And the Apostle John gives us confidence in His mercy, saying:

> My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin; but if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and He is the propitiation <note>original: "p̃pitiatio"—an atoning sacrifice</note> for our sins, and not for ours only but also for those of the whole world.

And likewise:

> In this we have known the charity <note>original: "charitatem"—divine love</note> of God, because He laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.

But the Apostle Jude, brother of James, demonstrated under the example of Moses' successor <note>original: "successoris Moši"—referring to Joshua (whose name in Latin is also 'Iesus'). Medieval scholars saw Joshua leading Israel out of the desert as a "type" or precursor of Jesus leading humanity out of sin.</note> that Jesus Christ led us through the Cross out of the spiritual Egypt—that is, from the power of darkness—and destroyed the unbelieving, saying thus:

> I want to remind you, though you once knew all things, that Jesus, saving the people out of the land of Egypt,

...secondly, he destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not keep their own positions of authority <note>original: "principatum"</note> but abandoned their proper dwelling, he has reserved in eternal chains under deep darkness for the judgment of the great day. 

Paul, indeed—the Apostle and teacher of the nations, who was the last of all the Apostles in his calling but labored more than them all—is so multifaceted in his speaking as he commends to us Christ’s passion, resurrection, and redemption through His blood, as well as His dominion in heaven and on earth, that he is almost entirely occupied with this theme. But because he who wrote more about Christ than all the others ought not to be excluded from this praise, and since he is so well-suited to it that he can easily be summarized briefly while others are set aside: let us nevertheless set down those testimonies which he specifically employed concerning the Cross. 

He says, therefore, to the Corinthians: *For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not in the wisdom of words, lest the Cross of Christ be made void. For the word of the Cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God,* and so forth. And likewise: *For I did not judge myself to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and Him crucified.* 

Likewise, he says to the Galatians: *But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.* 

Likewise, to the Ephesians: *He is our peace, who made both one, breaking down the middle wall of enmity in His flesh, making void the law of commandments in its decrees, so that He might create the two in Himself into one man, making peace, that He might reconcile both in one body to God through the Cross, killing the enmity in Himself,* and so forth. 

Likewise, to the Philippians: *Christ,* he says, *humbled Himself, becoming obedient even unto death, even the death of the Cross; because of which God also exalted Him, and gave Him the name which is above every name,* and so forth. 

Likewise, to the Colossians, preaching the majesty of Christ, he says: *In Him all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through Him and in Him, and He is before all, and all things hold together in Him. He is the head of the body, the Church; He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that He might hold the primacy in all things, because it pleased God that all the fullness of divinity should dwell in Him, and through Him to reconcile all things, making peace through the blood of His Cross, whether those things on earth or those in heaven.* And likewise, he says in the same Epistle: *Forgiving us all our sins, blotting out the handwritten record of the decree <term>handwritten record</term> <note>original: "chirographum," referring to a legal bond or record of debt</note> that was against us, which was contrary to us; and He took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross,* and so forth. 

In the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> as well, nearly all the praises and all the songs contained therein agree in preaching the glory of Christ’s passion and the grace of our redemption, as the author himself frequently and freely commemorates the slain Lamb who is in the midst of the throne. But we have judged it unnecessary to place any testimonies of these things here, because we have inserted many in other places in this book. 

There are, moreover, two <term>heroic verses</term> <note>Dactylic hexameters, the classic meter for epic and serious poetry</note> written with the same letters upon the image of the Holy Cross; the first of these, written along the length <note>the vertical beam</note> of the cross, is this: 

->**If I sound these measures for you as a gift, Jesus is in these songs.**<- 
<note>original: "Si dote tibi metra sono his te Hiesus in odis."</note> 

However, if this verse is read back with the same letters—that is, from the end to the beginning—it forms this second verse, which is written in the transverse path <note>the horizontal beam</note> of the cross: 

->**If you use His gifts, and if honor and song go toward this art.**<- 
<note>original: "Si donis vs ei & si honos artem ibit & odis." The symbol "&" is used here to represent the letters needed to complete the palindrome.</note> 

When this second verse is read back through the same letters, it returns to the first one—namely, the one that is in the length of the cross.

# DECLARATION.

In the New Testament, however, the examples of the writers concerning the life-giving passion and resurrection of our Lord are so abundant that one cannot easily choose the most evident testimonies from such a great multitude. One hardly knows which to select as the most important, since there are so many they could not be gathered into a single small book; all are of such great dignity that even the most learned cannot worthily value which among them are the most clear and proven. But just as we selected certain things from the Old Testament—that is, from the books of the Prophets—which served as a presage of the Lord’s future and not yet completed passion, let us likewise select only those things from the New Testament which are suitable for preaching the magnificence and praise of the holy Cross, and which pertain to glorifying the goodness of the Creator and the mercy of our Redeemer for our liberation. For those things which the former group predicted would happen, the latter group preach as already done and completed. Indeed, it is fitting for the acts of the holy Cross to be preached from both Testaments, because Christ is the administrator and mediator of both. He himself, therefore, who invisibly ruled the minds of the Prophets through the inspiration of His Spirit, took on a visible body: He taught the Apostles by words and examples, He who promised salvation and life to His people through the Patriarchs and Prophets. Having been made man, He fulfilled the promise through the power of His cross—He who said through the Prophet: *Strengthen the weary hands, and firm up the weak knees; say to the faint-hearted: take courage, and do not fear; behold, your God will bring the vengeance of retribution, God himself will come and save us,* and so forth. 

He showed this as already accomplished through the Apostle, when the Apostle Peter said: *You know, brothers, what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism which John preached: how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all those oppressed by the devil, because God was with him; and we are witnesses of all that he did in the region of the Jews and in Jerusalem, whom they killed by hanging him on a tree.* <note>original: "suspendētes in ligno" — the Latin 'lignum' means wood, log, or tree, and was a common scriptural way to refer to the Cross.</note> *This man God raised on the third day, and granted that he become manifest, not to all the people but to witnesses preordained by God—to us, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead; and he commanded us to preach and to testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. To him all the Prophets bear witness, that all who believe in him receive remission of sins through his name.* 

The same Peter says something similar in his epistle: *Christ died once for our sins, the just for the unjust, so that he might offer us to God, having been put to death in the flesh but brought to life by the Spirit.* And likewise: *Christ,* he says, *suffered for us, leaving you an example so that you might follow in his footsteps.* And a little later he added: *He gave himself up to the one who judges justly, he who bore our sins in his own body upon the tree* <note>original: "super lignum"</note>; *so that, being dead to sins, we might live for justice: by whose wounds you have been healed.* 

James also, the brother of the Lord, exhorts us to the same example, saying: *Take as an example of labor and patience the Prophets, who spoke in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Behold, we call blessed those who have endured; you have heard of the suffering of Job and you have seen the end intended by the Lord, for the Lord is compassionate and merciful.* 

And the Apostle John grants us confidence in His mercy, saying: *My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin, but even if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins; and not only for ours, but also for those of the whole world.* And likewise: *In this we have known the charity of God, because he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.* 

Moreover, Jude the Apostle and brother of James, using the example of Moses' successor <note>referring to Joshua, whose name in Greek/Latin is the same as Jesus</note>, demonstrated that Jesus Christ led us through the Cross out of spiritual Egypt—that is, from the power of darkness—and destroyed the unbelievers, saying thus: *But I want to remind you, though you once knew everything, that Jesus, saving the people out of the land of Egypt,*

But because he who wrote more about Him than all others should not be excluded from this praise, and since he is so fit for it that he can easily be summarized briefly while others are passed over, let us nevertheless set down those testimonies which he specifically employed regarding the Cross. 

He says therefore to the Corinthians: *For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel, not with the wisdom of words, lest the Cross of Christ be made void. For the Word of the Cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those of us who are being saved, it is the power of God,* and so forth. <note>original: 1 Corinthians 1:17-18</note> And likewise: *For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and Him crucified.* <note>original: 1 Corinthians 2:2</note> Likewise to the Galatians he says: *But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.* <note>original: Galatians 6:14</note> Likewise to the Ephesians: *He is our peace, who made both one, and breaking down the middle wall of enmity in His flesh, abolishing the law of commandments in decrees, that He might create the two in Himself into one man, making peace, that He might reconcile both in one body to God through the Cross, killing the enmity in Himself,* and so forth. <note>original: Ephesians 2:14-16</note> Likewise to the Philippians: *He humbled Himself,* he says, *Christ having been made obedient even unto death, even the death of the Cross; for which reason God also exalted Him, and gave Him the name which is above every name,* and so forth. <note>original: Philippians 2:8-9</note> Likewise to the Colossians, preaching the majesty of Christ, he says: *In Him all things were created, those in heaven and those on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through Him and in Him, and He is before all, and all things consist in Him. He is the head of the body of the Church; He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things He might hold the primacy, because it pleased God that in Him all the fullness of the divinity should dwell, and through Him to reconcile all things, making peace through the blood of His Cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven.* <note>original: Colossians 1:16-20</note> And likewise he says in the same Epistle: *Forgiving us all our sins, blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us, which was contrary to us, and He took it out of the way, pinning it to the cross,* and so forth. <note>original: Colossians 2:13-14</note> 

In the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> as well, almost all the praises and all the songs contained therein agree in preaching the glory of Christ’s passion and the grace of our redemption, as he himself frequently and freely makes mention of the slain Lamb who is in the midst of the throne. But we have judged it unnecessary to place any testimonies of these here, because we have inserted not a few in other places of this book. 

There are, however, two heroic verses <note>Dactylic hexameters, the "heroic" meter of epic poetry</note> here in the image of the holy Cross written with the same letters; the first of these, written along the length <note>the vertical beam</note> of the cross, is this: **If by a gift I sound rhythms for you, Jesus is in these songs.** <note>original: "Si dote tibi metra sono his te Hiesus in odis."</note> This verse, if read with the same letters backward—that is, from the end to the beginning—forms this verse, which is written across the path <note>the horizontal beam</note> of the cross: **If you are for him with gifts, and if honor goes to art, it will go also to songs.** <note>original: "Si donis vs ei & si honos artem ibit & odis." Note: This is a palindrome-like wordplay where the sequence of letters is nearly identical in reverse.</note> This, when read back through the same letters, returns to the former verse, namely the one which is in the length of the cross.

<meta>This page contains Figure 28 of Hrabanus Maurus's *In Praise of the Holy Cross*. It follows the previous page's theological justification for the Cross with a direct, personal poetic devotion. The author, Hrabanus, includes himself visually and textually in this composition.</meta>

### Figure XXVIII. On the Adoration of the Cross by the Author.

<page-num>XXVIII</page-num>

<note>This "pattern poem" (carmen figuratum) is a masterpiece of Carolingian art and literature. The text is arranged in a perfect grid, and within that grid, specific letters are highlighted in red ink to form shapes. Here, the red letters depict a large Cross and a kneeling figure of the author himself, Hrabanus Maurus, at its base. The poem below is a translation of the horizontal lines of the grid.</note>

Omnipotent power, high majesty, Lord of Hosts <note>original: "Sabaoth," a Hebrew title for God meaning "of hosts" or "of armies."</note>
Exalted Lord of virtues, highest creator,
Fashioner of the world and of men, you true redeemer.
You are my praise, my strength; you are all glory and salvation.
You are King and Teacher, you are the Ruler, the dear Master.
You are the Shepherd, feeding and protecting the true sheepfold.
You are my portion, holy Savior and author.
Leader, way, light, life, good reward, gate of the kingdom.
Voice, sense, word, joyful offspring of virtues.
To you I have directed, and now piling up words, I direct them again.
My mind speaks to you, the whole intention of my mind:
Whatever the tongue, the hand, or the mouth prays and blesses,
A humble heart and a just life, a consecrated will.
All things praise you and sing to you, serene Christ.
For I, prostrate and joyful, adore you as Lord,
And bowing here to your cross, I speak my greeting.
**I pray for hope, O branch; I pray to consume the altar from this bed.**
<note>original: "Spem oro te ramus aram ara sumare toro hinc." This line is a palindrome, meaning it reads the same (or nearly the same) forward and backward, a display of the poet's immense technical skill.</note>
This is my ardor, this the clear fire of love.
This my mind first asks, this hunger holds my mouth.
This is the thirst of the soul, the great desire of the spirit:
That you, good Christ, may piously receive me through the altar,
As an offered servant, so that I may be your victim, Jesus.
A sacrifice let me be, all of me crucified to your cross.
Now may your passion consume and mitigate the heat of passion,
May it crush carnal vices and suppress anger,
May it restrain the tongue and restore words of piety,
May it pacify the mind and lead an honest life.
For when your fiery advent shines through all the high heavens,
It will scorch the unjust with heat and fire.
The storm hisses, the horn now bellows throughout the world,
When the sign of the cross appears in the air before us.
Then I ask that the cross itself may snatch me from those avenging flames,
And defend the poet as his own from great wrath.
To whom I rightly sing, I, Hrabanus <note>Hrabanus Maurus (c. 780–856) was a Benedictine monk, scholar, and the Archbishop of Mainz.</note>, with words from my mouth,
With heart and hand, I always sing a memorable song to the Lord.
Because He had mercifully given me to the altar of life.
When, I pray, that merciful Jesus Himself appeared from the lowest depths,
Now may Christ grant rest in the heights of the heavens.
Give this to me, I ask; I hope and believe all these truths
Which you promised; I hold this by piety and faith:
That you, the Truthful One, make all things in order and true judgment.
Go now to the dwellers above in the heavens with a rightful triumph;
O nourishing praise of the cross, may it always prevail without end.

<summary>In this final visual poem of the first book, Hrabanus Maurus presents himself kneeling in prayer before the Cross, offering his own poetry and his very life as a sacrifice to Christ. The text serves as a personal plea for salvation and protection during the Last Judgment.</summary>

<keywords>Hrabanus Maurus, Holy Cross, carmen figuratum, Carolingian poetry, Last Judgment, prayer of adoration, religious art, Benedictine spirituality</keywords>

# BOOK ONE. LEAF LVIII.

Omnipotent power, high majesty, exalted Lord of Hosts, <note>original: "Sabaoth," a Hebrew title for God meaning "of hosts" or "armies."</note>
Highest creator of virtues,
Fashioner of the world: you are truly the redeemer of men.
You are my praise, my strength, you are all my glory and my health;
You are King, you are teacher, you are the ruler, dear Master,
You are the shepherd feeding us, the true protector of the sheepfold.
And you are my portion, holy Savior and author,
Leader, way, light, life, good reward; you are the gate of the kingdom,
Voice, sense, word, the joyful offspring of virtues.
To you I have directed, and now piling up words, I direct them again:
My mind speaks to you, the whole intention of my mind,
Whatever my tongue or my hand prays, and whatever my mouth blessedly speaks,
With a humble heart, and a just life, and a consecrated will.
All things praise you and sing to you, serene Christ.
For I, prostrate and joyful, adore you as Lord,
And bowing here to your Cross, I speak my greeting:
**I pray for hope to you, O branch; may I be taken up by the altar, from the altar I pray.** <note>original: "Spem oro te ramus aram ara sumar, & oro hinc." This is a palindrome, a sacred word-game where the line reads the same forward and backward, symbolizing the perfection and eternal nature of the Cross.</note>
This is my bright passion, this is the fire of my love,
This my mind seeks first, this my speech and my mouth desire,
This is the thirst of my soul, a great hunger for consuming:
That you, pious and good Christ, might receive me,
Your servant offered through the altar, so that I, Jesus, might be your victim. <note>Hrabanus uses "Hiesus" here as the object of his devotion, identifying his own sacrifice with that of Christ.</note>
That I might be your sacrificial host: let your passion now
Consume me entirely in my crucifixion; let it mitigate my carnal
Heat, shatter my vices, suppress my anger,
Bridle my tongue, and restore words of piety.
May it bring peace to my mind: may it lead me to an honest life.
For when your fiery coming shall shine forth
Throughout all the heavenly heights, <note>original: "olympo." Medieval Christian poets often used the classical term for Mount Olympus to refer to the highest Heaven.</note> and that heat shall scorch the wicked,
When the tempest roars and the horn now bellows through the world,
When the sign of the Cross shall first appear in the air:
Then, I ask, let the Cross itself snatch me from the avenging flames;
And let it defend the Lamb’s own poet from wrath,
To whom I sing: by right I, Hrabanus, sing with verses, with my mouth,
With my heart, and my hand, always a memorable gift in song:
Because He had mercifully placed me upon the altar of life.
When merciful Jesus himself, I pray, has rescued me from the depths
Of hell, grant me now, O Christ, rest in the citadel of the heavens;
This I ask, this I hope, and I believe all the truths
Which you have promised; this I hold through piety and faith.

# EXPLANATION.

> Because you, the Truthful One, make all things true in order and judgment.
> Go now to those above; in the heavens, you triumph as is right.
> O nourishing praise of the Cross, hail forever without end!

### Explanation of the Figure.

Almighty God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, you who willed that your only-begotten Son, born before all ages, should in time take on human flesh and a human soul, and undergo the Cross for the salvation of the human race: I adore you, I give you thanks, because you have granted your grace to me, your wretched servant (though I am unworthy and weighed down by a mass of many crimes), so that I might bring forth the passion of your beloved Son in songs of praise—which, though not fully worthy, are nonetheless devoted. To you, Lord Jesus Christ, only-begotten Son of God, I offer humble prayers and pay the vows of my mouth: because you have deigned to inspire me, a sinner, to sing out the honor of your holy Cross as much as I am able, and to preach our common salvation to my fellow servants. Nor did the consciousness of my own sins hold me back from this beginning; rather, it gave me greater confidence, because in this poem I might celebrate that in which you destroyed the kingdom of sin and gave forgiveness for all crimes to the whole world. To you, Holy Spirit, the Comforter, <note>original: "Spiritus paraclete," from the Greek 'Parakletos', meaning advocate or helper.</note> I return thanks with all my heart, because you have deigned to help and console me by your grace in this very work. I pray to you that if, through my frailty, I have set down anything unbecomingly or have not understood it rightly, you might deign to enlighten me through your visitation, so that I may properly correct those things and obtain through you the forgiveness of my error; so that you yourself, whom I called upon for help before the work began, might lead me without shipwreck to the longed-for shore.

To you, eternal and perpetual God in Trinity and inseparable Unity, I worship, adore, long for, and desire with all my heart, all my soul, all my mind, and all my strength. You are my illumination, you are my salvation, my praise, my strength, creator, redeemer, restorer, father, judge, teacher, bliss, fortitude, joy, eternity, felicity, serenity; one almighty God, Lord of Lords, creator of all things, God who is the light and life of the faithful; living life, life from the living, <note>original: "vita viuens, vita à viuente," a theological expression of the eternal generation of the Son and the procession of the Spirit.</note> giver of life to the living, loving and beloved, and most friendly love; begetter and begotten, and powerfully regenerating; the Speaker and the Word and the one proceeding from both; the Loving and the Loved, and the love of both; true light, light from light, true illumination, counselor, counsel, and communication, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist: to you be praise and glory for everlasting ages. 

I ask you, most merciful Father, that as you first willed me to complete this work by writing it—which pertains to the praise of our redeemer and savior—I may deserve to obtain his grace of redemption and salvation through him. And whatever work I may do hereafter, may you cause it all to come to your praise from your grace, through your grace, and in your grace; and command me hereafter to be safer from sins and stronger in good works. As long as I live in this small body, let me always offer some service to you. After the departure of my soul from the body, grant that I may obtain the forgiveness of all sins and receive eternal life through him, who lives and reigns as God, co-equal with you and the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages, Amen. Indeed, in the Cross of the preceding...

# BOOK ONE. FOLIO 59.

...of the preceding <note>The Latin text begins with "dentis," completing the word "praecedentis" from the previous page.</note> page, there is one verse written in 27 letters, which can be read and re-read with the same letters in this manner: **I pray to you, branch of the altar; may I be incensed by the altar and I pray.** <note>original: "Oro te ramus aram ara fumar & oro." This is a palindrome—it reads the same forwards and backwards.</note> Truly, my image, which I had depicted beneath the Cross, kneeling and praying, is composed in <term>Asclepiadean meter</term> <note>A classical Greek and Latin poetic meter named after Asclepiades of Samos.</note>, holding a <term>heroic hexameter</term> <note>The standard meter for epic poetry, like the Aeneid.</note> in the first verse, and a <term>heroic half-verse</term> in the second, thus: **O merciful Christ, I ask you to protect me, Rabanus: O pious one, in your judgment.**

Moreover, this entire book contains 28 metrical figures <note>Hrabanus refers to his "carmina figurata"—poems where the letters form visual shapes on a grid.</note> with their following prose, excluding the threshold page and the prologue. This number is a "perfect number" within the first hundred according to its parts <note>In medieval mathematics, 28 is a "perfect number" because its divisors (1, 2, 4, 7, and 14) add up to 28.</note>; and therefore, I wished to complete the work according to this sum, for I have sung of that form in this book which is the finisher and perfection of all things.

## Index of the contents of this book by chapter counts and the distribution of page numbers in each.

I. The first chapter contains the Image of Christ, extending his arms in the manner of a Cross, where the names of the Savior pertaining to both of his natures <note>Refers to the divine and human natures of Christ.</note> are explained. Book 1, folio 1; and Book 2, folio 1.

II. The figure of the Cross written within a <term>tetragon</term> <note>A four-sided geometric shape, such as a square or rectangle.</note>: it is demonstrated to encompass all things. Book 1, folio 4; and Book 2, folio 1.

III. Concerning the nine orders of Spirits <note>The hierarchy of angels (Seraphim, Cherubim, etc.).</note>, and concerning their names arranged into the form of a cross. Book 1, folio 6; and Book 2, folio 2.

IIII. The Cherubim and Seraphim are arranged around the cross: with their significance added. Book 1, folio 8; and Book 2, folio 2.

V. Four square figures are arranged next to the cross, with the building of the house of God joined to them. Book 1, folio 10; and Book 2, folio 3.

VI. How the four principal virtues <note>The Cardinal Virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note> pertain to the Cross: and how the fruits of all virtues are conferred upon us through the Cross of Christ. Book 1, folio 12; and Book 2, folio 3.

VII. In what manner the four elements, the changes of the four seasons, the four regions of the world, and the four quarters of the natural day are arranged and sanctified in the Cross. Book 1, folio 14; and Book 2, folio 4.

VIII. The mystery of the number twelve <gloss>the duodenary</gloss> is shown in the Cross: where the months, the signs <note>The Zodiac signs.</note>, the winds, and also the preaching of the Apostles are manifested by the number twelve. Book 1, folio 16; and Book 2, folio 4.

IX. The days of the year in four hexagons and the <term>leap-year monad</term> <note>The "monad" refers to the single extra day added during a leap year.</note> added as an increase: how they are arranged and consecrated in the form of the holy Cross. Book 1, folio 18; and Book 2, folio 4.

X. The sacred power of the number seventy <gloss>the septuagenary</gloss>, how it may be adapted to the holy cross. Book 1, folio 20; and Book 2, folio 5.

XI. How the five books of Moses are renewed through the cross of Christ. Book 1, folio 22; and Book 2, folio 5.

XII. How the name of Adam <term>the first-formed</term> <note>original: "protoplasti," a Greek-derived term for the first human.</note> signified the second Adam <note>That is, Jesus Christ.</note> and His passion. Book 1, folio 24; and Book 2, folio 6.

XIII. The days of conception in the womb of the immaculate virgin are indicated by four Crosses, that is, 276 <note>Medieval theologians calculated the duration of Christ's gestation as exactly 276 days.</note> with the mystical significance of that number added and joined. Book 1, folio 26; and Book 2, folio 6.

XIIII. The years from the origin of the world to the time of the passion of Jesus Christ, mixed with Greek letters, the form of the Cross being observed, with that which is revealed in this sacrament annexed. Book 1, folio 28; and Book 2, folio 7.

XV. The four Evangelists with the Lamb portray the appearance of the Cross. Book 1, folio 30; and Book 2, folio 7.

XVI. The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, according to the enumeration of the Prophet Isaiah. Book 1, folio 32; and Book 2, folio 7.

XVII. The series of the eight beatitudes noted in the appearance of the Cross. Book 1, folio 34; and Book 2, folio 8.

XVIII. What mystery the number forty <gloss>the quadragenary</gloss> contains. Book 1, folio 36; and Book 2, folio 8.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book Two of Hrabanus Maurus’s "In Praise of the Holy Cross." Having concluded the table of contents on the preceding pages, the author now transitions from his complex grid-poems (the "verse" or "meter" version) to a prose commentary intended to explain their difficult symbolism.</meta>

# PREFACE TO THE SECOND BOOK.

a

<meta>catchword: light is,</meta>

It was a custom among the ancients to compose their own works in a twin style <note>original: "gemino stilo"; this refers to the "opus geminum" tradition where an author wrote two versions of the same work, one in poetry and one in prose.</note>, so that their talents might be both more pleasing and more useful to their readers. Thus, among both secular and ecclesiastical writers, many are found who have described one and the same matter in both poetry and prose. To say nothing of others: what else are Prosper and the venerable man Sedulius seen to have done? <note>Prosper of Aquitaine and Coelius Sedulius were influential 5th-century Christian poets. Sedulius famously wrote the "Paschale Carmen" in verse and the "Paschale Opus" in prose.</note> Do they not publish their double work in this twin character of style for this reason: so that the variety itself might remove boredom from the readers, and if by chance someone understands something less in one version, they may soon recognize it more fully explained in the other?

Following this example and for this reason, I, a most lowly little man, have taken care to turn into prose the work which I composed in a metrical style in praise of the holy cross. Because of the difficulty of the arrangement and the necessity of the figures <note>Hrabanus refers to his "carmina figurata" (shaped poems) from Book One, where letters are arranged in a grid to form images; this constraint made the poetry very difficult to read.</note>, the speech seems obscure and the meaning less clear in the verse; at least in the prose it may become more lucid. For I did not strive to use the same words in this work as I used in the verse, but rather to speak with the same meaning. The sharp and learned man Horace instructed the skilled translator in this same way in his *Art of Poetry*, saying: *As a faithful interpreter, you will not care to render word for word.* <note>original: "Nec verbum verbo curabis reddere fidus interpres." A famous maxim from Horace’s Ars Poetica (133–134) advocating for "sense-for-sense" rather than "word-for-word" translation.</note> For in a way I am an interpreter in this work—not of another language, but of another mode of speech—so that I may explain the truth of that same meaning.

Therefore, I ask the reader not to receive our labor with disdain; let them know that I do not wish to strive for superfluity, but for utility. I do not envy anyone, but rather, out of brotherly charity, I wish to contribute whatever I am able through divine grace for the benefit of my neighbor through my writing. May the goodness of Almighty God grant me that whatever good I hold in my mind, I may complete in my work; and may whoever receives our labor in a brotherly spirit, by God's bounty, become a sharer with us in the joys of eternity.

->*Here ends the Preface to the Second Book.*<-

### *Concerning the first figure, in which the image of Christ spreads his hands in the manner of a cross.*

<margin>I.</margin>
Behold, the Son of God and Lord of Lords shows here, with his hands outstretched, the form of the Restorer to be honored. And rightly the holy flock of the Church worships this one shepherd as just; and in that manner in which he allowed his limbs to be weary upon the cross, all peoples duly acknowledge the Redeemer; for Holy Scripture proclaims him to be the parent of all law. Recognizing this also, I, unworthy as I am, according to my small measure adore the Lord Jesus, the height of all summits; and I believe that he himself is the King of Kings. But Judea, which through the stimulus of envy is the inventor of evils, unjustly killed its king. <note>In the medieval theological context, "Judea" is often used to represent the opposition of the Jewish authorities to Christ, a common theme in the "In Praise of the Holy Cross."</note> Yet rising again with glory, he powerfully overthrew the weapons of the impious through the word of his Gospel, according to the promise of the Prophets.

But let us who believe in him rejoice in him; while whoever does not confess him to be the eternal Lord may doubt wickedly and perilously, because he is worshiped throughout the whole world as the author of all things, to whom it is fitting that all things be subject. For the upright and holy right hand of the highest Father snatched the offered prey from the depths of hell with his own blood; and having been placed thus upon the cross, he granted the heavenly kingdom to his faithful. He is of himself the beginning of all things; here is God with us; here is the origin and end of the universe: the true light, the image of the invisible God the Father; the Mouth of the Lord, the splendor of eternal light; who is consubstantial <note>term: consubstantial (original: "consubstantialis"); a theological term meaning "of the same substance" or "of the same essence," defining the relationship between Christ and God the Father.</note> with the Father, the sun of justice, the word of God, and from light [light]...

<note>The page ends mid-sentence; the final words "ex lumine lu-" are the beginning of "ex lumine lumen," meaning "light from light," a phrase from the Nicene Creed.</note>

BOOK TWO.

This is the cornerstone for those who believe, and a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense for the unbelieving: and he is the same as the door of life. Behold, Christ the Truth is clothed in a garment; I shall explain what this signifies mystically. Christ’s garment is also the divine Law <note>original: "lex diuina"</note>: which, under the humble covering of letters, in a certain way embraces the Author of all things who contains all. To him belongs the whole world, the heaven and the earth, and the sea and the entirety of creation: he who measures the heaven with a span and encloses the earth in his palm. Likewise, our nature, which he took up for our redemption, is like a garment of his divinity. For this nature both conceals the splendor of his majesty from human sight and encloses the rays of his brightness, hiding them from the eyes of the impious; yet he himself, through flashing miracles and the thundering Gospel, has become known as the true God. He was also sent to the people of God as the Angel of Great Counsel <term>Angelus magni consilii: A title for Christ from the Greek Old Testament (Isaiah 9:6), identifying Him as the messenger of God’s ultimate plan.</term> and with the highest devotion: namely, a teaching wisdom, and a peaceful guardian, the fountain of eternal life, the arm of the Lord, and the living bread who came down from heaven. Christ is indeed the rock, the rising morning star, and the true physician, the key of David, the way of life, and the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world; the serpent <note>A reference to the bronze serpent raised by Moses in the wilderness (Numbers 21), which healed those who looked upon it, serving as a "type" or foreshadowing of Christ on the Cross.</note> who, being exalted, brings life to those about to die, and the mediator between God and men, a worm and a man, leading captivity captive: the mountain of God. An eagle seeking the heights, an advocate for us. The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the good shepherd, and the goat bearing our sins: the foundation of faith, the innocent sheep, a priest after the order of Melchizedek, offering bread and wine: for he was sacrificed for us as a victim, both calf and ram. He who is the Son of the eternal Father is the same who was condemned to the punishment of the wood. He indeed was begotten from the Father’s womb before the morning star and before every creature: and in time, in a moment, he proceeded from his mother’s womb, and so that he might save the human race, Christ the eternal Creator came to the cross: who is God over all, blessed forever.

### *Concerning the second Figure, in which the holy Cross is depicted within a square.*

<margin>III.</margin>
O Holy Cross of Christ, which by the power granted to you excels above all things: you, in the supreme height of the heavens, rule the powerful ranks of the heavens: because the power and divinity of the King crucified upon you made you all-powerful and all-holy, especially since the evidence of his passion always exists within you. Therefore, we rightly call you Queen by Christ the King, because through you we first earned entrance to the heavenly kingdom; and while you merited the grace of his humanity and divinity by carrying him, you joined the Christ-worshippers <note>original: "Christicolas"</note> in sacred confession to the praise of the one almighty God. For you stir up manifold praises to God in the holy assemblies of the Angels: and by a similar reason, you render the devoted inhabitants of the lands ready to glorify God. Generally, the whole world, the air, the sea, and the fiery stars of the heavens sanctify you: and specifically, every single species of creature from the four parts of the world celebrates you with great devotion. The united confession of all also professes this: that, illustrated by eternal light, you demonstrate to us the joys of the heavenly kingdom, and may it grant the things demonstrated to those who seek them piously; since you do both by divine dispensation, so that with a believing heart and true confession we may confess God Christ, and through this faith we may merit to reach him. O cross of Christ, who are blessed through his longed-for victory: how bright and how great the Creator of all has rendered you by his love.

For He has enriched you with the gift of life-giving, and has raised you up for our health, so that the ancient enemy—who first cast out our forefather from paradise when he consented to him—might no longer harass his offspring, condemned to exile, with the mockery of his praise. <note>original: "irrisionis eulogio." The death-dealing Yew flies far from you; the aromatic Reed and the ever-green Pine subject themselves to your honor. The long-lasting Cedar too, which worms cannot pierce, the dripping Myrrh, and the Melilot <note>A type of sweet-smelling clover.</note> of most pleasant scent are amazed by your fragrance. Spikenard, and Cypress of good scent; Mastic also; the resin of the Lentisk, and Arabian Frankincense, the Gum of India, and Syrian Amomum, the Balsam of Judea, and the Bdellium of Phison <note>A fragrant resin mentioned in Genesis 2:12 as being found near the river Phison in Eden.</note>—all fearing your majesty, exalt you above themselves with their vows. Though you may be harsher in name than these, while you echo of torture, yet by the virtue of our redemption you surpass them; you who grant the faithful to receive the fruits of good works before the judgment seat of Christ. O sacred Cross, which, having burst the enclosures of hell, had snatched away the people of the saints and placed them in heaven.

### Concerning the form of the Third Figure, in which the nine orders of Angels are depicted.

<margin>A III</margin>

O You holy salvation, and joyful passion of Christ, hail! Venerable Cross of God, you who are the wisdom, light, and teacher of the whole world: you who are the true praise, the friend of virtue, and clear philosophy among those who dwell in heaven and those born of earth, you thrive without ceasing. You are already among the armies of Angels, who remain in the brightness of eternal light, and among men, for whom you have stood as salvation and beautiful renewal after long-standing infirmity and the ancient age of sins. The whole world blesses you; the hosts of heaven praise you together. Through you, in the name of Jesus (who bows all the scepters of the world and the empires of kings alike), every knee is bent, whether by will or by force—namely, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. 

But Michael, the leader and prince of God’s people, records in his confession that you rule all the stars of the heavens by your virtue and cover them by your power, because you are the altar of God, upon which was sacrificed the Lamb who took away the sins of the world. In this shield of benevolence he himself continually exults; trusting in this sword of confession, he enters into war against the horrid dragon and the ancient serpent: and triumphing over the enemy, he rejoices with thousands of holy ranks, seeking this for himself as a place of reward, that he may perpetually sing your praise before the judgment seat of the Lord. 

Therefore, this act of forming letters, and this manner of positioning the nine orders <note>Refers to the nine choirs of angels: Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones, Dominions, Virtues, Powers, Principalities, Archangels, and Angels.</note>, and also the lot itself by which the sacred ranks of Angels are first ordered to praise the Redeemer, rightly establishes this cross thus suspended as the altar of our High Priest and Redeemer: so that the true life itself, witnessing within itself, may show the venerable senate of powers offering praise, as is fitting; so that upon the cross, which is our true salvation, good and healthy writings may appear. 

And therefore Christ, humbling himself, descended from the citadel of the heavens, so that he might powerfully lead us to himself, the solid foundation of faith and the increase of all good things. He taught by words, and left behind examples for us by his deeds: and so finally redeeming us on the holy Cross, he completed his works. This you, Gabriel, Archangel of the Most High and betrother of the heavenly marriage, joyfully revealed to the Virgin with clear speech, when you [recounted] the power of Christ’s kingdom and the work of his salvation in a brilliant sermon...

...as you had pronounced with your voice. And what of you, O Raphael, the <term>Medicine of God</term>? <note>The name Raphael in Hebrew means "God heals."</note> Did you not, in that mystical work by which you opened the eyes of Tobit, anointing them with fish-gall, signify the power of the holy Cross? For through the bitterness of Christ’s death, the darkness of sins was removed, and eternal light was restored to the human race. Therefore, we must believe that the deeds of the Angels recorded in the Old Testament signify the coming and glory of our Redeemer; just as the New Testament describes how, at the very beginning of his birth, they sang "Glory in the highest" to God with a great joyous dance, and proclaimed peace to men. Wherefore, we also humbly beseech you, O illustrious armies of Angels: that you may unceasingly give worthy thanks to our Savior and bless his holy name forever. For he has delivered us from perpetual death through the Cross, and has filled your number in the celestial citadel with holy souls (so that it might not remain diminished on account of the lost angels). <note>Medieval theologians often taught that God created humanity to replace the "fallen angels" who followed Lucifer, ensuring the heavenly court remained at its intended full capacity.</note>

### Concerning the form of the fourth figure, where the Cherubim and Seraphim are depicted next to the Cross.

<margin>IIII.</margin>

But you, heavenly hosts of Cherubim and Seraphim, now praise from heaven the name of your King, Jesus Christ. For the fire of your love and wisdom burns so brightly if it shines with pure breath in the praise of the Redeemer. For that praise is true and divine by which our <term>Pasch</term> <note>original: "Pascha." Referring to the Passover/Easter mystery of Christ's sacrifice.</note>—which is the passion and resurrection of our Redeemer—is truly proclaimed to be our life. Certainly, the true fruit of light is Christ, whom you celebrate with shared praise as the Lord God of <term>Sabaoth</term> <note>original: "Sabaoth." A Hebrew title for God meaning "of Hosts" or "of Armies."</note> together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. He, in the hour of his passion, conquered the sorrow of death, and now reigning everywhere, exults in the joy of the resurrection. O blessed Seraphim, tell us what the heat of your love is; and show us if your heavenly conditions are manifested in this celebration—if you signify this great and mighty praise, reveal the heavenly Victor. 

Here, I confidently answer on your behalf for myself and my people. For there is one thing they show us: they affirm by the position of their wings that the altar of the holy Cross, and the sacred beauty of the <term>Victim</term> <note>original: "hostiae." Refers to Christ as the sacrificial offering.</note> sacrificed upon it, was long ago foretold to us in figures. They also voice Christ's vows of praise—what the power of our redemption is, and the goodness of the rewards which King Christ decreed to grant us. For when he suffered on this altar according to his purpose, he consumed the iniquities and the sins of our crimes in the flame of his passion. Overcoming all opposing powers at the moment of his death, he conquered them; and casting out the prince of this world, he broke through his shattered enclosures. He wiped away the old age of our sins, and as the kind Lord and King of Virtues, he restored to us the very realms of paradise in which the first man had been created and placed. The mouths of all the faithful prove this, and the virtues and miracles that God performs in this world through his saints testify that God gave the aid of his commandments to the human race—which was justly condemned to the prison and darkness of this world—for the sake of escaping perpetual death. Truly, he is our Creator and King, who was fixed for us upon the high stake of the Cross. It is more fitting for this to be called an imperial throne than a slave’s torture; for our Emperor, King Christ, won for himself a kingdom on it, and power in heaven and on earth. He overcame his enemies and reconciled the world to God. This is the banner of the Christian people; this is the sword <note>original: "framea." A word used in the Latin Bible for a sword or spear.</note> with which we wage war against the enemy; this is the sign of our victory. With this, we trample our enemies.

He argues that the Cross is not a tool of execution but an imperial throne and a victorious banner that restores humanity to Paradise.</summary>

## BOOK TWO

<note>original: "hac arma..." The text continues from the previous page: "...by this [the Cross] we break the weapons of iniquity..."</note> with this we break the weapons of iniquity, through this we are lifted to the crown and receive the rewards of virtue. Therefore, you fire of greed, forever an exile and stranger to good, know what slaughter is prepared for you in the death of Christ. Therefore those Cherubim, who in the construction of the tabernacle and temple <note>Refers to the golden figures of angels placed over the Ark of the Covenant in the Old Testament temple.</note> stood next to the altar behind the Altar of Incense <note>original: "altare Thymiamatis"</note>, showed this holy altar by the extension of their wings and by the whole position of their placement, this banner of the Cross; which, anointed with mystical oil, prefigured the triumph of Christ and the palm of his struggle. And so these living beings <note>original: "animalia," referring to the four living creatures of Ezekiel’s vision, often identified with the highest orders of angels.</note>, that is, the Cherubim, made joyful by their spread wings, bring forward the deeds of Christ: and they hand down with manifest signs that those deeds are nourishing and exalted.

<margin>VII</margin>
The Seraphim themselves also open their mouths for this purpose: so that when they proclaim heaven and earth to be full of the glory of God, the time is now near when carnal luxury shall depart from here, and vices shall recede. Finally, let all things say, together with these living beings by the duty of their wings, they especially signify that the Savior’s arms are stretched out on the Cross: and in these, all those are now drawn and lifted up by mercy, whom

<margin>IV</margin>
he himself afterwards, in the universal judgment, repaying things worthy of their merits, will place in a blessed seat: then openly proving them through examination, whom he already previously approved by loving them, as they were known to him and increased by good works. Therefore, the prophecies of the righteous seers concerning the Lord's passion do not disagree in any way: nor do the signs of those living beings deceive.

### Concerning the form of the fifth figure, where four squares stand around the Cross.

<margin>V</margin>
I beseech you now, holy Cross of God, that by your power you may bless my weak heart: so that I may be able to sing of the trophy of the eternal King upon you with worthy praises: how you join together heavenly and earthly things alike in one treaty, confirm the pact, and dissolve the bonds of death. O you holy assembly of the Apostles, and laureled order of martyrs: by right you have laid the foundations of the house of Christ, whom he himself carries in a most beautiful citadel. Indeed, by your voice and examples you have acquired a holy people for God, and you have rightly placed the holy and saving Cross of Christ in the first foundation of preaching: because the power of the Lord crucified upon it has properly strengthened the entire structure of the Lord’s Church to carry it. Truly also the Cross itself has dedicated the human race to life, and stands as a firm pillar: desiring to show that through it an eternal house rises, to be placed in the heavenly kingdom: namely, the court of the righteous king and the bridegroom of the Church. By this, O Lord Christ, you have quickly erected a new trophy in the world, by right of lordship, by the blood of redemption, and by the way of guidance: so that the race of Christ-worshippers may keep the covenant of justice, spurn the devil as rightly damned, and overcome the enemy man through piety: because you are the promoter of praise for him, and the fear of preservation for each good work, as well as the palm of victory, and the crown of reward. O glorious Cross of the Lord, precious foundation of Christ's court: you are more beautiful than the flowery appearance of all seeds: you are taller than the Cedars of Lebanon: you are more precious than white Parian stone <note>A fine-grained semi-translucent pure white marble from the Greek island of Paros, highly prized by ancient sculptors.</note>: you who, being square, join the rocks, the living stones in the firm foundation of faith. Also the assembly of Patriarchs and the most ancient rite rightly lay the first foundations at the beginning of the entire building: who first, by sound doctrine, joined the hearts of those devotedly obeying them to the house of God reigning over all things, through faith.
