### *Concerning the Twenty-Fifth Figure, where "Alleluia" and "Amen" are placed.*

<margin>25</margin>
O praise, pious and perpetual, of the holy Cross, which the assembly of created beings <note>original: "factorum coetus," the gathering of those made by God, i.e., the angels</note> frequents in heaven: assist those born of earth, so they may be able to bring forth something decent and worthy concerning you, and preach your glory with a full mouth. For I, as much as I was able, have sung of you, holy Cross, in rhythmic meter, greatly desiring to satisfy you in this; but you, exceeding in dignity the measure of our strength, have also surpassed the bounty of our gifts. Nor is it a wonder, since you surpass all things both heavenly and earthly at once, nor is anyone sufficiently able to do justice to your majesty or adapt words worthy of your honor. Therefore, I have tried to take certain words from heavenly odes to praise you, which would also suit your appearance and figure: I have arranged these same words on the page of verses, not continuously but scattered, and I have inserted Angelic songs: namely, placing **Amen** in the middle of the Cross and filling its corners <note>original: "cornua," literally "horns," referring to the four extremities of the Cross</note> with **Alleluia**, so that in this way I might mark this sacred image with a heavenly song and suggest a mystery through it. For all the faithful and just servants of God triumph over the scepters of the world from this point, and they despise the beauty of its gifts, publicly preaching this: that the hope of eternal things—the fire of faith resonating through the mouths of the chosen—prepares heavenly rewards for its companions and puts to flight the ancient enemy <note>the devil</note>, who first brought the cruelest death to the human race and had dragged the whole lineage from our <term>first-formed parents</term> <note>original: "protoplastis parentibus," referring to Adam and Eve</note> down to the places of hell until the coming of Christ. But let us, whom the desire for eternal things lifts in spirit to the heavens, come before the face of the Lord in confession, and duly shouting for joy in psalms, let us strive to find grace in His sight: exulting in His praises in such a way as the order of justice requires and as the ranks of saints in heaven celebrate perpetually together. This will then be done rightly, if we strive to fulfill the commands of the <term>Thunderer</term> <note>original: "tonantis," a classical poetic epithet for God</note>, and not only with the tongue, but also in thought and...

HEADER: BOOK TWO.

c ij

...striving to speak most grateful praises in both state and work. For a profession of faith brought forth only by the mouth, without the harmony of mind and deed, is not sufficient for salvation: because such praise is not pleasing to God, which, though it promises great things to itself, nevertheless deserves little: for it is written, <note>original: "non est pulchra laudatio in ore peccatoris"</note> *praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.* I therefore pray to you, heavenly hosts of angels and spirits, and the souls of the just, who truly exult in the sight of the glory of the divine majesty: just as you sing *Alleluia* without ceasing and a perpetual *Amen* to Christ the Lord forever, so also strive to help our lot with your prayers, so that we may at last deserve to receive through the grace of Christ that true blessedness which you already possess perfectly.

### Concerning the Twenty-Sixth Figure, in which the prophetic sentences are denoted.

<margin>XXVI.</margin>
Therefore, O holy Cross of Christ, the oracles of the prophets honor you well, their deeds proclaim you, and their virtues exalt you, because whatever that most sacred people, inspired by the Divine Spirit, brought forth by prophesying about the coming of Christ, revealed the glory of your power within it: since the Savior Himself appeared in the world for no other reason than to save the human race through you. Let us see, therefore, what the prophet and psalmist David said, if by chance he spoke anything signifying you. For he said: <note>original: "Foderunt manus meas & pedes meos, dinumerauerunt omnia offa mea"</note> *They pierced my hands and my feet, they numbered all my bones.* What else is it to pierce the hands and feet, and to number all the bones, if not to fasten the members of Christ stretched out upon you with nails? Likewise David says: *They gave me gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.* This certainly signifies what the Evangelist explained concerning Christ, saying: *Afterwards,* he says, *Jesus, knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled, says: I thirst. Now a vessel was set there full of vinegar. And they, putting a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop, offered it to his mouth.* And elsewhere it is written: *They gave him wine to drink mixed with gall.* From here also the prophet Isaiah, prophesying, says: *A child is born to us and a son is given to us, and the government is placed upon his shoulder,* and so forth. And likewise he says from the person of Christ: *I gave my body to those who strike me, and my cheeks to those who pluck them.* And again: *I turned not away my face from those who rebuked and spat upon me.* And *the Lord shall lift up a sign among the nations, and shall gather together the fugitives of Israel,* and so forth. In all these sentences, therefore, he expressed both your erection and the truth of Christ’s passion and the cruelty of the Jews. Jeremiah indeed describes Christ as an innocent lamb led without a voice to be sacrificed, and says that the unfaithful would <note>original: "lignumque in panem eius missuros"</note> *put wood into his bread*: which signifies that the Bread of Life was to be lifted up upon you, and would taste the death of the flesh. Ezekiel, moreover, asserted that the letter **T** <note>the letter Tau, which in ancient scripts resembled a cross</note>, mimicking your image, was placed upon the foreheads of the men who groaned and grieved, for their liberation from the slaughter of the destroyer. Thus you also, holy Cross, were shown to the holy prophets not as a weakness or ignobility, but as firm virtue, chief praise, and the most faithful ship or harbor in relieving the shipwreck of the whole world. For Daniel foretold that Christ the Lord would be killed by the faithless, and thus the guilt of sin would be ended. Hosea describes the slaying of death and the salvation of the people: and Joel foretold the darkness of the stars that would occur at the death of Christ. Amos predicted that the festivals of the iniquitous would be turned into mourning, and all their songs into lamentation.

### Concerning the Twenty-Seventh Figure, in which the sentences of the Apostles are placed.

<margin>XXVII.</margin>
The letter of the New Testament testifies no less to your rights, O holy Cross, than the scripture of the old law, because the gifts of divine grace which that law promised for the future, this one teaches have been completed through the incarnation of the Savior. From this it is most clear that Christ Jesus is the Lord of both laws, because with his own mouth he had opened a double abyss to the world: namely, explaining the Law and establishing the Gospel. He refreshed the ancients with the hope of holy desires, and he satisfied those who came after with the revelation of the things themselves—he who is good, true, and just to all. From this it happens that the Apostolic company brought forth a most joyful discourse concerning your most holy construction and showed your magnificent work with a most wholesome report. 

For **Peter**, who is first in the order of the Apostles, strongly took an example of persuasion from you, saying thus: <note>original: "Christus pro nobis passus est fratres, vobis relinquens exemplum, ut sequamini vestigia eius"</note> *Christ suffered for us, brothers, leaving you an example, so that you should follow his footsteps.* And likewise, he says: <note>original: "Peccata nostra ipse pertulit in corpore suo super lignum"</note> *He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, dead to sins, we might live to justice, by whose stripes you were healed.* From this also I believe that he, who laid down his life for the wicked and ungrateful, inclines the ears of his mercy to the prayers of those devoted and faithful to him. 

Therefore, I, a wretched man, if his majesty deigns to receive any small gift of human art, desire to offer this poem to him with my greatest effort, because I trust in his goodness, that the gifts of pious devotion are not displeasing to him if we persevere in the true confession of his name. But the blessed Apostle **James** exhorts us from here, showing us an example of Christ’s patience: <note>original: "Exemplum accipite fratres laboris & patientiæ"</note> *Take, brothers, an example of labor and patience, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Behold, we call blessed those who endured; you have heard of the suffering of Job, and you have seen the end of the Lord.* 

From here also the beloved of the Lord, **John**, provokes us to mutual love, bringing Christ into the midst: so that just as he laid down his life for us, we also should lay down our lives for our brothers. **Jude** also, the servant of Christ and brother of James, using the example of Joshua <note>The Latin "Hiesu" refers here to Joshua, Moses' successor, again as a type of Jesus</note>, the successor of Moses, demonstrated that Jesus Chri-

HEADER: BOOK TWO, I

...the Author of life led us out through the Cross from a spiritual Egypt—that is, from the power of darkness—and destroyed the unbelieving. Paul, therefore, spoke not just a little but magnificently of you, saying to his listeners: "For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified" <note>original: "Non enim iudico me inter vos aliquid scire nisi Christum Hiesum, & hunc crucifixum" — 1 Corinthians 2:2</note>. And he forbade himself to boast except in the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to him, and he to the world; he affirms that Christ, because of his death on the Cross, received power in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. Behold, O holy Cross of Christ, how harmoniously the Apostolic order brings forth your praises alongside the ancient prophets, so that they disagree in nothing; for what the prophets sang would happen in the future, the Apostles affirm is completed in you. For you, as the sign of true harmony, bring to perfection all things—celestial and terrestrial, old and new—at once.

### Concerning the Twenty-eighth Figure, where the maker himself adores the holy Cross.

<margin>XXVIII</margin>
Omnipotent majesty, exalted power, creator of heavenly beings and shaper of earthly ones, Lord God of <term>Sabaoth</term> <note>Sabaoth: a Hebrew title meaning "of hosts" or "of armies," emphasizing God's supreme authority over all creation</note>, who are the true founder and redeemer of men: you are our praise, you are our strength and glory with true salvation; you are the King of kings, the Teacher of the ignorant, the Ruler of the faithful and the Master of believers; you are the highest Prince of shepherds, the merciful protector of your sheep. You, O holy Savior, are the author of all good, the good leader, the right way, the true light and perpetual life, the bright reward, and the door of eternal salvation. From you proceeds all sense, voice, word, and the fruit of every virtue. Toward you, therefore, I have directed my speech at the beginning of this work, and whatever I have added in the following parts, I have desired to reach your praise. My heart lifts itself to you, the whole intention of my mind cries out to you; whatever the tongue produces anywhere in a confession of right faith, or the hand in a work of good service with a devoted and pious mind, all of it belongs to your praise. For all things—those in the depths and those in the heights—glorify and bless you. And I also, the smallest part of your creation, adore you as the true Lord, a suppliant and joyful, and greeting your Cross submissively and humbly, I say: O <term>vital wood</term> <note>original: "lignum vitale" — a reference to the Cross as the new Tree of Life</note> and health-bringing altar, I adore you, praying for the hope of eternal life, so that through you, the most holy structure, I may exist as a sacrifice pleasing to God. This is my desire, this the strong fervor of my love; this the whole intention of my mind and the speech of my tongue pray for; this is the hunger of my heart and the thirst of my soul: that through the grace of your passion you may receive me, your servant, as an offering to you, and that your crucifixion may consume everything in me that is contrary to you. May it temper carnal heat, extinguish anger, restrain the tongue from wicked and vain speech, and place words of piety in my mouth; may it pacify every disturbance of the mind and lead me to an honorable life. Therefore, Lord Jesus, when you come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire, and the flame has consumed your adversaries—all those who hated your name—amidst the final trumpet and the powerful storm, when according to your Gospel the sign of the Son of Man appears in heaven and all the tribes of the earth mourn for themselves, looking upon him whom they pierced: I beseech you, that then the holy Cross may snatch me from the avenging flames, and defend its own poet from the wrath of the Lamb. To him I sing this present song, and I pray that until the end of my life it may be pleasing and honorable to him...

<header>BOOK TWO.</header>

...may I always sing, I Rabanus, the least of all your servants and a sinner, with hymns, praises, heart, mouth, hand, and every gesture of my body, always remembering with how much goodness you, our creator, made us, and with how much piety you redeemed us when you freed us from the prison of the underworld <note>original: "inferni carcere"</note> and the flame of Gehenna. And now, good Savior, I pray that you give me that rest which you promised to give your faithful in the height of the heavens <note>original: "arce polorum" — literally "the citadel of the poles," a poetic way of saying the highest point of the sky or heaven</note>: where your people truly keep the Sabbath, enjoying a perennial Sabbath-rest. Meanwhile, as long as I am in this little body, guide me in the right path of the Catholic faith: sustain me with firm hope, and refresh me with your love, so that you yourself may be my refreshment on the way, you whom I desire to have as my rest in my true homeland. For without any doubt, I believe all your promises to be most true, I fear your most just judgments, and I look forward to your sweetest gifts. Grant that, rejoicing in you, I may remain with you in eternal joy. O nourishing Cross of God, up to this point, as much as I was able, I have sung your praise: but because you seek a perpetual triumph, which you do not find fully and perfectly among these mortals, take yourself to the celestial ranks of the Angels, and there perpetual praise shall sound for you through all ages.

->THE END OF BOOK TWO.<-

## CONCLUSION.

You have now, sweetest reader, Rabanus in his wonderful poem *In Praise of the Holy Cross*, upon which our salvation hung, and which we use against foul enemies at every moment. Read these verses, setting aside those that are base, obscene, and immodest. Accustom yourself from now on to read Christian poets, who can supply you with Latinity, elegance, <term>figures of speech</term> <note>original: "tropos"</note>, good morals, and the measurements of syllables no less than the pagans. Let Rabanus now be taken into your hands instead of Lucretius; Sedulius instead of Virgil; Alcimus instead of Ovid; Lactantius instead of Propertius; Arator instead of Statius; Prosper instead of Catullus; Juvencus instead of Tibullus; Prudentius instead of Horace; the Epigrams of Engelhard Scintilla and Hermannus Buschius instead of Martial; Walter instead of Lucan; and Baptista Mantuanus instead of Juvenal. In this way, Christian youths will be instructed in a Christian manner by Christian teachers from Christian poets, to the honor of Christ. 

Our Augustine confesses that he learned many useful words in the vain sentiments of the pagans, which can also be learned in matters that are not vain, and that this is the safe path in which children should walk. For those words are not learned more conveniently through such filthiness; rather, that filthiness is committed more confidently because of those words. Add to this that Ovid himself, the author of most shameful verses, driven by the impulse of natural conscience, agrees with us in these verses:

> *I will speak unwillingly: do not touch the tender poets,*
> *I, though impious myself, remove my own gifts.*
> *Flee Callimachus: he is no enemy to love,*
> *And you also, poet of Cos <note>Refers to Philitas of Cos</note>, do harm alongside Callimachus.*
> *Certainly Sappho made me more indulgent toward my mistress,*
> *Nor did the Teian muse <note>Anacreon</note> give me rigid morals.*
> *Who could have read the songs of Tibullus in safety?*
> *Or yours, [Propertius], whose work was Cynthia alone?*
> *Who could depart sternly after reading Gallus?*
> *And my own songs sound with some such thing.*

<meta>catchword: In quo. This page concludes the editor's preface and includes the self-written epitaph of Rabanus Maurus. The editor, likely Jakob Wimpfeling, is contrasting Rabanus's Christian virtue with the "obscene" classical poets favored by the Italian Renaissance.</meta>

If Ovid <note>original: "Naso" — referring to the Roman poet Publius Ovidius Naso, famous for his erotic poetry</note>, that pagan and obscene man, urged such things, then Italian teachers should henceforth blush to interpret, annotate, and read those shameless poets to impressionable young men <note>original: "mollibus ephæbis"</note>. For what profit is there in adding fire to fire? To stir the blood, to increase madness, to instill evil thoughts, to press in the stings of love, to incite the imagination, to harm the reason, to pull one away from shame, modesty, and every virtue, to turn one from more useful study, to set one on fire for beastly pleasure, to render a tender age perpetually corrupted, to provoke the movements of the flesh and the lust that comes of its own accord, to infect adolescents, to hand poison to boys—and what they otherwise consider a small vice, to persuade them through the fame of the authors that hereafter it is no vice at all. "Woe to the world because of scandals," says the Highest Truth <note>original: "summa veritas" — a reference to Christ in Matthew 18:7</note>, and "it is a horrific thing to fall into His hands." Farewell, most noble reader. From the suburbs of the noble city of Strasbourg <note>original: "vrbis Argentinæ"</note>, on the 11th of July, 1502.

Farewell, happy Germany, inventor of the art <note>The printing press, which had been developed in Mainz only about 50 years prior to this publication</note> by which one man in one day can print as much as many could barely write in a whole year. Happy, too, is the inventor of such a marvelous and astounding poem, which both the Italians and the French have greatly celebrated in their histories.

And you also, reader, farewell—you who do not disdain to devote your waking hours to many mocking poets endowed with light, cold, and futile rhythms, who are under manifest condemnation. May you allow this work to nest and dwell with you. We wish it to be sought and obtained, for it is well known that it was created with incomparable mastery, skillful and most wise in the knowledge of healthy things. If you weigh the very force of the meanings and the power of the words through successive and secondary readings (unless you have been ill-taught by unfairness and made more irritable by envy), you will find them most sufficient.

Among the inscriptions <note>original: "Epigrammata"</note> of the bishops of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinorum"</note> on Mount Saint Alban, it is said that the following was carved and sculpted for our Rabanus <note>original: "Mauri quoq; noſtri"</note>. Lest it should be lost to antiquity, with the tips of the letters being illegible or deleted and worn away by some other filth, we present to your eyes, reader, as much as has reached us. If you wish to consult a cleaner and more beautiful version, so that not even a single flaw appears, we pray that you yourself compare it with the original characters and strive for it, so that you do not decide that this too must be forgiven as our own lack of skill. Once and again, farewell.

> *The holy Rule was the standard of my life.*
> *But although I might have held to this incautiously and not always firmly,*
> *Nevertheless, my cell was a pleasing dwelling for me.*
> *But when many years of time had already passed,*
> *Men gathered to change the destiny of the place:*
> *They drew me, weak, from my home, and brought me to the King,*
> *Demanding that I perform the office of a Bishop.*

*And true rest always in the heights of heaven <note>original: "arce poli" — literally "the citadel of the pole," a poetic term for the highest heaven</note>.*

->They say he held his office <note>original: "sedisse," meaning "to have sat" in the bishop's chair</note> for 9 years and died in the year 856. He was once buried at Mainz <note>original: "Moguntiæ"</note> on the hill of Saint Alban, but has now been moved and rests in Fulda <note>A major monastery and center of learning founded by Saint Boniface</note>.<-

### FROM THE PRINTER TO THE READER: AND CONCERNING THE AUTHOR OF THE EPIGRAM.

->You yourself know the Mastership <note>Referring to the skill of the work or the status of the author as a Master</note> well enough:<-
->But if you wish to know the homeland and name of the craftsman?<-
->My birthplace is Baden; my seat is Pforzheim <note>original: "Phorcys"</note>:<-
->And I am called Thomas Anshelm, the bookseller <term>Bibliopola</term> <note>From the Greek 'bibliopolos,' meaning a bookseller, though in this era it often referred to the printer-publisher</note>.<-

->PFORZHEIM. IN THE HOUSE OF THOMAS ANSHELM,<-
->In the month of March, 1503. Under the illustrious prince Christopher of Baden.<-

---

->REPRINTED AT AUGSBURG <note>original: "Augustæ Vindelicorum" — the Roman name for the city of Augsburg</note>,<-
->IN THE YEAR 1605.<-
